#6281. In 1991, NASA sent 2,478 jellyfish into space, and some born in orbit came back pulsing abnormally

In 1991, NASA sent moon jellyfish into space aboard Columbia. Those formed in orbit showed abnormal pulsing after returning to Earth's gravity.

In June 1991, the space shuttle Columbia carried thousands of tiny moon jellyfish, Aurelia aurita, into orbit. NASA’s life sciences records list 2,478 of them on the flight.

Some of the young jellyfish formed in orbit. Back on Earth, 18.3 percent of them pulsed abnormally, compared with 2.9 percent of those that developed on the ground.

Dorothy Spangenberg of Eastern Virginia Medical School in Norfolk led the experiment. Her goal was to learn whether the animals’ gravity sensors could form normally without gravity.

Columbia launched on June 5, 1991, on the STS-40 mission and landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California on June 14. The flight, commanded by Bryan O’Connor with a crew of seven, lasted nine days, two hours and 14 minutes.

It carried Spacelab Life Sciences 1 (SLS-1), the first Spacelab mission dedicated solely to life sciences.

Of its 18 investigations, ten involved humans, seven involved rodents and one used jellyfish. Six body systems were studied in all, from the heart and lungs to the blood, bones and muscles.

The neurovestibular system, which helps people sense gravity and balance, was one of them.

Both polyps and young jellyfish flew. Polyps are a stalk-like stage that lives attached to a surface, and they can metamorphose into tiny, free-swimming ephyrae.

Ephyrae on the mission measured about 0.04 to 0.08 inch (1 to 2 millimeters) across, according to a 1997 NASA report on jellyfish thyroxine by Spangenberg.

Before the flight, about 25,000 polyps were mixed together and divided into flight and ground control groups. A NASA educational guide to the experiment says 60,000 jellyfish were grown for the mission.

The team triggered metamorphosis with iodine or the hormone thyroxine at 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius). Some groups were treated 48 or 24 hours before launch, and others eight hours after liftoff.

Ephyrae formed in orbit as well as on the ground, so the jellyfish apparently could still make the hormone needed for metamorphosis in space. Even two groups of polyps that received no trigger formed ephyrae there.

Some ephyrae were preserved on the eighth day of the mission. Others were preserved after landing for study under light microscopes and scanning and transmission electron microscopes.

Under the microscope, the flight ephyrae looked very similar to those raised on Earth. Counts of their arms showed no significant differences.

Like adult moon jellyfish, ephyrae swim by pulsing, rhythmically contracting their bodies. That movement is where the space-grown animals stood out.

The abnormal pulsing suggested problems in the development of the gravity receptors or the neuromuscular system, or in how the two worked together.

The 1997 report raised another possibility. The animals may have been unable to readjust to Earth’s gravity after landing.

Ephyrae in microgravity also showed more looping and circling behavior than ephyrae on Earth, Spangenberg and colleagues reported in a 1996 study of touch-plate formation. That paper drew on SLS-1 and a later flight.

Sensory hair cells in ephyrae that developed in microgravity also had fewer lipid droplets near their bases than those of ground controls.

Moon jellyfish sense gravity with organs called rhopalia, found around the edge of the bell. Each holds a statocyst filled with tiny crystals called statoliths.

Space-grown ephyrae formed rhopalia that looked much like those of ground controls. They had statocysts with statoliths, light-sensing ocelli, ciliated mechanoreceptor cells and immature touch-plates, according to a 1994 study of graviceptor development.

The number of rhopalia per arm did not differ significantly between the groups. Ephyrae induced to form in space with iodine even made more statoliths per rhopalium than one set of controls.

But statolith loss from the rhopalia was significantly higher in ephyrae kept in space in artificial seawater, compared with their controls on the ground.

Normal pulsing depends on normal development and function of the rhopalia.

Humans have similar calcium-containing crystals, called otoconia, in the inner ear. They help people keep their balance.

When Columbia flew, the effect of microgravity on human otoconia had not been studied, the NASA guide noted.

Many developing jellyfish structures resemble human ones but are less complicated. That could help predict what happens to the embryos of more complex animals during spaceflight.

Jellyfish flew again on the later IML-2 mission. Spangenberg suspected that a buildup of the jellyfish version of thyroxine might be linked to the statolith loss.

On Earth, thyroxine given to the animals increases statolith demineralization. A planned third experiment would have measured the jellyfish hormone in space-grown ephyrae, but NASA deselected it in August 1997.

The study was published in the journal Advances in Space Research.

#6280. The 6 Best Electric Snow Shovels for Quickly Clearing Sidewalks and Driveways

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

These models deliver fast cleanup with minimal effort when there isn't enough accumulation to take out the snowblower. Here are our recommendations.

Winter will be here before you know it. Easily one of the most laborious and hated chores of that season is shoveling the snow. Not only that, it can be dangerous. Beyond the strain it puts on your back, the American Heart Association says it can increase the risk of a cardiac event for those with heart issues, and the cold weather can hide symptoms that otherwise would give you pause. That’s why the best electric snow shovels not only make the task easier, but safer, too, for those at risk.

Of course, you should not mistake these for full-blown snowblowers. Because of their compact size and throwing range, electric snow shovels are best used for small homes with shorter walkways and fewer steps. Like their larger counterparts, they use augers to scoop up snow (no more than 6 to 8 inches, ideally) and launch it up to 25 feet through the air so you don’t have to bend or lift as you dig out after a storm.

They also work well as supplemental tools for clearing out outdoor stairs, walkways, patios, decks, and anywhere else a snowblower may not be able to reach. If that sounds like it could help you out of a blizzard-induced jam this winter, we can steer you toward the best electric snow shovels that can make the chore as painless as possible.

Toro Power Shovel 60-Volt 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

Ego Power+ EGO POWER+ 12-Inch Electric Snow Shovel

We leaned on our personal experience with snow removal machines and conducted extensive research to inform our selections. Specifically, we looked at each machine’s clearing area, weight, battery life, and throwing distance. Because snow removal needs vary from property to property, we included larger models that can clear up to 6 inches of snow from two- to four-car driveways, along with lighter electric snow shovels that are easy to lift and maneuver in smaller areas, such as walkways and patios.

Though we still include one corded model as our best budget pick, we primarily focus on cordless models because for most people these days, the convenience of battery power beats having to drag a cord around on a cold day.

Most electric snow shovels max out with a fairly narrow clearing width and low clearing depth, potentially forcing you to do multiple passes to clear a proper path. This Earthwise model is an exception.

With a broad clearing width of 16 inches and a depth of 8 inches, it’s capable of clearing paths through deeper snow. And since it launches snow up to 32 feet away, you can use this machine to clear small driveways along with your walkways, deck, and patio.

On the other hand, this electric snow shovel is quite heavy. It has wheels, though, which make it easier to push and maneuver. It’s a tradeoff, but one that pays off if you live in an area that routinely gets 6 to 8 inches of snow in a night.

You may notice that our best overall is a bit cheaper than our best value pick. This is because we felt the wide clearing width and the fact that it has wheels to support your efforts made this a solid choice for many people.

Though higher in price than some of the other models on our list, there’s a lot that you get for the price, namely power and run time. With a larger battery than most, this electric shovel from Greenworks runs longer on a single battery than any other cordless electric snow shovel out there.

It packs a good amount of power with a large 80-volt 4.0-amp-hour battery powering a brushless motor; you’ll get about 45 minutes of run time on a single charge. This snow shovel clears a 12-inch path through up to 6 inches of snow, then blows it 25 feet away, making it ideal for uncovering a large area after a light snowfall.

Just remember that with great power and runtime comes great weight. With the battery loaded, this machine weighs more than 19 pounds, so moving it around for 45 minutes can turn into a real workout.

If you want the most clearing power possible from an electric snow shovel, Earthwise is your brand. This corded model can carve a 16-inch-wide path through snow up to 8 inches high, which is significantly more than what you can expect from other brands. It’s also significantly more powerful, moving up to 430 pounds of snow per minute.

For reference, most of our other picks move around 300 pounds per minute. As a result, it can handle deeper, slushier snow than most electric snow shovels. It also has a longer throwing distance than most corded or cordless electric snow shovels out there.

At 16 pounds, it’s pretty heavy, but like other heavy models, it has a pair of wheels so you can push it most of the time. In short, it offers the best snow removal capability of any machine this side of a snowblower.

Ryobi makes several types of cordless electric snow shovels, but this model is a head attachment for its Expand-It 40-Volt String Trimmer that you can swap in when the snow starts falling. The advantage here is that you aren’t limited to just one tool; you can swap in a variety of attachments to run on the same primary unit and battery. This makes a lot of sense if it only snows a couple of times where you live, and you only need a snow thrower infrequently.

During our testing, we were impressed with this tool’s performance. In mere minutes, we were able to clear a wide path through 8 inches of snow (more than the max height of 6 inches this model is rated for) on a patio outside our office. It was not fresh snow, either; it was densely packed after sitting for several days. There were times when the shovel head froze up while trying to push through too much at once, but this was quickly rectified by pulling back and pushing through again. The snow flies quite far, too, for such a small toolhead, at least 10 to 15 feet by our estimation.

Being able to fling snow that far is a good thing because this thrower can only send the snow straight forward (some models have adjustable fins that allow you to send it to either side). You need to be strategic about the direction you push to avoid creating more work for yourself if you have a long path to clear.

We must admit, too, that while this electric snow shovel makes the job easier than a manual shovel, it does take a bit of strength to operate, especially since it doesn’t have wheels to help you stay balanced and moving. You can move it along the ground, but you may need to lift it slightly if the snow is packed or icy at the lower levels, and it doesn’t come with a shoulder strap to help you do that. If you aim to greatly reduce the physical strain of snow removal, models from our list that feature wheels and directional fins may be a better option.

Overall, if you already have the Ryobi 40-volt-compatible string trimmer, adding this attachment to your arsenal would be a good move if you only need to clear snow from a small driveway, walkway, deck, or patio. The 40-volt, 4-amp-hour battery will give you up to an hour of power, which is more than enough for a small job like that, and buying into this multitool system will keep it from being a tool that just sits in the toolshed or basement for most of the time.

The lightweight design of this cordless electric snow shovel makes it a great option if other electric snow shovels are too heavy for you to manage. Whereas most electric snow shovels weigh around 18 pounds, this one weighs just 13.5 pounds.

Along with being lighter, the Snow Joe electric snow shovel also has a dual-handle design that allows you to operate it while standing up straight, taking pressure off your back. Despite its lighter weight, it can still clear a foot-wide path of snow up to 6 inches deep. The Snow Joe does have a shorter runtime than most, which limits it to lighter-duty snow removal, such as clearing walks, decks, and patios.

With its two 20-volt rechargeable batteries, the Worx electric snow shovel is both versatile and powerful. It can clear a path a foot wide and up to 6 inches deep and throw snow up to 25 feet, so it's suitable for clearing tighter spaces.

The two-battery design gives you the option to mix and match larger-capacity 20-volt Worx batteries to increase this shovel’s run time for larger jobs, such as clearing small driveways. It also comes with a dual charger, so you can charge both batteries simultaneously for a shorter turnaround time.

Another plus is that this model's batteries are compatible with other 20-volt Worx yard machines, making it a great option if you’ve already bought into the Worx product line.

We’d be remiss if we didn’t point out that this whole category of yard machines has some limitations. Most electric snow shovels can only handle snow depths up to 6 inches—8 inches if you’re lucky—and lack the power to handle heavier slushy snow. They are ideally suited to powdery snow on walkways, patios, decks, and maybe a small driveway. If you see heavy snowfalls regularly or have a large number of driveways and parking spaces to clear, get a snowblower before you buy an electric snow shovel. For big jobs, go with a gas snowblower. An electric snowblower works for small to moderate-sized driveways.

When push comes to shove, we recommend looking for a cordless electric snow shovel rather than a corded one. Having the freedom to move without worrying about a cord makes the whole shoveling or snowblowing process much easier. That said, if you’re on a tight budget or only need to clear a short walk or a small patio or deck that’s near an outdoor outlet, you can get by with a corded model.

Much like a snowblower, electric snow shovels are rated by how much snow they can move. The wider the shovel, the fewer passes it takes to clear an area. Most electric snow shovels move a 10- to 16-inch-wide path of snow. A small, narrow shovel is lighter and more nimble, making it useful for creating pathways. Wider, larger models are better equipped for clearing a patio or driveway, but are also heavier and more difficult to maneuver in tighter spaces.

Electric snow shovels can handle snowbanks around 4 to 8 inches high, depending on their clearing depth. Technically, you can remove deeper snowfall with these machines, but you’ll have to make more passes to do so.

For an electric snow shovel to be useful, it should be able to propel the snow far enough that it’s off the deck, walkway, or driveway that you’re clearing. Most electric snow shovels launch their snow between 20 and 30 feet, which is on par with entry-level, corded electric snowblowers, but shorter than cordless and gas snowblowers that can throw snow a distance of 40 feet or more. With that in mind, consider the route you plan to take while clearing, and make sure you’re moving the snow somewhere out of the way so it can sit until spring arrives.

Electric snow shovels process and throw snow like a snowblower, so you won’t need to bend over and scoop up snow as you would with a shovel. However, you should still look for the lightest possible option. While you won’t have to lift and throw snow as you would with a conventional snow shovel, you have to hold it upright and apply some force to push it through the snow. At the very least, you should look for a shovel that you can lift easily whenever you need to clear steps or multiple levels of patio.

Electric snow shovels typically weigh between 10 and 20 pounds. As you might expect, more powerful shovels that can move more snow and feature large batteries tend to be heavier than smaller, narrower models. Some large electric snow shovels have a set of wheels mounted to the rear of the base for standing upright on their own, so you can maneuver the machine with minimal lifting.

Similar to standard snow shovels, electric models come in both straight and curved handle varieties. A curved handle allows for standing more upright while operating the machine, putting less strain on your lower back and decreasing the risk of injury. A straight handle gives you more leverage for lifting loads of snow, but since an electric snow shovel has an auger that lifts and blows the snow for you, it’s not an advantage for electric models.

Electric snow shovels operate similarly to single-stage snow blowers. The shovel end of the machine has an auger that’s powered by an electric motor. As you push the shovel through the snow, the rotating auger collects snow, mashes it up, and then propels it through a shoot that throws the snow off to the side

The average electric snow shovel can churn through about 300 pounds of snow per minute. That means a snow shovel with a 12-inch wide intake and a clearing depth of 6 inches can remove about 4 inches of powdery snow from a 1,000 square foot driveway in about 20 minutes.

Just keep in mind that a shovel’s snow-clearing ability varies depending on certain conditions, such as the heft of the snow itself.

It’s never a bad idea to have a standard snow shovel around. While the electric snow shovel can reach most spaces that a standard push-behind snowblower can’t, it may not always be able to clear hardened snow or wet slush.

Plus, a manual shovel ensures that you can always dig out in an emergency, like when you’ve lost power after a snowstorm.

#6279. Scientists want to improve photosynthesis to help feed the world, but it isn’t so simple

Scientists screened about 15,000 bacterial Rubisco variants, revealing promising changes and unexpected obstacles to improving photosynthesis.

Plants look like experts at turning air and sunlight into food. But a key enzyme in that process, Rubisco, is slow and sometimes captures the wrong gas.

Scientists have now tried to improve a faster bacterial version of that enzyme, and the single changes that helped often stopped helping once they were combined.

Even the computer models built to predict such changes struggled to say which combinations would work.

The team screened about 15,000 altered versions of the enzyme inside living photosynthetic cells. What came out is a long list of which changes help and which hurt.

The list comes with a limit: the enzyme was bacterial, not a plant’s, and any use in a crop would need further testing in plant cells and whole plants first.

Paul Hudson, a professor of systems biology at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, led the work with Ute Hoffmann and Axel Knave, who share first authorship.

Colleagues at SciLifeLab, the University of the Balearic Islands in Spain and Kobe University in Japan took part.

Every plant carries Rubisco, and so do some bacteria.

Sunlight supplies the power, and the enzyme captures carbon dioxide from the air and attaches it to a sugar, the first step in building the rest of the plant.

When Rubisco captures oxygen instead, it produces a byproduct the cell has to break down and recycle, which costs energy.

Plant Rubisco is a 16-piece assembly that is hard to produce and alter in the lab. Some bacteria carry a simpler form, built from identical copies of one piece, that fixes carbon faster.

Versions like it have been proposed as replacements for the plant enzyme in crops.

Hudson’s team chose one from a bacterium called Gallionella. This type of Rubisco evolved mainly in places with little oxygen.

Chemists call capturing carbon dioxide carboxylation and capturing oxygen oxygenation, and the fast bacterial enzyme does more of both.

“But they also catalyze the oxygenation reaction more readily, meaning that they are less selective for carbon dioxide,” Hudson said.

“Our idea was to take these fast Rubiscos and make them even faster, or at least reduce their oxygenation rate while retaining a high carboxylation rate.”

The team put the altered enzymes into Synechocystis, a photosynthetic bacterium, or cyanobacterium.

Its own Rubisco had been switched almost entirely off, so each cell could grow only as fast as the bacterial Rubisco it carried allowed.

Each altered gene also carried a 20-letter DNA tag. These tags let researchers track which variants became more common as the cells grew together in one pooled culture.

The library had two parts. One tested individual changes at selected positions in the enzyme.

The other combined changes at seven positions, with 16,200 possible combinations in its design.

None of the positions was a guess. Most came from two programs that compare the enzyme with thousands of related Rubiscos and flag the spots most likely to tolerate change.

The pooled cells then grew for 12 generations in bioreactors, with or without oxygen in the gas feed. The cyanobacteria grew more slowly whenever oxygen was present.

Cells carrying about 8% of the single-swap variants grew faster than cells carrying the starting enzyme, compared with under 1% of the multi-change variants. The helpful swaps clustered in a few places.

Two of them were in a flexible loop beside the enzyme’s active site, a stretch thought to help Rubisco tell carbon dioxide from oxygen.

Another helpful swap was at the seam where two copies of the enzyme meet, beside a tunnel that runs between the two active sites.

Swaps there helped more when oxygen was present.

One short stretch couldn’t be changed at all: it forms a helix above the opening where the enzyme’s sugar partner enters and leaves, and every swap there made growth worse.

To check the tag readings, the team grew six of the best variants on their own. Cells carrying each of the six variants outgrew cells carrying either the starting enzyme or the natural enzyme.

The cells held about the same amount of each enzyme, which argues against the idea that they were simply making more Rubisco.

The obvious next step is to combine the winners, and it mostly didn’t work. On average, the more changes a variant carried, the worse the cells holding it grew.

Cells carrying one variant with three particular changes grew more slowly than cells carrying the starting enzyme. Cells carrying a fourth change on its own also grew more slowly.

Put all four together, and the cells grew noticeably better.

The computer models struggled with combinations too. Three programs that score a mutation by how it fits the pattern across related Rubiscos did reasonably well on single swaps.

On variants with several changes, their predictions pointed the wrong way, largely because of one swap they kept recommending that hurt every variant it appeared in.

A model trained on the team’s own data did better at predicting the combinations already in the dataset.

But when the team built 11 new variants it recommended, each with six to 12 changes, eight of them didn’t support growth at all. Only two beat the starting enzyme.

The best enzyme in the whole study, called Ad1, came from the simpler approach of adding proven changes together. Give Ad1 one more swap that had helped on its own, and growth collapsed.

The team purified Ad1 and a six-change variant called C6 and measured them in the test tube with radioactive carbon dioxide.

Both reacted with oxygen more slowly than the starting enzyme, and Ad1 was choosier about carbon dioxide over oxygen.

Carbon-fixing speed changed in opposite directions, with C6 about 25% faster than the starting enzyme and Ad1 about 15% slower.

There was a cost. Both variants needed more carbon dioxide around them to work at full speed, so their overall efficiency at fixing carbon was lower too.

The better growers the team tested were also generally less heat-stable than the starting enzyme, which the authors wrote may reflect a looser fit between the two halves.

Inside the cells, the Ad1 strain held less of the sugar Rubisco works on and more of the product it makes. That fits a smaller bottleneck at that step.

The strain also grew better than the starting enzyme’s cells in ordinary air, not only in the carbon-rich bioreactors.

The cells were cyanobacteria, not plants, and the enzyme was bacterial.

Moving a bacterial Rubisco into a crop would also mean moving the machinery that concentrates carbon dioxide around it, which the authors call an outstanding challenge.

The starting enzyme was itself a slower version of the natural one, and even Ad1 still fixed carbon more slowly than the natural enzyme.

The pooled screening also ran at 5% carbon dioxide, far above the level in air, which may have hidden differences in how the enzymes handle scarcer carbon dioxide.

And the team measured only two enzymes in detail, so it can’t yet say that less reaction with oxygen is what sped up growth.

Next, Hudson’s team wants to cut the oxygen reaction further in the promising variants and work out which parts of the enzyme help it choose carbon dioxide.

With funding from the European Union, the researchers are also testing new enzymes in plant cells and in cyanobacteria engineered to produce useful chemicals.

They have publicly shared their analysis code and results, including successful and unsuccessful changes, so others can train their own models.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

The powerful Euclid space telescope is making the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos, and ESA has just shared the first enormous piece of it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope, including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.

"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell, ESA's director of science, said in a statement. "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."

Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.

Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.

A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.

Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These "Einstein rings" ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein, who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.

In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Over 10 years ago, we forecast that Euclid would revolutionise the field of strong lens discovery," Natalie Lines, a Euclid Consortium member working at the University of Portsmouth in the UK, said in the statement. "That day is finally here."

The "grand design" spiral galaxy M81, imaged by Euclid.

The Messier 81 galaxy (seen on the right) is one of the brightest in the sky. With fully developed spiral arms stretching to its bright core, M81 is known as a "grand design spiral" galaxy.

While M81 is relatively close to Earth and can be seen with a good pair of binoculars, Euclid's field of view captures it alongside the elliptical galaxy NGC 3077 (bottom left) and crisp clouds of interstellar dust.

The ring galaxy NGC 1291, imaged close up at Euclid's highest resolution.

Among the nearly 1 billion galaxies charted by Euclid is NGC 1291, also called the Golden Eye galaxy. The galaxy is located 33 million light-years from Earth, and Euclid shows a close-up view of it here at the telescope's highest resolution, according to ESA.

Ring galaxies like this contain a central bulge disconnected from a surrounding ring of stars; astronomers think these galaxies form when a smaller galaxy plunges through the middle of a larger one.

The first piece of the Euclid Wide Survey, covering about 14% of the total sky area that the telescope plans to survey.

This image shows the entire sector of the Euclid Wide Survey, the telescope's mission to map vast swatches of the northern sky. The Wide Survey is accompanied by the Euclid Deep Survey, which will spend about 10% of the telescope's observing time taking repeated observations of three relatively small spots of sky, according to ESA.

With about 85% of its survey left to go, Euclid is on track to collect one of the most comprehensive datasets of the universe ever. Now, it'll be up to the scientific community to make good use of those observations and find something extraordinary.For more stunning space images, check out our Space Photo of the Week.

#6277. Does everyone carry disease-linked DNA variants? What nearly a million genomes revealed

The average human genome holds about 5 million variants, and one to three of them are already labeled as causing a genetic disease.

A DNA test may flag a variant linked to disease, but that result alone does not mean you will develop the condition.

The typical adult carries one to three rare variants already labeled as causing a genetic disease, plus about 50 more whose meaning is still uncertain.

Most of them do not cause disease in the person carrying them.

The counts come from the largest attempt so far to describe the average human genome.

Caroline Wright, a professor at the University of Exeter, led a team that read the full genomes of nearly a million adults in two large health studies.

The volunteers in UK Biobank and the All of Us program in the United States were not chosen because of any disease. Their DNA shows what ordinary variation looks like.

“Whole genome sequencing has become such an important tool in diagnosing genetic disease, and we’re increasingly moving towards genetic screening for predicting disease. Yet most people are unaware of just how much genetic variation is present in every genome. Actually, variation is the norm,” Wright said.

Scientists compare each person’s DNA with a reference genome, a standard copy of the 3.1 billion letters in human DNA.

A typical person differs from that standard at 4.3 million to 5.3 million spots, or roughly one letter in every 600 to 700.

People whose ancestry is genetically closest to African populations carry about a million more differences than everyone else.

The authors think that may be partly because the reference itself was built mostly from people of European ancestry, so it matches the DNA of people with African ancestry less well.

Most of those differences are single letters swapped, or a few letters added or dropped. The typical genome has 68 stretches longer than 10,000 letters that are either missing or present in extra copies.

Almost all of this variation is shared. In the typical genome, 98.4% of the variants are common, meaning they turn up in more than 1% of people from the same ancestry group.

Only about half a percent land in the parts of genes that spell out proteins.

Protein-coding variants can affect the proteins our bodies make.

A typical person has 21,000 to 26,000 of them, and the team predicts that about 48% change the protein in some way.

Even so, a computer score that flags protein changes likely to do harm picked out just 28 of the roughly 9,600 protein-altering variants in a typical genome.

Each person also carries about 229 variants predicted to break a gene outright, 165 of them with high confidence. That count is in line with earlier surveys of human variation, the authors wrote.

ClinVar, a public database at the U.S. National Institutes of Health, lists about 4 million variants, and around 300,000 of them are rated as causing or probably causing disease.

Eight to ten of those are in the average genome.

The team then narrowed the search to 4,262 genes with solid evidence of causing a single-gene disease and kept only rare variants. That leaves one to three disease-causing variants per person.

Most are in genes for recessive conditions, which need a broken copy from each parent before anyone gets sick.

One copy makes a carrier, and the average person may be a carrier for two to six such conditions.

Variants predicted to disrupt the gene for filaggrin, a skin protein linked to eczema, turn up in about 1 in 15 people of European ancestry in the study.

Not everyone who carries one gets eczema.

For genes associated with dominant conditions, in which one altered copy can cause disease, about 1 in 9 people carries a rare variant rated as disease-causing.

“Importantly, we found that everyone carries a small number of genetic variants linked to disease, although many of these will not actually cause disease in that individual,” Wright said.

“It is therefore crucial to consider context when interpreting findings from genetic testing, including symptoms or family history of disease as well as other clinical and environmental risk factors.”

Common diseases such as diabetes and heart disease usually involve many genetic variants alongside environmental and lifestyle factors.

Thousands of common variants each nudge the odds a little, and a polygenic risk score adds those nudges up to rank a person against everyone else.

Wright’s team used scores already calculated for 28 common diseases across UK Biobank. The average person ranked in the top 10% of risk for about three of them.

Among 450,209 participants of European ancestry, 102,831, or about 1 in 5 people, scored in the top 1% for at least one disease.

A high score for at least one condition is therefore relatively common. Participants of other ancestries landed in the top 1% even more often, about 1 in 3 people.

The authors read that as a flaw in the scores, which perform poorly outside the population they were built in, rather than as extra disease.

Run 100 such scores on one person, the authors calculate, and about 99% of people would land in the top 5% for at least one disease.

About 63% would be in the top 1%. Screening programs that run many scores at once, they wrote, carry significant potential for overdiagnosis.

Some variants come from neither parent. In 2,334 sets of two parents and an adult child, the child carried an average of 61 mutations found in neither parent, ranging from 30 to 113.

Typically only one of them fell inside a protein-coding stretch.

Three-quarters to four-fifths of those new mutations came from the father’s side.

Each year of a father’s age at the child’s birth added about 1.2 more of them, and each year of a mother’s age added about 0.4.

All three members of a trio had to be adults to join the studies, so the parents in this sample were young at the birth. That puts the average toward the low end of earlier estimates.

The volunteers came only from Britain and the United States, and 91.5% of the UK Biobank group was of European ancestry. So the figures say little about most of the world.

Sequencing read short fragments of DNA taken almost entirely from blood, which misses some kinds of variation and any change confined to other tissues.

Uncertainty is unevenly spread. People of European ancestry carried more variants with a known disease label, while everyone else carried more variants of unknown meaning.

The authors trace that gap partly to who has been sequenced so far, and it can affect who gets a diagnosis.

The largest open question is one the study did not try to answer.

The team did not assess whether participants had the diseases associated with their flagged variants, so it cannot say how often those variants were linked to illness.

Wright’s team is presenting the work at the American Society of Human Genetics annual meeting this week.

The authors call for genomes from more diverse populations, read with longer-range sequencing and from more than one tissue, and they urge caution as genetic screening of healthy people expands.

The full study was published in the journal Genome Medicine.

#6276. A NASA Veteran Claims to Have Used Mind-Bending Physics to Conquer Gravity

Charles Buhler’s claim could change how spacecraft fly. But experiments show how much work it takes to establish that a mysterious push is real.

In April 2024, Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist who helped establish a laboratory at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center, made a remarkable claim. His company, Exodus Propulsion Technologies, had built a device that could produce thrust without expelling propellant. He attributed the push to what he called a “New Force.”

As we reported in our earlier coverage, Buhler’s claim would have big consequences for spaceflight. That promise depends on whether researchers outside Exodus can reproduce the push and rule out an ordinary explanation.

One physicist has spent years investigating similar claims. Martin Tajmar, a professor and chair of space systems at Dresden University of Technology in Germany, has spent two decades measuring the forces produced by charged capacitors, including lopsided ones like the designs Buhler describes.

“It’s all negative,” he tells Popular Mechanics. Meaning, his tests found no evidence of that force within the limits of his equipment. He hasn’t tested Exodus’s hardware, but his experiments show what an independent test would need to account for.

A capacitor stores electric charge. Apply a high enough voltage to certain designs, and they can set the surrounding air moving, producing a push on the device itself. Tajmar calls this corona wind, “a discharge in air that drags air molecules with it.” In those cases, the device moves by pushing air backward, much as a fan does.

Tajmar’s team wanted to see whether a capacitor would still produce a push with almost all the air removed. For their 2024 study in Scientific Reports, they put the capacitor and its battery-powered electrical equipment together on a sensitive balance inside a vacuum chamber. At 10,000 volts, an asymmetric capacitor produced no clear sign of an unexplained force, even with instruments sensitive enough to detect a push measured in billionths of a newton.

Exodus hasn’t sent Tajmar a device, so he built his own capacitors for those experiments. He says his asymmetric design follows the principles in the company’s patent, though he doesn’t know the exact dimensions of its hardware.

“It’s Exodus who have to say why my asymmetric capacitor does not produce any thrust,” he says.

He believes his results challenge the company’s explanation, but he’d need its hardware to put its particular device through the same checks.

Keeping the battery and high-voltage equipment on the balance removes outside power cables that could interfere with the reading. Researchers also have to watch for electromagnetic forces or parts shifting as they heat up, either of which could look like thrust.

Tajmar also recommends swapping the device for an electrical dummy that draws power but should produce no thrust. If the balance still registers a push, something else in the setup is causing it. Researchers would need to track that down before treating the reading as evidence of a working drive.

Buhler has also said the devices can keep producing thrust after the power is switched off. Electrical charge can linger in insulating materials, leaving an electric field even after the supply is disconnected. Researchers would need to work out whether that leftover charge explains the reading and, if there really is a push, where it comes from.

In a short white paper, Exodus says other experimenters have reproduced the effect and argues that the device pushes against the vacuum itself, allowing momentum to be conserved. But it doesn’t include their laboratory reports. Without those details, readers can’t tell how the experiments were done or whether the researchers ruled out other causes of the push.

What leaving the propellant behind could change

Spacecraft have to bring along the propellant they’ll use to speed up, slow down or change course. That adds weight, which takes more propellant to move. The rocket equation puts numbers to that trade-off, showing how much a spacecraft can change its speed with the supply it carries.

If a drive could produce useful thrust without using up propellant, engineers could plan missions differently. A spacecraft could keep changing course as long as it had enough power and the drive kept working. Some of the weight now devoted to propellant tanks and their contents could go toward other equipment.

But the drive would bring its own baggage. It would need a power source and a way to get rid of waste heat, and all of that would have to travel with it. Engineers would need to find out whether the thrust was worth the weight of the complete system. Getting a reliable push in the lab would give them a reason to start working that out.

Light can give a spacecraft a push, too. When a laser sends light in one direction, the laser gets a tiny push in the other, because light carries momentum. Tajmar points out that this already offers a way to produce thrust without using up material propellant.

“If you just power a laser with the power that we use in our experiments, the thrust is also propellantless and actually already exists,” he says.

The catch is how much power it takes. To hold up a 1.2-ounce object, roughly the weight of the devices Buhler described, a laser would need to send about 100 million watts of light downward. A drive that produced a useful push with much less power would be worth engineers’ attention. Researchers would also have to explain what carries momentum in the opposite direction, as the light does for a laser.

“You have to test it in an independent laboratory. And then with a different method,” Tajmar says. He wants the results published so other experts can examine the work, including the equipment itself. Getting the same push on a different instrument would help show that the device deserves the credit.

Nobody needs to make the whole apparatus float. Even a small sideways push would warrant attention if it survived those checks and other researchers could reliably reproduce it. Then engineers could start asking whether it was strong enough to put to work aboard a spacecraft.

Buhler’s claim promises freedom from the propellant tank, which would change how we travel through space. The next move is closer to home. Put the drive in another lab, let someone else take the controls, and see whether the promise still has any push behind it.

#6275. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

Z. Yu et al. High fiber diet mitigates exposure risk of nanoplastics in male mice. Nature Communications. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78675-7

#6274. Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is changing color, and plastic may be the reason

Water near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch brightened in blue and green over 20 years, and microplastics are the likely cause, a study finds.

Satellites cannot see tiny pieces of plastic in the ocean, but they can see the color of the water. Over the last 20 years, the ocean near the Great Pacific Garbage Patch has actually changed color.

New research suggests that microscopic plastics are to blame. If this is true, scientists might soon be able to track invisible plastic pollution from space just by looking at the color of the sea.

Shea Cheatham, Daniel Koestner, and Børge Hamre of the University of Bergen in Norway carried out the study. They didn’t collect water samples. Instead, they compared three satellite records with computer simulations of how light travels through seawater.

Between Hawaii and California, clockwise surface currents carry floating plastic into an area called the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.

In the summer of 2015, The Ocean Cleanup, a nonprofit group, ran a survey in which boats towed nets in and around the patch 652 times. The group then tallied the catch piece by piece.

Using that survey, the group’s researchers estimated the patch’s area at about 620,000 square miles (1.6 million square kilometers) in a 2018 study. The group describes that area as twice the size of Texas.

The researchers put the number of plastic pieces at 1.8 trillion. They estimated that larger objects made up 92% of the weight, while microplastics made up 94% of the pieces.

But the plastic in the new study is too small to be in that count. Its pieces are no bigger than about a hundredth of an inch (0.3 millimeters), roughly the thickness of three sheets of printer paper.

Plastics that small are the most likely to enter the ocean’s food chain at its lowest level, the authors wrote.

These plastics are also hard to measure at sea, and cleaning them up on a large scale would be difficult, if not impossible.

The color of the ocean depends on what’s in the water. Microscopic algae called phytoplankton absorb some colors of light far more than others.

Plastic behaves differently. In earlier lab work, Koestner and his colleagues measured how water with microplastics mixed in absorbs and scatters light.

The plastic absorbed light fairly evenly across colors. It also scattered a lot of light back the way it came.

In the team’s simulations, seawater with these particles in it looked brighter from above. Blue-green light increased the most.

When the amount of phytoplankton or other natural material changes, blue light tends to get brighter while green gets dimmer, or the other way around. Plastic should brighten both at once.

The team analyzed three records of ocean color. Each ran from August 2002 through September 2022.

One came from an instrument on NASA’s Aqua satellite. The other two, from the European Space Agency and the Copernicus Marine Service, combine readings from several satellite sensors.

Large parts of the ocean have changed color in recent decades, often because of shifts in ocean life. So the team compared the patch with the water around it.

In all three records, areas in and near the patch grew brighter in both blue and green light. Together, those colors make cyan.

The cyan areas were shifted west and north of the patch’s densest part. That may be because wind pushes large floating objects, while microplastics travel with the water, the authors wrote.

Elsewhere, the three records didn’t always match. Farther south, the NASA record showed much more brightening in red light than the other two.

Two likely causes, the authors wrote, are an aging NASA instrument and differences in how the records were processed.

The European Space Agency record showed the fewest areas of clear change. Even so, it showed cyan in and near the patch.

How much plastic would it take to change the ocean’s color enough for a satellite to detect? The team ran 1,100 simulations to find out.

By their calculation, it would take about 5 milligrams of small microplastics in a cube of seawater 3.3 feet (1 meter) on each side.

At that level, the plastic brightened the simulated water more than satellite readings normally vary from one pixel to the next.

Suppose plastic alone caused the change in the brightest area on the patch’s western edge. In that area, a cube of water that size would have gained 11 to 25 milligrams of plastic over 20 years, depending on the satellite record.

The authors called those amounts reasonable. Net surveys by The Ocean Cleanup suggest that larger microplastics may reach similar concentrations near the surface.

In 2018, the group’s researchers also reported that the amount of plastic in the patch appeared to be rising exponentially, and more quickly than in nearby waters.

A color that fits plastic isn’t proof of plastic, the authors wrote, so they tested what natural changes could do alone.

The team simulated 500 versions of the ocean in which only natural material varied: phytoplankton, other natural particles, and colored material dissolved in the water.

In 500 more versions, the amount of microplastics varied too.

Then they compared the versions two at a time and sorted every case of brightening by its color: blue, cyan, green, or red.

With only natural material varying, 3% of the brightening cases were cyan. With microplastics added, 13% were cyan.

In the simulations, adding plastic made a cyan change more than four times as likely.

Without plastic, cyan appeared only when phytoplankton shifted from mostly larger kinds to mostly smaller ones, usually with less living material overall. With plastic, much smaller natural changes were enough.

Blooms of plankton called coccolithophores can brighten seawater too. But these plankton haven’t historically been active here, and their blooms would likely turn the water greener than the satellites recorded.

Mineral dust can brighten the ocean as well. But a dust record at Station ALOHA, north of Hawaii, appears to show no significant change between 1980 and 2025.

The study can’t say for certain that plastic is the cause. The satellites recorded color, and more than one thing in seawater can change it.

In one plausible scenario, the authors wrote, moderate changes in ocean life and a buildup of microplastics are both adding to the brightening.

Plastic could also be acting indirectly, they wrote. Chemical pollutants that come with plastic could be disrupting ocean life, and that disruption could change the water’s color.

Scientists haven’t directly measured how much plastic this small is in the patch.

The team also built its simulated seawater to match a measurement from the South Pacific. No complete set of light measurements exists for the patch’s own region.

Researchers will need to measure light and particles directly, at different depths near the patch, to check the result.

If those measurements confirm the pattern, satellites that already record ocean color could help scientists monitor where small microplastics are building up.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

#6273. The 8 Best Portable Power Stations for Outages and Outings

Be prepared for unexpected power failures and off-the-grid camping trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Portable power stations are handy for backup power during outages, off-grid electricity for an RV, or simply charging your laptop and phone while working remotely. They’re effectively large bundles of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, which provide a quiet, exhaust-free alternative to noisy gas-powered portable generators.

Portable power stations come in a broad range of sizes from brands like Jackery and EcoFlow, including smaller models capable of charging a few devices and high-capacity backup units to keep your lighting and critical appliances on during a days-long blackout. Plus, most can be recharged using solar panels.

We evaluated eight power stations of varying sizes, focusing on each model’s maximum output, capacity, charging time, and portability. To test max output, we connected enough electronics and appliances to each power station to meet or slightly exceed their listed max output to see how well they could operate at maximum load. We then tested capacity, using an electricity usage monitor to record the total watt-hours each power station produced while running them under a consistent load.

Once they were drained, we charged each power station from 0 to 100 percent using its AC adapter, timing how long it took to get to 80 and 100 percent capacity. Finally, we evaluated each power station’s portability by attempting to carry it or roll it. Other factors that weighed into our decisions included the number and power output of each power station’s inputs and its charging options.

Our test team for this article includes David Dritsas, an editor who covers generators, lawn and garden, and more; Bradley Ford, an editor with more than five years of experience testing and writing about generators, generator maintenance, power tools, and lawn and garden equipment; and Tony Carrick, a frequent Popular Mechanics contributor who covers landscaping, home improvement, gardening, and home security.

Bluetti manages to pack a lot of power into the Elite 200 V2. It has a max output of 2,600 watts with 3,900-watt startup power and a 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, all while being relatively compact.

We hooked up a miter saw, blender, and space heater, all three of which it powered simultaneously. It easily handled the spike to 4,000 watts to start up the saw, above its listed 3,900-watt starting power, before maintaining an even flow of around 2,500 watts.

The Elite 200 V2 also impressed with the quality of its battery. We recorded 92 percent of its listed 2,073.6-watt-hour capacity, well over the 85 percent average for most portable power stations. It has a quick recharge time for its capacity, going from 0 to 80 percent in 81 minutes and to full in just 107 minutes. And because it uses a LiFePO4 battery, it discharges and recharges for 6,000 cycles before it drops below 80 percent capacity.

The Elite 200 V2 gives you plenty of output and input options for its size, too. Four AC outlets allow you to load up multiple appliances. There are four USB ports for charging smaller devices, a car accessory outlet, and a DC output. Along with its power cord, there’s a port for charging from a car accessory port or with up to 1,000 watts of solar panels.

With a great power-to-weight ratio, the latest version of the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 is a great portable power station for powering a camper or providing backup power for the essentials.

A new and improved version of Jackery’s extremely popular Explorer 1000, the Explorer 1000 V2 features a slightly larger storage capacity, up 70 watt-hours, and a much higher 1,500-watt output—a 50 percent jump from 1,000 watts of the original. This allows you to power devices with higher loads, like an electric grill or a large microwave. Jackery managed this while maintaining the Explorer 1000’s compact size and weight, so it’s still easy to carry with you on a camping trip.

The Explorer 1000 V2 features three standard 120-volt AC outlets, two USB-C ports (30- and 100-watt), one USB-A port (18-watt), and one 12-volt DC outlet. Paired with Jackery’s app, you can monitor the power station locally via Bluetooth or from anywhere when it’s connected via WiFi. The app allows for checking charge levels and estimated run time, as well as toggling any of the outputs on or off. Plugged into the wall, the power station charges in under two hours. It’s also possible to charge it from your vehicle in up to 12 hours.

Performance-wise, the 1000 V2 did well powering a 25-cubic-foot refrigerator for 18 hours and 22 minutes, which is better performance than we’ve gotten from other tested 1000-watt models. Under a constant load of 475 watts (that’s a little less than a small coffee maker), it ran for 1 hour and 57 minutes.

This power station offers a lot of bang for the buck. Sure, it isn’t going to power your house through a days-long outage, but it offers a lot of nice features for the price, making it one of the better values out there, especially if you pick it up on sale.

What is most impressive about the Anker S2000 power station is its ability to maximize its runtime. During our testing, we were able to run a full-sized refrigerator for just over 24 hours, which is nearly six hours longer than other power stations we’ve tested with comparable capacity.

It does this using a technology that recognizes the type of device plugged in and adjusts the inverter's frequency to match the type of demand. This, in theory, helps reduce the amount of wasted power. From what we can tell, it works very well.

The S2000 is fairly well equipped, too, with five outlets for AC power (two are in the back) and a bank of USB ports for home use, and can operate as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) for 10-millisecond automated backup. With only 1,500 watts of output, it may struggle with some high-power appliances like a large microwave, but for many people, this station can deliver power during a blackout and keep you up and running for a long time.

With the Bluetti Apex 300, the name of the game is flexibility. Alone, it delivers up to 3,840 watts of continuous power and handles up to an impressive 7,680 watts of surge power. Capacity is a solid 2,764.8 watt-hours for decent runtime, though it depends on the amount of power you intend to draw from it. If you happen to have 240-volt appliances or circuits, this model has you covered, too.

But everything on this power station is scalable. It’s possible to add up to six additional batteries for a very high capacity of 19,353.6 watt-hours, and connect up to two other Apex 300 units and run them in parallel. This expandability makes it a great entry-level home power station that expands into a larger backup system that delivers whole-home power.

The Apex 300 features four 120-volt outlets across the front, plus a 120-volt 30-amp outlet and a 120/240-volt 50-amp outlet on the side for powering devices individually, plugging into an RV, or delivering home power through a transfer switch.

One downside for me was the lack of direct DC outputs, e.g., USB-C ports. For that, you have to purchase an optional hub. There are also power inputs for a standard AC plug, a 30-amp connection, and two solar connections. The Apex 300 uses two inverters as opposed to one, giving you two banks of 120-volt, 1,920-watt output (two outlets in each bank). We easily ran two high-powered appliances at the same time, including a space heater and a toaster, with no issues at all.

This station is serious about solar recharging, too. There are two ports for connecting solar panels up to 1,200 watts each. Having the option of 2,400 watts of solar input is uncommon in a station of this size and price point. Plus, you can reach even higher input by pairing with a Bluetti SolarX 4K voltage regulator, which is designed for connection to larger solar arrays.

Most of the control options are accessed with the Bluetti Mobile app, and it’s one of the best we’ve seen. It’s easy to finely tune settings in ways that other companies don’t offer, such as adjusting the recharging level from as little as one amp to 50 amps.

If you’ve been eyeing power stations but aren’t sure if you want one more for portable power or more for home backup power, this is the model for you. It delivers a great amount of power for portable use, but lays the groundwork for building a more dedicated system in the future.

This is one of the most rugged power stations we’ve seen yet. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra features an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system and cooling structure that help keep water out of the enclosure. All work together to resist the elements better than most power stations can.

The unique cooling system was particularly interesting. A titanium alloy plate within the structure helps dissipate heat without the need for multiple fans, and eliminates the need for any side vents (typical in most power stations) that could allow droplets of water in. Meanwhile, you can remove an external plate on the bottom and dry it if water does make its way in.

The 1,800 watts of output power and 1,536 watt-hours of battery capacity are decent if you’re taking this camping for the weekend and need to recharge devices, run a low-powered small appliance or two, and plug in some lighting. But don’t expect to run something like a space heater for very long, though.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The S5000 is the second power station in Anker's S-series, which features inverter efficiency technology that helps to reduce wasted energy when the inverter is idling or running lower-powered devices. We were impressed with how this technology performed in the S2000, and this model matched that performance.

We ran this through several tests, and the battery efficiency proved to be around 97 percent (the industry average is around 89 percent). For example, we left the AC inverter idling for 18 hours, and the battery remained at 100 percent capacity. Meanwhile, another station we idled at the same time lost 19 percent of its available power. That was impressive.

The next most impressive attribute about the S5000 is its size. It’s at least half the size of other power stations that feature 5,000 watt-hours of capacity and includes just as many outputs, including a 240-volt, 30-amp outlet. It also has both high- and low-powered DC inputs that enable up to 3,000 watts of solar power input if you have the panels to generate that. You can also recharge at up to 4,500 watts using a direct DC connection to Anker's 5500 Smart Tri-Fuel generator.

With only 4,500 watts of total output, we wouldn’t call this a contender for true whole-home backup (Anker’s E-10 system is a better option for that), but the S5000 can deliver a decent amount to power an RV, run lights and appliances during an emergency, or even a couple of critical circuits.

During our hands-on test, Goal Zero’s newest Yeti 1500 impressed us with its capable performance and sturdy construction. It’s the replacement for an older model and improves on its predecessor with improved weatherproofing, more outputs, and a better battery.

This 2,000-watt power station is clearly designed for outdoor use with an IPX4 water-resistance rating and new outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs when you’re not using them. That’s great for dusty conditions. Each section is nicely illuminated by an LED light and can be individually turned on/off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a duration of time). These additions make it perfect for camping or other outdoor uses. You can’t leave it out in the rain, but getting a bit of water on it won’t be a concern.

We loved the increased number of outputs on the Yeti 1500. There are now four 120-volt AC outlets and six USB ports: four USB-C (two are high-powered) and two USB-A ports, plus four 12-volt connections (though two of those are proprietary for Goal Zero accessories and not all that useful in our estimation). There are also inputs for AC power, 12-volt DC, and inputs for both low- and high-voltage solar power that can be used simultaneously. Theoretically, you could recharge this station with up to 900 watts of eco-friendly electrical current.

As part of our test, we simulated a blackout at home and managed to run a cable modem/Wi-Fi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while simultaneously charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

The mobile app was easy to use and chock-full of great information on energy consumption. The only problem we had was maintaining a stable Bluetooth connection. It needed to be manually paired every time we went to use it, which was annoying. Wi-Fi is available, but that’s not so useful when you are off-grid.

We should warn you that the Yeti 1500 is heavy at 53 pounds. If you’re taking it on a trip, you’ll need a bit of strength to lug it around. That aside, the 2026 Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping, especially when there are dusty or wet conditions. We’d happily take it on our next camping trip.

Though it’s no longer EcoFlow’s flagship backup power solution, the original Delta Pro is still a massive power station with a good amount of electrical output. The brand claims it powers nearly any appliance, and after testing, we’re inclined to agree. With an output of 3,600 watts, it can handle multiple appliances, and it’s possible to bump the output to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if you need more power.

In testing, we ran it with a continuous 470-watt load for 6 hours and 57 minutes, as indicated on the Delta Pro’s display. Of course, in a home backup during a power outage situation, we would run only the bare essentials to conserve power. To that end, we used it to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator, which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes.

Recharging the power station from empty using a standard 120-volt home outlet, it recharged to full capacity in 2 hours and 36 minutes. There’s also an included adapter for charging the system at EV charging stations, with solar panels (sold separately), with a car charger, or combinations of these to speed things up.

The Delta Pro’s display screen provides all the important information you need to manage your power consumption. We frequently checked the screen during testing to see the unit’s charge level, current load, and estimated run time at the current discharge rate.

All of this information is accessible through EcoFlow’s app, which was the most intuitive and easiest to use of those tested. We connected the app both locally using Bluetooth and remotely via Wi-Fi to monitor the power station from anywhere. We could also toggle outlets on and off remotely, which is helpful if you’re trying to manage power station output to extend the battery life.

We’ve tested the brand’s Whole-Home Backup Kit, which includes two of the power stations and a dual-voltage hub used to connect to your home service panel, via a transfer switch. We used this setup to power critical circuits in a Northeast Pennsylvania home in late winter.

The Delta Pro Whole Home Kit ran just over 24 hours, powering kitchen outlets, a full-size refrigerator, a chest freezer, a cable modem and wireless network, and a hot water boiler. Plus, having charged these two Delta Pro power stations previously, we found that they were able to hold a full charge over a full 8 months.

Testing was performed under normal usage conditions—run time could easily be extended by employing standard power-conservation strategies like lowering the thermostat, powering the fridge and freezer for four hours on and four hours off, and only opening them when absolutely necessary.

EcoFlow’s Delta Pro Whole Home Kit is a legitimate home backup system that can operate inside your home, with none of the risks or potential hassles of running a generator, such as dangerous carbon monoxide gas from exhaust fumes and dealing with fuel and oil.

A portable power station’s maximum output tells you the total watts it can produce, which determines what you can and can’t power with it. Look for a power station that can handle the combined wattage of the electronics you plan to plug into it.

Some power stations also have surge power that allows them to produce higher wattage for short bursts. This is designed specifically for appliances that draw more watts (known as starting watts) in the first few seconds that you first start them up, including power tools, refrigerators, blenders, and window air conditioners.

A portable power station’s capacity, listed in watt-hours (Wh), determines how much energy a power station can deliver over time. Generally, power stations with more watt-hours can run for longer, but exactly how long depends on the amount of watts the devices connected to the power station draw. You can roughly estimate how long a power station will last by dividing the total watt-hours by the watts drawn (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, if you have a power station with 2,048 watt-hour capacity, and are consistently drawing 400 watts of power: 2,048 ÷ 400 = 5.12 hours of runtime.

Keep in mind that the usable watt hours are not the same as the watt hours listed on the power station’s label. You’ll typically get about 85 percent of the listed watt-hours due to power lost in connections and the electricity that the power station itself uses to power its inverter and display. Given those losses, expect to get about 85 percent of a power station’s listed watt-hours in usable power. So, a fully charged 2,000-watt-hour power station will typically give you about 1,700 watt-hours of usable power.

These days, most portable power stations, including all those we recommend here, use LiFePO4 batteries, which are capable of holding far more cycles, which is the number of times a battery goes through a complete discharge and recharge, than older lithium-ion batteries, while also being less likely to combust. Their one drawback is that they have a lower energy density, which means it takes more LiFePO4 batteries than lithium-ion batteries to produce the same amount of power. Still, this is the battery type of choice for portable power stations, both large and small.

While all these power stations are portable, some are easier to transport than others. A power station’s portability is directly related to its power capacity and output.

Small power stations with around 300 watt-hours of capacity and a max output of 300 watts typically weigh under 10 pounds and are about the size of a lunch box.

Mid-size models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 portable power station, which have a max wattage of between 2,000 and 2,600 watts and a 2,000-watt-hour capacity, are about the size of the printer in your home office and weigh around 60 pounds, just small and light enough for one person to carry from one room to another.

Large portable models can weigh up to 135 pounds and are about the size of a suitcase. While these monsters are too large for one person to lift, they do sit on wheels that allow you to move them over flat surfaces, technically making them portable.

Portable power stations have an array of output ports, including USB-C, USB-A, car accessory, AC, and RV. Consider what types of appliances or electronics you’re planning to charge and the type of connections they use when choosing a portable power station.

Since the wattage of the output can vary, also consider the maximum charging output of each port to avoid disappointing recharge times. For example, a power station with a USB-C port that has a 15-watt max output will take a much longer time to charge a laptop than one with a 140-watt USB-C port.

If you’re looking for a large capacity power station that will back up critical circuits in your home or power an RV, you’ll need a station that features a single 30-amp connection that can connect to an RV input or transfer switch.

Portable power stations have control panels with LED displays and buttons that turn inputs off and on and display usage and remaining power. Most portable power stations are also compatible with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi, allowing you to monitor and control them remotely from a smartphone app.

Often, what makes a power station great is the kind of software it includes and what features it offers to help you best manage your power station. For example, some stations that you leave plugged into a wall—so that they stay charged and at the ready—will automatically only recharge your station during low-peak hours when rates may be lower from your electric utility. Features like this one can be incredibly helpful when trying to get the most from your station.

Most large power stations, including the EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus and Anker F3800 Plus, can serve as a UPS (uninterruptible power supply) for your home. To use these power stations as a UPS, plug them into the wall, then plug whatever devices you want backed up into the station’s AC output ports. When the power is on, those devices use energy from the grid. When there is a power outage, the power station instantly switches these devices to battery power. If you live in an area prone to power outages, this can be useful to prevent data loss from a connected computer, keep medical devices running, or run the pump and filter on a fish tank.

Portable power stations heat up when operating for extended periods or when they’re providing power for multiple devices. Internal fans will kick on to keep the power station from overheating. While these fans are far quieter than the roar of a gas-powered generator, they do still create some noise. Smaller power stations are about as loud as a small fan, while larger ones produce about the same amount of noise as a refrigerator.

A portable power station’s lifespan depends on the type of battery inside. Most new portable power stations, including all the models we recommend here, feature LiFePO4 battery technology, which lasts far longer than older lithium-ion technology.

How much more? LiFePO4 power stations will last for more than 3,000 charge cycles, or about 10 years. That’s far longer than the 500 or so charge cycles and 3 to 5 years you’ll get from an older power station with a lithium-ion battery.

That depends on the capacity of your portable power station, the wattage of your solar panels, and the weather. To figure that out, divide the station’s total capacity by the total input power of the solar panels (Wh ÷ W = Hrs).

For example, a 1,000-watt-hour power station that’s receiving a consistent stream of 200 watts of power from a solar panel would take about 5 hours to recharge. Keep in mind, this is assuming uninterrupted, direct sunlight conditions, which, even then, may produce varied results.

Some power stations have ingress protection (IP) ratings, indicating they have been tested for water and dust resistance. The Bluetti Elite 200, for example, has an IP65 rating, which means it can withstand water sprays from all angles. However, other portable power stations do not have a weather rating, so it’s important to check if you plan on using your power station outdoors. Regardless, it’s a good idea to protect your power station from any water or severe weather conditions as much as possible.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Her background is in service journalism and earlier in her career she worked as a daily newspaper reporter and book editor. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.
