#6118. The Hidden Math Behind Delta Air Lines Being The Only US Carrier Flying Mainline Jets With Under 110 Seats

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

Delta Air Lines operates some of the smallest mainline aircraft in the United States (US), including the 109-seat Airbus A220-100 and 110-seat Boeing 717. While most major carriers rely on larger narrowbodies, Delta has maintained a niche for smaller jets within its extensive domestic network, allowing the company to reach markets with more modest passenger demand.

Pilot agreements, buying aircraft at affordable rates, and operational flexibility have helped ensure that these planes are viable. However, the 717's gradual retirement raises questions about how Delta will continue reaching out to these destinations and whether its small-aircraft strategy will evolve as the airline adjusts its fleet and domestic operations in the years ahead.

Delta Air Lines has an unusual selection of narrowbody aircraft as compared to other major US air carriers. Its mainline fleet includes two jets with approximately 110 seats: the 109-seat Airbus A220-100 and the 110-seat Boeing 717. Delta is the only major US airline to operate mainline aircraft within a particularly small seating arrangement, according to Simple Flying. While other carriers generally rely on larger narrowbodies for their mainline flying, Delta has retained a place for smaller jets, allowing it to serve routes where a larger plane may offer more capacity than needed.

Highlighting the difference between mainline and regional operations is important when looking at Delta's fleet. Mainline aircraft are operated directly by the airline, utilizing its own pilots and cabin crew. Regional flights, however, are typically outsourced to partner carriers operating under the Delta Connection brand.

These operators generally fly smaller planes, including the Embraer E175 and Bombardier CRJ900. However, the pricing and labor arrangements vary when an airline operates a smaller jet itself rather than relying on a regional partner. As Simple Flying explains in its overview of scope clauses, pilot agreements can significantly influence how airlines divide their flying between mainline and regional operations.

Delta's decision to keep jets such as the 717 and A220-100 in its mainline fleet is therefore about more than passenger demand. Its pilot agreement limits the number of aircraft regional partners can operate, while also incentivizing the retention of certain smaller jets in the mainline fleet. This helps to explain why Delta's fleet composition differs from those of its competitors. A comparison by AeroHaber also illustrates how Delta uses the A220 alongside other US operators.

Discover the secrets behind Delta's A220-100 cabin configuration.

One of the main reasons Delta operates smaller mainline aircraft comes down to an agreement with its pilots known as a scope clause. These provisions are included in collective bargaining agreements and determine how much regional flying an airline can allocate to regional partners. These agreements became increasingly important during the 1990s, when regional flights and routes grew in popularity. As a result, mainline pilots raised serious concerns about airlines shifting more routes to lower-cost regional operators. Aircraft Commerce explains that these restrictions put in place by scope clauses were intended to "protect the pilots of the major airlines."

Under the scope clauses used by many major US airlines, Simple Flying reports that regional partners are generally limited to planes with up to 76 seats and a maximum takeoff weight (MTOW) of 86,000 lb (39,009 kg). Delta's agreement, on the other hand, includes an additional provision that gives the airline more room to expand its regional fleet.

Cranky Flier states that Delta can operate up to 153 regional planes with 71 to 76 seats. It can add another 70 aircraft in that category if it operates an eligible small narrowbody in its mainline fleet. Delta met that requirement by introducing the reliable Boeing 717, and later the Airbus A220-100. Further, Cranky Flier explains, the agreement gives Delta a larger regional aircraft allowance than it would otherwise not have.

United Airlines has a similar provision in its pilot agreement, but it has not introduced an eligible small narrowbody into its mainline fleet, which would allow it to gain an expanded regional fleet allowance. American Airlines negotiated a different arrangement, allowing a larger number of regional planes with up to 65 seats, alongside separate restrictions for larger regional jets. The agreements are not identical, but Delta's provision gives it a particular reason to retain smaller aircraft in its mainline fleet.

Have you ever wondered who was flying the plane?

Operating smaller planes with mainline crews can be expensive, but Delta found ways to make its Boeing 717 and Airbus A220-100 fleets work. The terms under which it purchased the aircraft were an important part of that equation. In 2012, Delta stated that it reached an agreement with Southwest Airlines and Boeing Capital to lease or sublease 88 Boeing 717s previously operated by AirTran Airways. This gave Delta access to a sizable fleet without having to purchase an entirely new aircraft type.

Delta had intended to use the 717s to replace smaller regional jets. In its announcement, the airline said the jets would "primarily replace small 50-seat regional jets on a capacity-neutral basis." Then-CEO Richard Anderson also said the 717s would provide "a significant improvement in economic efficiency relative to the aircraft they are replacing." The arrangement gave Delta a way to bring smaller aircraft into its mainline operation while improving the economics of some existing routes.

The Airbus A220-100 offered another opportunity. Delta placed its initial order for 75 aircraft in 2016, when the jet was still known as the Bombardier C Series. During the ensuing trade dispute between Boeing and Bombardier, Boeing alleged that Bombardier had offered the aircraft to Delta for approximately $19.6 million (£14.61m) each, well below the reported production cost. That figure originated from Boeing, rather than a publicly listed contract price, but it illustrates the highly competitive pricing at the center of the dispute.

The two aircraft also perform different jobs within Delta's wide-ranging network. The 717 is primarily used on shorter, high-frequency routes, while the A220-100 is better suited to longer domestic services. According to The Points Guy, the A220-100 frequently operates routes of around 900 miles (1,450 km), including markets popular with business travelers that were previously served by the CRJ700, CRJ900, and Embraer E175.

Further, Delta equipped the aircraft with spacious 18.6-inch (47.24 cm)-wide economy seats, providing a wider seating arrangement than many competing narrowbodies. Between the terms of purchase and the different roles the aircraft fill, Delta has been able to make a relatively small mainline fleet work across a range of domestic routes.

How Brazil's most popular puddle jumper keeps Americans in the air.

Delta's strategy could look different as the airline continues retiring its Boeing 717 fleet. The aircraft has played an outsized role in Delta's domestic network for more than a decade, particularly on shorter routes where its capacity makes it a practical replacement for smaller regional jets. With the 717 gradually exiting stage left, Delta will need to decide how best to maintain its presence in those markets. The airline is not necessarily throwing in the towel on smaller mainline aircraft, however. Its A220-100, A220-300, and Airbus A319 provide other options for routes previously served by the 717.

Age is also becoming a factor in the 717's future. Delta's 2025 annual filing listed 80 Boeing 717s in its fleet at the end of the year, with an average age of 24.3 years. In June 2026, Air Data News indicated that Delta planned to retire six planes earlier than expected as they approached major maintenance inspections. The 717 is no longer in production, and its Rolls-Royce BR715 engines are unique to the aircraft. Keeping an aging fleet in service under those circumstances can become increasingly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

Replacing the 717s may not necessarily be a straightforward one-for-one swap. Although the A220-100 is newer and has greater range, its capacity and operating characteristics are different. Delta could use a combination of A220 variants and A319s, putting larger aircraft on some routes while reducing frequencies in markets that cannot support the additional seats. View From The Wing summarized the possible changes: "Replacing 717s would probably mean some larger A220-300s, some reassignment of comparable A220-100s and Airbus A319s, and fewer frequencies in some markets."

Delta's use of smaller mainline aircraft is likely to change as the 717 fleet leaves service, but there is still a place for jets below the capacity of its larger narrowbodies. The A220 family and A319 give the airline further options for serving destinations that may not need a larger aircraft, although they cannot replicate the 717's role on every route. How Delta deploys those aircraft will determine whether it can maintain the same level of flexibility across its domestic network.

The retirement of six aging Boeing 717s by Delta, nearly four years earlier than expected, may mark the beginning of a measured transition strategy.

Delta Air Lines' use of smaller mainline aircraft demonstrates how fleet planning involves more than simply matching passenger demand with aircraft capacity. Pilot scope clauses, favorable acquisition agreements, and the ability to serve markets with smaller jets have all played into the airline's distinctive approach. The Boeing 717 and Airbus A220-100 have allowed Delta to maintain flexibility across routes that may not require larger narrowbody planes.

However, as the 717 gradually makes its exit from the fleet, Delta's strategy is likely to evolve. The A220 family and A319 will continue to provide smaller-capacity options, although replacing the 717 will not always be straightforward. Ultimately, Delta's ability to balance aircraft economics, labor agreements, and passenger demand will shape its future domestic fleet strategy.

My husband and I have always dreamed of visiting London, but we knew we wanted to do it the right way: comfortable flights and a chic hotel stay, with room left in our budget for things like afternoon tea, souvenirs and even a day trip.

All of that can sometimes require some pretty deep pockets, which is why we spent the past year allocating our spending strategically, using my to earn points toward both our flights and our hotel stay.

But like anyone on a budget, we wanted to get the most bang for our “point.” So when American Express last offered a 30% transfer bonus to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers, I knew I had to jump on the opportunity and book our trip asap. The good news? Amex is offering this same transfer bonus to Virgin again, now through Nov. 30, 2026.

Here’s how I made the most of the transfer bonus, including the redemptions I made and how you can do the same with the current offer.

First, let’s break down how the bonus works:

The American Express Membership Rewards® program is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club for eligible U.S. cardmembers until Nov. 30, 2026. That means every 1,000 Membership Rewards points you transfer becomes 1,300 Virgin Points®. Terms apply. Note that Amex points must be transferred in multiples of 1,000, with a minimum of 1,000 points.

Now I’m no math whiz, but I do know that means 100,000 Membership Rewards points would convert to 130,000 Virgin Points, instead of the standard 1:1 ratio. That's one of the best transfer rates Amex offers.

Several Amex cards earn transferable Membership Rewards points, including:

Editor tip: If you’re new to transferring Membership Rewards, like I was, I highly recommend checking out our beginner-friendly guide that breaks down how to transfer Membership Rewards points to partners like Virgin step by step, along with any restrictions you need to be aware of.

The best part about Virgin as a transfer partner is its surprising breadth. You can redeem your points for flights on Virgin Atlantic, as well as stays at Virgin Hotels and cruise sailings with Virgin Voyages.

I had built up a solid balance of Membership Rewards points through a combination of the Gold Card's welcome offer and my everyday spending, but the limited-time window of that bonus meant I couldn't afford to think about it for too long.

I live in Central Florida, and luckily for me, Virgin Atlantic offers nonstop flights from Orlando

International Airport (MCO) to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR). However, Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop to LHR from airports across the U.S., including:

Personally, I’ve always been curious about Virgin’s premium economy cabin after hearing so many great things about it from my fellow TPG colleagues. So for our outbound flight, we booked premium economy, which comes with perks like extra legroom and an elevated meal service.

It cost me 35,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. With the 30% bonus, I only needed to transfer 54,000 Amex points for the two of us, which means I saved 16,000 Amex points on the outbound leg alone.

Note that taxes, fees and charges apply in addition to the points price for reward flights in all classes. These vary depending on factors such as your destination and travel dates, and the applicable amount is shown at the time of booking.

From check-in to landing, the premium economy cabin proved to be the perfect balance of value and comfort. Extra touches like a dedicated check-in desk, a glass of bubbly after boarding, upgraded dining and amenity kits made the experience feel so special. The wide leather seats with extra legroom meant we arrived in London well-rested and ready to explore. I could see why so many people rave about it; it was the perfect middle ground between budget-friendly and comfortable.

The real splurge was our return flight, which turned out to hardly be a splurge at all because I found a nonstop Upper Class flight home from LHR to MCO for just 29,000 Virgin Points per person, plus taxes and fees. Thanks to the bonus, I only needed to transfer 46,000 Amex points total for two people. That's 12,000 Membership Reward points saved on an already incredible redemption. Needless to say, I felt like I’d won the lottery.

I’ll be the first to tell you that it doesn’t get any better than Virgin’s Upper Class for R&R on a nine-hour flight across the Atlantic. The direct-aisle-access seats converted into lie-flat beds, and the amenity kits were well curated. Not to mention that the dining and inflight service made me feel like, well, royalty.

By the time we touched down in Orlando, I had slept through most of the flight, which is a rarity for me as a nervous flyer. We arrived home feeling restored rather than depleted.

Combined, our flights cost us 128,000 Virgin Points plus taxes and fees, which took 100,000 Amex points to cover. The transfer bonus saved my husband and me 28,000 Membership Rewards points across both flights, and we used them to redeem on Virgin Red for a rewards stay at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch.

Once I had committed to the Virgin Atlantic booking, staying at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch was a no-brainer with that 30% transfer bonus. And yes, when you transfer Membership Rewards points to the Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you can use them toward a stay at a Virgin Hotels property.

Editor tip: Once you’ve transferred your Membership Reward points to Virgin,  check out our easy-to-follow guide to booking Virgin Hotels with Virgin Points.

On our dates, the stay came out to about 60,000 Virgin Points per night. For our four-night stay, I was looking at 240,000 points in total, which felt like a lot to give up. With the 30% transfer bonus, though, I only needed to transfer 185,000 Membership Rewards points, which was much easier to wrap my head around.

When I booked the hotel, I had a feeling using my points would be well worth it, and from the moment we arrived at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch, my suspicions were confirmed. The hotel sits in trendy East London, far enough from the crowds and tourist traps, but close to the Old Street Tube station for easy access to activities and dining across the city. It’s also a convenient 10-minute walk from Liverpool Street Station, which has direct access to LHR.

The hotel has quintessential Virgin design, with red accents everywhere, from the lobby carpets to the Smeg fridges in the guest rooms. Beyond the rooms, the property has a rooftop pool for the warmer months and a retro hi-fi listening bar called Hidden Grooves, which serves creative cocktails that are perfect after a long day exploring London.

As for how it compares to cash pricing, a comparable room size runs around $450-$550 per night. Our four-night stay on Virgin Points was equivalent to saving roughly $2,000 in cash, which suddenly made the Amex transfer bonus feel like money in the bank.

With our flights and hotels covered by points, we had cash to spend on our most anticipated experiences in London. Here are a few of my favorite trip highlights:

My Membership Rewards transfer to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club covered nearly every big-ticket item on our London trip: flights in both directions, including a lie-flat Upper Class seat home, and four nights at Virgin Hotels London-Shoreditch. With the 30% transfer bonus stretching every point further, we were able to spend our cash on experiences, dining and souvenirs.

If you've been sitting on a stash of Membership Rewards points, this is one of the best ways to use them right now, and you don’t need to go to London. Virgin Atlantic also flies nonstop from the U.S. to Manchester and Edinburgh and connecting through Heathrow opens up destinations like Barbados, Cape Town, Dubai, Mumbai and the Maldives.

Your points aren't limited to flights, either. You can put them toward a stay at Virgin Hotels or even a Virgin Voyages cruise. Just keep in mind that the 30% transfer bonus, available to eligible U.S. cardmembers, ends Nov. 30, 2026, so whether you're dreaming of a lie-flat seat across the Atlantic or days in the sun at sea, now is the time to book your next trip.

#6116. Air Algerie Business Class Review: An Odd Avion Express Airbus A320 Wet Lease

For the next portion of my Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, I flew Air Algerie’s Airbus A320 business class on the one-hour flight from Algiers (ALG) to Tunis (TUN). Okay, Air Algerie doesn’t actually operate A320s, so this flight was operated by Lithuanian and Maltese charter operator Avion Express (which Air Algerie is really bad at disclosing during the booking process).

I mean, what can one really say about this flight, especially after coming off of Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, which was possibly the worst long haul business class I’ve ever flown? Truth be told, for a short haul flight this wasn’t terrible, but it also wasn’t good. It was just… whatever. As an aviation geek, I always do love a wet lease adventure!

As I explained in the last installment, I booked an attractive one-way business class cash fare on Air Algerie, even though it didn’t start or end where I actually wanted to go. 😉 I booked the following in business class for $1,171 in cash:

10/03 AH2701 Montreal to Algiers departing 4:10PM arriving 5:00AM (+1 day)10/04 AH4000 Algiers to Tunis departing 7:10AM arriving 8:30AM

So in the last installment I reviewed Air Algerie’s A330neo business class, and then this installment is my review of the connecting flight.

I’ve already reviewed the Air Algerie VIP Lounge Algiers, which gives strong furniture store vibes and is nothing remarkable, but is still much better than Air Algerie’s onboard experience.

My flight to Tunis was scheduled to depart at 7:10AM, and my boarding pass indicated that boarding would start at 5:40AM. Yes, 90 minutes before departure… for an Airbus A320. Not surprisingly, that was completely inaccurate. I get that airlines don’t want people to miss flights, but I do find it frustrating when airlines don’t actually tell you when you should realistically be at the gate.

Anyway, my flight was departing from gate nine, roughly a five-minute walk from the lounge. Algiers Airport is fairly pleasant — it feels sterile and there’s not much to it, but compared to some other airports in the region, it isn’t half bad. But of course let me remind everyone that nothing holds a candle to Cairo Airport (CAI), easily one of the world’s finest facilities. 😉

I showed up at the departure gate plenty early, but even by 6:10AM (30 minutes after the alleged boarding start time), there wasn’t actually anyone at the gate.

The crew showed up at around 6:20AM, and boarding actually started at 6:35AM. The boarding process was rather strange on a variety of levels.

For one, before boarding started, the gate agent and security staff walked onto the jet bridge and then lit a cigarette and smoked. Nice… real professional.

Second, when boarding did start, it was just a free for all, with no priority give to business class passengers.

Third, there were three separate passport and boarding pass checks on the jet bridge by airport police. So first the gate agent checked documents, then upon entering the jet bridge a security officer checked both, then 100 feet later another security officer did the same, and then at the door of the plane, another security officer checked. After all that hard work protecting us, they definitely deserve a cigarette!

At the forward door to the plane I was greeted by the crew, and then headed toward my seat. I was flying on an 18-year-old Avion Express Airbus A320 with the registration code 9H-AMJ. While Avion Express is a Lithuanian company, this plane was registered in Malta.

This A320 has seen quite some things, as it started its career in 2008 at Wizz Air Ukraine, then in 2015 it moved to the main Wizz Air fleet when the Ukrainian subsidiary shut down, and then in 2021 it was taken over by Avion Express. Since then, it has flown on a wet lease basis with carriers like Eurowings, British Airways, Viva, and more.

For those not familiar with the concept of wet leasing, this is when an airline leases out its plane to another airline, including the crews. So while it’s sold just like any other Air Algerie flight, and the catering is like any Air Algerie flight, the crew and planes are from Avion Express.

This Avion Express A320 had a total of 180 seats, spread across 30 rows in a 3-3 configuration. Unfortunately unlike most of Air Algerie’s own planes, this one didn’t have a dedicated business class cabin with different seats. Instead, the first three rows were designated as business class, and they just had economy seats with blocked middles. That means business class had the capacity for 12 passengers.

I assigned myself seat 3F, the window seat on the right side in the third (last) row. This was a pretty old school cabin, which is a double edged sword. On the plus side, this meant seats were well padded, which you don’t typically find nowadays, given the emphasis on slimline seats.

Legroom was okay when you consider these are really economy seats, so it could’ve been worse.

The seat had a standard tray table, which folded down from the seat in front.

Given how old school the cabin was, it definitely wasn’t in very good condition, though. I mean, just look at the liner inside the window, and how that was coming apart.

Also, given the age of the cabin, it was clear that nothing had really been updated — there were no power ports, there was no Wi-Fi, and there was no streaming entertainment. That’s of course not a huge issue for such a short flight, but I’m just trying to help people manage expectations here.

The overhead console was typical for an A320, and had individual air nozzles and reading lights.

The cabin stayed really empty — there were only two other commercial passengers, and then one pilot who seemed to be commuting to Tunisia, for whatever reason.

Boarding was really efficient, and wrapped up by 6:55AM, as the flight wasn’t very full. That was still 15 minutes before the scheduled departure time. Before departure, the crew came around with juice or water as pre-departure drinks. I opted for a water, and was also given a packaged refreshing towel.

Ironically enough, on this flight the safety demonstration was exclusively performed in English (compared to my previous Air Algerie flight, where it was in French and Arabic, but not in English).

At 7AM the main cabin door closed, and at 7:05AM we began our pushback (sorry for the quality of the pictures, as the windows were super dirty)…

On the taxi out, we saw another Avion Express A320, which looked identical to ours (we also had an all-white A320).

There were quite a few Air Algerie planes parked on the ramp, as very few seemed to actually be at gates. I’m not sure if Air Algerie’s aircraft utilization is just terrible, or what.

By 7:25AM we made it out to runway 23, and were immediately cleared for takeoff.

Our climb out was smooth, and I loved the views on departure… I wish I could’ve actually visited Algiers, but the visa situation is complicated (and after my review, I’m not sure they’d be happy to have me anyway). 😉

The seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff. At that point the crew closed the curtain between the cabin and galley, and got started with the service.

On this morning flight, breakfast was served. There was no choice, but I was served a hot dish with scrambled eggs, veggies, and some sort of meat. There was also a yogurt, a croissant, and a pastry, and additional bread rolls were offered (though I passed).

It sure seems like Air Algerie instructs Avion Express flight attendants to not deviate from their service protocol, which is to say that everything must simply be thrown on the tray, with zero effort put into presentation. 😉

So I couldn’t help but reorganize the tray a little bit, to make it look a little more presentable.

Drinks were also offered. I asked for a coffee, and it was a rather disgusting powdered coffee that I didn’t at all enjoy.

Before the descent, I checked out the lavatory, located at the front of the cabin. It was very basic and worn, though at least it wasn’t dirty.

Since this was a wet lease, the flight attendants onboard worked for Avion Express. I couldn’t actually figure out what country they were from (and they weren’t really friendly enough that I felt like being conversational). But anyway, they went through the motions, and weren’t rude, and they spoke a little bit of English (more than the Air Algerie crew on my previous flight).

There was also one Air Algerie flight attendant onboard, I guess to “oversee” the service, as is common with wet leases like this. In this case, he just plopped down in a business class seat and relaxed for most of the flight.

Around 30 minutes after takeoff, at roughly the halfway of the flight, the captain made an announcement, informing us we were at an altitude of 10,700 meters (35,000 feet), and that we’d be descending in around five minutes. Sure enough, we started our descent as planned, and the seatbelt sign was turned on 10 minutes after that.

The views on approach were gorgeous. Tunis is of course a coastal city on the Mediterranean Sea, so the views are tough to beat. I fondly remember my visit to Tunisia around a decade ago.

On our approach, we ended up flying out over the Mediterranean, and then circling back to land toward the south.

We ended up touching down on runway 19 at 8:25AM.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival gate, where we pulled in at 8:30AM next to an Etihad A321LR (probably the nicest plane that serves the airport).

From there I cleared transit security, and had an extended layover, before connecting to Marseille (MRS) in Tunisair economy (due to a downgrade from business class).

My Air Algerie flight operated by an Avion Express A320 was perfectly whatever. For an hour-long flight, I thought the meal was quite good. However, the Avion Express A320 wasn’t terribly inspiring in terms of its modernness, seating, amenities, or service. So yeah, I don’t really have strong feelings on this one, other than appreciating that the flight was at least on schedule.

What do you make of Air Algerie business class, operated by an Avion Express A320?

#6115. Global Airlines Liquidating: The Senseless A380 Dream Finally Dies

Over the past few years, I’ve extensively covered Global Airlines, the strange “airline startup” that had a single Airbus A380, with which it wanted to bring back the “golden age” of travel. The carrier’s A380 has been parked since the spring of 2025, and just several months ago, I covered how the company faced several winding up petitions. Well, there’s now an update, which seems long overdue…

Public records in the UK show that Global Airlines has finally been given winding up orders, which is the equivalent of liquidation. This is in response to a petition that was filed on May 29, 2026, and a court approved that order on November 4, 2026. This has only been added to public records today, as there seems to be a one week period between when these decisions are made, and when they’re published for the public.

This means that a government officer from the Insolvency Service will now become the liquidator, and take control of the company, investigate its affairs and the conduct of directors, and collect whatever assets still exist for creditors. This means that the directors no longer have control of the company.

What’s amazing about this entire story is that in the spring of 2025, the company actually operated two roundtrip flights to New York out of Europe, for reasons that most of us couldn’t really make sense of. For that matter, this was part of a wet lease agreement with Portuguese charter company Hi-Fly, given that Global Airlines lacked its own operating certificate.

James Asquith, founder of Global Airlines, gate crashes travel guru Simon Calder's interview with Mike Graham.@james_asquith: "Did you get a cupcake?"@Iromg | @SimonCalder pic.twitter.com/etMVj1TcPu

Shortly after the A380 operated those flights, it entered long term storage, as it needed to undergo heavy maintenance, which costs millions of dollars. The company’s founder, James Asquith, had insisted that the reason the plane was parked for so long was due to delays with being able to get heavy maintenance.

Just months ago, Asquith suggested that the airline would be flying to the Maldives before the end of 2026, despite no progress having been made on the heavy maintenance front.

A post shared by Robyn Asquith (@robynasquith)

Obviously on the surface, the whole Global Airlines thing sounds a bit odd. But let me simply say that the public knows only a tiny fraction of what was really going on here. That’s true both in terms of what Asquith was showing investors to get them onboard with the concept, and also what he claimed the goals for the company were.

My skepticism with this concept wasn’t because I don’t like to see other people succeed, or because I’m against innovation, or anything like that. Instead, it’s because things aren’t always what they seem, and when you’re raising millions of dollars of other people’s money and selling them a dream, there has to be some chance of that actually becoming a reality.

Keep in mind that in 2025, Asquith appeared on The Times’ 40 richest people under 40 list, which claimed he had a net worth of £183 million, making him richer than Adele. Right.

I’d encourage those who just went along with Asquith to be a little introspective here. For example, when you have publications like SimpleFlying that publish things about Global Airlines without even an ounce of skepticism, and then you have people like Captain Chris who latch on to people like Asquith as if they’re Richard Branson (which he literally compared him to, while pointing out that he was proving the doubters wrong), that’s a problem.

A post shared by Captain Chris | Aviation Life (@captainchris)

Many people lost many millions of dollars on this venture. Now, I’d also encourage them to perhaps be a bit more careful next time. And if you just want to make a donation to someone with no expectation of any return, I’m also happy to wire you my bank account details. 😉

It’s the end of the road (or runway) for Global Airlines, as the A380 “airline” has had its winding up petition approved, meaning the company will now be liquidated. It was only a matter of time before this was going to happen, so I don’t think anyone will be surprised. Hopefully one day the entire story can come to light…

What do you make of Global Airlines liquidating?

American Airlines is planning to add more flights from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), as part of a “gradual build” at its West Coast hub.

The Fort Worth-based carrier said it's about to add more LAX service to its schedule, with a focus on places executives describe as “important markets.”

It’s not clear whether that means entirely new routes or more frequent service on existing ones.

But either way, it comes after a long stretch where American seemed to focus far more of its attention on other parts of the country.

After the pandemic, the airline doubled down on its Sun Belt hubs, fortifying its strongholds in Dallas, Charlotte and Miami.

More recently, American reignited a longstanding Chicago turf war with United Airlines when it rapidly reinstated flying at O’Hare International Airport (ORD).

It looks like LAX will be its next project.

“We’re going to grow," American chief commercial officer Nat Pieper said, speaking this week at an industry conference. "We’re going to tailor a schedule to the local market."

American has a smaller presence today in Southern California than it did several years ago.

This year, the carrier will operate about 32% fewer flights than it did in 2019, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

That’s a significant drop-off at LAX, which is one of the nation’s most competitive airports — and the only where each of the “big three” legacy carriers operates a hub.

By contrast, top L.A. rival Delta Air Lines has solidified its place as the airport’s top carrier, and plans operate its largest-ever schedule there next year.

United Airlines has also signaled it has future growth aspirations at LAX.

Speaking earlier this year, United’s top network planner, Patrick Quayle, lamented the fact that the airport is United’s only hub where there’s another airline with a larger presence.

“I don’t like being No. 2,” Quayle said during a company event at LAX in March. “And so I will, today, put Delta on notice here in L.A. — we will be No. 1, as well.”'

Pieper said the carrier needs to start by catering more to local Los Angeles customers — not just using the airport as a hub to route connecting traffic.

Doing that, he acknowledged, will likely require AA to offer a longer list of unique destinations.

Today, for instance, the carrier only serves four long-haul cities from LAX: London, Tokyo, Sydney and Auckland.

“People don’t only want to fly domestically. They want to go to Latin America. They want to go to Europe. They want to go to Asia,” Pieper said on stage this week at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York. “We need to be able to serve that with our own airplanes.”

United is clearly following that formula. The carrier already serves more than a half-dozen transpacific destinations from Southern California — and will expand next year with a new route to Osaka.

Delta, for its part, is also pointing to LAX as a linchpin of its Pacific growth aspirations, having launched nonstops to Hong Kong and Melbourne within the past year. New flights to Manila will begin in 2027.

Delta’s Los Angeles growth is also thanks, in part, to massive infrastructure investments the carrier has made at the hub which, among other things, is the only airport that's home to two Delta One Lounges.

American’s LAX digs, meanwhile, are still a construction zone.

The carrier had to consolidate its presence at the airport last year to make way for a rebuild of the airport's Terminal 5.

American will grow at a "gradual" pace, Pieper said, until its LAX facilities are "ready to roll." That's expected to happen in late 2028, at which point the carrier will have access to 30 gates.

“Our facility will be as good as anybody’s,” he said.

That, along with more flights — plus connectivity to American's Pacific partners like Qantas and Japan Airlines— have the airline more bullish about its hub that's grabbed far fewer headlines in recent years.

“You combine all those things together,” Pieper added, “I think we’re going to have a compelling offering there.”

#6113. Alaska Adds Service to Four New U.S. Cities

Alaska Airlines will bring four new destinations into its domestic network next summer.

The carrier announced Thursday that it will serve Charlotte, North Carolina, Jacksonville, Florida, Norfolk, Virginia, and Des Moines, Iowa, from Seattle. Three of the four cities – Jacksonville, Norfolk, and Des Moines – have never had nonstop flights to Seattle.

Currently, only American Airlines connects Charlotte and Seattle.

The Des Moines service will also mark Alaska’s debut in Iowa.

All four connections will operate daily, year-round. Flights to Charlotte and Norfolk will begin June 10, 2027, with Jacksonville and Des Moines launching later that month, on June 24.

Alaska will also offer seasonal service from Seattle to Guadalajara, Mexico, from March 18, 2027, to Aug. 9. Flights will operate three times weekly, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

#6112. Emirates Is Stripping Its Airbus A380s To 'Bare Metal' While Qantas Retires Its Superjumbos 4 Years Early

Wikimedia Commons, Markus Mainka | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

While much of the airline industry is moving away from the Airbus A380, Emirates is taking a very different approach, stripping its Superjumbos back to bare metal and investing billions in rebuilding their interiors. The strategy reflects the aircraft's continued value on high-demand international routes, particularly at airports where limited takeoff and landing slots make replacing its enormous passenger capacity difficult.

Meanwhile, Australia's Qantas is bringing forward the retirement of its A380 fleet, turning instead toward newer, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft. The contrasting strategies highlight why the world's largest passenger aircraft remains valuable to some airlines while becoming increasingly difficult for others to justify.

The Airbus A380, widely known as the Superjumbo, is an incredibly important aircraft for Emirates and has been part of its fleet since August 1, 2008, when it received its first aircraft of the type, registered as A6-EDF. According to Mogaz International, this elderly A380 is 20.5 years old and had logged 45,892 flight hours across 7,539 flights by May 31, 2026.

However, the average age of Emirates' A380 fleet is approximately 11.6 years. Airbus states that its "A380-800 offers several payload capabilities ranging from 400 passengers in a very comfortable multiclass configuration, up to 853 passengers in an all economy class configuration." Actual seating arrangements vary from airline to airline, depending on their individual requirements.

For Emirates, the A380 is a key connector and revenue generator due to its ability to concentrate large numbers of passengers within a single fuselage on high-demand routes and deliver them to key destinations. This capability is particularly important when serving airports with restricted slot availability, such as London Heathrow Airport (LHR), Amsterdam Airport Schiphol (AMS), and Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD). Without the aircraft's substantial passenger capacity, the airline would need to operate more flights to transport the same number of passengers, placing additional pressure on airports where takeoff and landing slots are already limited.

Regarding the highly lucrative nature of the Superjumbo, Aviation Week quoted Sir Tim Clark, President of Emirates, as saying, “Last year, the A380 was the most profitable asset in our fleet, and that was the most profitable year we’ve ever had,” he said. “It tells you how successful, how popular that airplane is.” According to Emirates' financial data released last May, the company recorded an eye-watering profit during its 2025–26 financial year, amounting to $6.6 billion.

Due to these factors, Emirates will not be retiring the iconic aircraft in favor of smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft, as Qantas is doing. Rather, Emirates reportedly plans to maintain its A380 fleet until 2041, as no other aircraft currently in production offers anywhere near comparable passenger capacity. To keep the vast majority of its massive fleet of 116 Superjumbos looking their best and maximize passenger comfort, Emirates embarked on an ambitious and extensive retrofit program, the likes of which the company had never undertaken before.

Nine new SFO connections expand Pacific reach and bolster year round East Coast feeds while adding seasonal Midwest and Florida service.

As noted in the previous section, the A380 is a massive moneymaker for Emirates. Keeping these aircraft looking and feeling their best for the passengers who travel aboard them is a major priority, particularly as the average age of the fleet is nearly 12 years.

In an effort to keep these aircraft in top shape, Emirates is roughly halfway through one of the most ambitious retrofit programs in commercial aviation, which, according to the company, is worth $5 billion (£3.75 billion). Once completed, the airline will have completely retrofitted the interiors of 219 aircraft, including 110 A380s and 109 Boeing 777s.

The project began in November 2022, with the first A380 undergoing its retrofit at the Emirates Engineering hangars in Dubai. Since then, Emirates has stated that 47 of its Superjumbos and 53 Boeing 777s have received a complete nose-to-tail refresh, with the company averaging work on 28 aircraft per year. Completing the first 100 aircraft was an incredible milestone in this ambitious program.

The detailed work has involved 400 engineers and technicians who have collectively invested 4.4 million man-hours in transforming these aircraft. Incredibly, each revamped A380 requires more than 4,000 new parts, while the 777 requires more than 2,500, according to Emirates. The completed A380s feature a Premium Economy section for the first time, with a 2-3-2 configuration, full leg and footrests, six-way adjustable headrests, side cocktail tables, and a 13.3-inch personal screen. Additionally, Emirates is installing Starlink WiFi across 232 aircraft.

Ahead of the A380's planned fleet retirement in 2041, Aviation Week reports that Emirates expects to begin receiving the Boeing 777-9 in 2027, although the aircraft will accommodate approximately 150 fewer passengers. However, this transition towards twin-engine aircraft is becoming a necessity, as A380 production has ended and the industry has increasingly shifted towards lighter, more fuel-efficient passenger aircraft.

The only way for engineers to expand the A340-300 without a cleansheet aircraft was to stretch it into the world's longest passenger jet at the time.

Qantas, an international airline based in Australia, operates seven aircraft types, and the A380 has been an important component of the company's ability to transport passengers to high-demand markets, such as Western Europe, Asia, and the US. While these aircraft have performed admirably, Qantas has officially stated that it will begin the process of retiring its 10 A380s as early as 2028. However, it remains unclear exactly how long it will take to completely phase them out, although they are expected to remain in service until at least FY2032.

The company made the decision to retire its fleet of Superjumbos due to two primary factors: fuel expenses and the arrival of new, long-haul-capable aircraft. Regarding the former, strong travel demand has not been enough to offset the impact of jet fuel prices, which have been affected by instability in the Middle East. AeroTime reports that "Qantas estimated that the overall impact of the fuel crisis could have been as high as AU$610 million (US$438 million), although claims to have managed to reduce this figure to AU$420 million (US$301 million) thanks to mitigation measures."

Aside from the expenses associated with operating older four-engine aircraft, Qantas will be receiving new-build aircraft with improved fuel efficiency. These new aircraft will be able to take over some of the A380s' routes and capacity, giving the company greater confidence in its decision to begin retiring the aircraft earlier than originally planned. Regarding the arrival of these new aircraft, at the end of August, Qantas Group CEO Vanessa Hudson announced:

“Our fleet renewal continued at pace, with 17 new aircraft arriving during the year and up to 31 more to arrive in the year ahead, with the majority joining Qantas . . . With our first Project Sunrise A350-1000ULR to arrive in April, and more A350s and 787s on the way, it’s a new era for Qantas’ international fleet with these next generation aircraft set to transform the way our customers travel. This means we can commence the retirement of our A380 fleet from 2028."

Regarding long-distance travel, the Airbus A350-1000 and Boeing 787 Dreamliner will form the backbone of the company's international flight strategy. While neither aircraft can fully replace the sheer passenger capacity of the A380, both can still carry substantial numbers of passengers over long distances.

Committed to these aircraft, in 2023, Qantas placed a multi-billion-dollar firm order for 12 Airbus A350s and 12 Boeing 787s, with deliveries expected to begin in FY2027. The order also included "access to up to 500 million litres of sustainable aviation fuel; enhancing pathway to reach the Group’s 2030 emissions targets."

Airbus states that its A350-1000 has a maximum seating capacity of 480 passengers and can comfortably accommodate between 375 and 400 passengers in a standard three-class configuration. It also offers a 40% increase in space within the premium seating category. Regarding fuel consumption, the A350-1000's Rolls-Royce Trent XWB-97 engines provide a 25% reduction in fuel burn and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation aircraft. Qantas expects to begin receiving these aircraft by FY2028.

Regarding the Boeing purchases, Qantas will receive four 787-9s and eight 787-10s. According to Boeing, the former can accommodate between 250 and 325 passengers, while the latter can carry between 300 and 375. In line with Qantas' commitment to fuel efficiency, the new Boeing 787s will be powered by General Electric GEnx engines. These aircraft offer improved fuel efficiency, with the 787-9 delivering a 20% reduction in fuel consumption and the 787-10 offering a 25% improvement, alongside a 60% reduction in noise.

They're all from Dallas, Charlotte, and Chicago, with some intriguing additions. Find them here!

The contrasting strategies of Emirates and Qantas demonstrate that the Airbus A380 still has a place in commercial aviation, although its long-term viability depends heavily on an airline's operating model. Emirates continues to see substantial value in its capacity, investing billions to keep its Superjumbos flying for years to come.

Meanwhile, Qantas is transitioning toward more efficient twin-engine aircraft, reflecting an industry-wide shift. Although the A380's era is gradually coming to an end, Emirates shows that the Superjumbo still has plenty of life left.

#6111. Wild: Stolen Delta Bag Tracked From JFK To DC Bus Stop, Thief Nabbed By Police

It’s not totally uncommon to see bags stolen (or perhaps in some cases accidentally taken) from baggage claim belts at airports. In the past that was basically a lost cause, but thanks to things like AirTags, they can often be tracked.

Here’s an absolutely wild version of such a story, where someone in the miles & points community had their bag stolen, and then someone else tracked it down… hundreds of miles away, and with the help of police!

JT Genter is Editor-in-Chief of AwardWallet and a member of the miles & points community who travels full time. On Tuesday, November 10, 2026, he took to social media to share that his checked bag had been stolen off the Delta baggage claim belt at New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) Terminal 4.

He filed a Delta missing bag claim and police report, and pointed out how “so many irreplaceable memories” were lost in the bag, including all his clothing, medicines, all his toiletries, etc. And he claimed that Delta agents didn’t seem like they gave a you-know-what.

God. So many irreplaceable memories lost in that bag. All of my clothing. Medicines. All my toiletries. Literally so many of my worldly possessions stolen right off Delta's baggage claim belt.And @Delta agents couldn't give less of a shit. Acted like it must happen all the time

That’s obviously incredibly frustrating, though this is a story that had a happy ending less than 24 hours later. JT did have a tracker in his bag, so could keep an eye on the movements of the bag, but he just didn’t say so initially. Apparently the person had pretty quickly taken Amtrak down to DC.

But this is where the story gets truly wild. Jamie Larounis, an Upgraded Points contributor and another member of the miles & points community, coordinated with JT to help. Let me just share Jamie’s version of events:

This might be a story for the history books. Man steals backpack in NY. He takes Amtrak train to DC. I decided to play detective and found the thief with the backpack sitting at a bus station. He boards a bus, but luckily I caught the bus number. I found 2 extremely helpful cops to assist and they found the thief a few blocks away and they nabbed him. They asked me to get in the cop car to ID the thief, and we headed to the police station to retrieve the items.

Gotta say, I didn’t have being in a Metropolitan Police cop car on my bingo card today, but with a little perseverance we got this thief locked up!!! Huzzah!

And by "we", I mean @TheForwardCabin! Jamie used the Tile tracking location to get a visual on our bag and found DC police who were ready to protect and serve.What an incredible end to this story!https://t.co/LvFthwBMqt

When asked what was missing from the bag after it was recovered, JT shared that the guy ditched some clothing, supplies, and custom medical equipment, plus “irreplaceable memories.”

When you consider the volume of bags that are checked, obviously a fair number get lost, stolen, etc. In theory, stealing a bag from a baggage claim belt is really easy — you just take it and leave. However:

Publicly, we of course don’t know anything about this thief. Are we to assume that he wasn’t actually flying, and was just there to steal a bag? And of all the bags he could steal, why did that black backpack catch his eye? And was he planning to travel to DC anyway, and if so, was that the plan all along, or was that just the “escape” plan with the stolen goods?

I recognize that people stealing bags off of baggage claim belts probably aren’t the most sophisticated criminals, but in this day and age, you’d think that checking every pocket of the bag for a tracker would be a best practice, given how common they are.

A traveler had their backpack stolen off of a baggage claim belt at JFK after a Delta flight. Fortunately he had a tracker, which showed that the bag was taken down to DC on Amtrak. After posting about this online, someone else coordinated and played detective, and found someone with the bag at a bus station in DC, and with the help of police, it was recovered.

It’s nice when a story like this has a positive ending, and it’s also a good reminder to put some sort of a tracking device in your bag, for situations where your bag gets lost or stolen.

What do you make of this checked bag recovery mission?

#6110. United Clears Halfway Mark on Starlink Rollout

Starlink satellite internet service is now available on more than half of United Airlines’ daily flights, the carrier announced Thursday.

The airline said it accelerated Starlink installations ahead of the Thanksgiving travel period. It expects to fly an average of 500,000 people per day between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

Customers can use United’s Starlink Wi-Fi tracker to check whether their upcoming flight is equipped with the service up to three days before their departure.

United selected Starlink as its onboard wireless internet provider in 2024. It first installed the technology on its regional jets and is now working on its long-haul widebody fleet.

Starlink Wi-Fi is free for MileagePlus members.

United expects to have Starlink on nearly 64% of daily flights by the end of the year. Installations should be complete by the end of 2027, officials said.

We didn’t have to wait long to find out how American Airlines is shaking up its route map in Los Angeles.

Just minutes after TPG reported the carrier was planning a route announcement at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), American revealed its plans. And there’s both good and bad news for AA flyers in Southern California.

Most notably, the carrier plans to bolster its service on four routes to major U.S. cities.

It’s also bringing back a route to Colorado that it hasn’t offered in a half-decade.

Plus, American will end service to two cities from LAX.

All told, Friday's changes cover nine routes from its West Coast hub. Here's what to know.

American confirmed it’s bringing back service to Grand Junction, Colorado, for the first time in five years.

It will operate seasonal regional service from LAX between May 27 and Aug. 9 with a Bombardier CRJ700.

American last operated LAX service to Grand Junction Regional Airport (GJT) in 2021, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

In 2027, this route will effectively replace American’s flight to Colorado’s Aspen/Pitkin County Airport (ASE), which will be closed next summer for construction.

American will fly its LAX-GJT route with one of its smaller CRJ-700 aircraft.

Elsewhere, American will turn to two routes it’s previously offered seasonally — and sporadically —from LAX into more regular service:

Both routes will operate with an Embraer 175 regional jet.

Starting next spring, American will also add extra daily flights from LAX to several major U.S. cities.

Denver, Las Vegas and Seattle will all get additional frequencies. Plus, American will double its daily service on one transcontinental route — from LA to Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

Starting in May, American will offer twice-daily Dulles service. That’ll make the IAD-LAX routes a stronger complement to AA’s cross-country Los Angeles service from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA).

American will cut ties with its LAX route to Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) effective Feb. 11.

That same day, it will also end service to Des Moines, Iowa.

This network revamp in LA comes a day after American executives said the carrier was rethinking the routes it offers at its Southern California hub.

American’s LAX service today sharply lags the flight offerings it had at the airport in 2019.

Speaking Thursday, American’s chief commercial officer, Nat Pieper, said the airline would aim to offer more flights from LAX to major U.S. cities in a push to win more L.A.-based flyers.

"We’re going to grow and we’re going to invest in the local market,” he said, speaking Thursday at the Skift Aviation Forum in New York.

That expansion, Pieper noted, will be gradual — and ramp up — as infrastructure work at LAX progresses over the next two years.

#6108. Bitter Christmas: A Bah Humbug to Moviemaking

Almodóvar’s loss of creativity and camp is cause for alarm.

Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas explores his own recent creative crisis. Using a prismatic structure, Almodóvar tells three stories that reflect one another with diminishing returns. These interwoven tales never blend due to the blockage suffered by gay male Spanish filmmaker Raul (Leonardo Sbaraglia, styled with a storm of gray-white hair to resemble Almodóvar himself). Viewers must do a meta reading about the nature and purpose of filmmaking and artistic expression.

Almodóvar makes the mistake of introducing Raul’s imaginary stories before revealing their real-life source. As Bitter Christmas becomes more and more convoluted and uninvolving, it undeniably reflects a peculiar Millennial crisis: the internalized post-Covid repression that has paralyzed many filmmakers. Once the most exciting filmmaker of the late 1980s, Almodóvar now suffers the same malaise that has also befallen comparable colleagues Martin Scorsese and Steven Spielberg. You don’t have to be a cinephile to realize that most contemporary filmmakers are bereft of fresh ideas and genuine inspiration.

Before getting to that core Raul/Almodóvar narrative, Bitter Christmas first presents stories in which a female filmmaker Elsa (Bárbara Lennie) imagines the drama of a woman, Patrizia (Victoria Luengo), who feels her same maladies and longs to escape an unhappy marriage, and then another woman, Natalia (Milena Smit), who is deep in mourning. This narrative contraption is the worst example of a gay male’s feminine empathy that Almodóvar has ever contrived. Unlike Law of Desire and Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown, this film lacks the camp buoyancy that made Almodóvar a comic hybrid of Jean Cocteau and Luis Buñuel, putting him at the vanguard of the world’s evolving sexual sophistication.

Now foregrounding his identification with female experience, Almodóvar seems to cater to political correctness rather than flout it. That a once-major pop artist can no longer make irresistible movies but instead succumbs to patronizing political trends is a cause for alarm more significant than any particular misbegotten film.

In one subplot, Raul is told, “You can lie in your life but not in your fiction,” referring to how he mistreats his partner Santi (Quim Gutiérrez) while also exploiting his assistant Mónica (Aitana Sánchez-Gijón) as fodder for his newest script.

This contorted set-up suggests that Almodóvar feels pressure to join the global progressivism that a former bad boy of the Spanish underground is now obliged to endorse. That’s why the ultra-bourgeois Bitter Christmas lacks comedy and eroticism. Raul’s sex life is transferred to the shallow, quasi-porn of Elsa’s relationship with boytoy Bonifacio (Patrick Criado), a firefighter and part-time stripper (probably an homage to the superior João Pedro Rodrigues satire Will-O’-the-Wisp.

Almodóvar has lost audacity. Sadness pervades the movie. Its title comes from “Amarga Navidad” (“Bitter Christmas”), a ranchera (folk torch song) performed by Chavela Vargas. But this is the least impassioned film Almodóvar has made; its emotions are distanced by artifice — in imagination, storytelling, and performance. The projection of Raul/Almodóvar’s true feelings into fakery distances real life so much that the melodrama is drab. It’s not fabulous or funny (despite ornamental design and another urgent Alberto Iglesias score), but arid like Lanzarote, the black-sand volcanic island where make-believe characters Elsa and Victoria retreat into a dull version of Ingmar Bergman’s Persona — another go at Almodóvar’s insipid The Room Next Door. None of these meta-antics result in moral summation like Fellini’s masterpieces La Dolce Vita and Otto e mezzo.

Although Almodóvar avoids obvious political pronouncement like those that ruined Killers of the Flower Moon, West Side Story, and Disclosure Day, the twisted autobiographical aspects of Bitter Christmas still indicate that he suffers a similar personal liberal panic. (Unlike Spielberg and Scorsese, Almodóvar has made foolish partisan comments on American politics.) Almodóvar can’t escape the private anxiety that Scorsese and Spielberg experience along with the rest of us. Almodóvar’s inability to disentangle primal emotional need from political confusion is evident on screen in Bitter Christmas and ultimately unsatisfying.

Armond White is National Review’s culture critic and the author of New Position: The Prince Chronicles and Make Spielberg Great Again: The Steven Spielberg Chronicles.

The Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ is Chase’s premium business card. While the card has a steep annual fee, it also has strong perks, and for many people, will prove to be more than worthwhile.

We’re currently seeing a highest-ever Sapphire Reserve Business bonus, which matches the best bonus we’ve seen on this card. I’d like to recap the details of the offer, including talking about eligibility, and why the card could be worth it. While this is a limited time welcome offer, the end date hasn’t been published.

Link: Learn more about the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠

The Chase Sapphire Reserve Business currently has a limited time highest-ever welcome offer of 200,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards after spending $30,000 within the first six months.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Chase Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each. That means to me, the welcome bonus on this card is worth $3,400, which is incredible, among the best welcome offers out there. Admittedly the spending requirement is big (you need to average $5,000 per month in spending over six months), but so is the bonus.

For context on the Sapphire Reserve Business bonus history, when the card launched in 2025, we saw the same offer that’s currently available, for 200,000 points. Then in early 2026 we saw an offer for 150,000 points, before the offer for 200,000 points returned. Initially the offer for 200,000 points was supposed to end in September 2026, but it was extended, though we don’t know the official end date.

When it comes to applying for the Chase Sapphire Reserve Business, eligibility is unrelated to that of any other Chase Sapphire or Chase Ink card. That means if you’re eligible for business credit cards, you should be eligible for the welcome offer on this card, making this offer pretty widely available.

Keep in mind the general rules of applying for Chase cards, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months (though select business cards don’t count toward that total).

If you’re trying to understand general Chase business card restrictions, the Chase Ink cards probably give you the best sense of what you can expect in terms of eligibility. You don’t need a corporation to apply for the Sapphire Reserve Business, as a sole proprietorship would qualify as well. So even a side gig (like freelancing or having a rental property) would potentially qualify you for the card.

There’s not a specific credit score you need to get approved for the Sapphire Reserve Business, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that goes into deciding on approvals.

#6106. ‘Somebody Hit Us’: UPS Boeing 767 Collides With Copa 737 In Miami After Taxiing Too Far

A UPS Airlines Boeing 767 freighter and a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 collided while taxiing at Miami International Airport (MIA) on Saturday night. According to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the wingtip of the Copa passenger jet struck the nose of the 767 as the cargo aircraft taxied for departure.

Air traffic control (ATC) had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the 737, and one of its pilots acknowledged the mistake over the radio moments after the collision, saying, "We went too far." The FAA has opened an investigation into the collision, which happened a day after a rare nationwide ground stop brought US air travel to a halt.

The collision occurred at approximately 9:15 PM local time at the intersection of two taxiways. Copa Airlines flight 427, operated by a Boeing 737-800, had just arrived from Tocumen International Airport (PTY) in Panama City, while UPS flight 358 was taxiing for departure en route to El Dorado International Airport (BOG) in Bogotá.

As the Copa jet taxied toward its gate, controllers instructed the UPS crew to give way and let the 737 pass before continuing toward the runway. However, the 767 continued too far and moved into the Copa aircraft's path. The 737's left wingtip then struck the nose of the freighter as it passed, bringing both aircraft to a stop on the taxiway.

Audio from ATC.com captured the radio exchange during the collision. After the Copa crew reported, "Somebody hit us," the controller reminded UPS 358 that it was "supposed to give way" to the 737. The following exchange occurred immediately after the taxiway collision:

"Controller: "UPS 358, did you hit that aircraft?"

UPS 358: "Yeah, we went too far and then he... he clipped us with the wing."

After instructing the Copa crew to hold position and confirming that fire trucks were on their way, the controller heard from the 737's pilot, who reported, "It seems that we are missing the left wingtip." Authorities later treated two people at the scene for minor injuries, but neither required transport to hospital.

The FAA has confirmed that controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, meaning the 767 was supposed to wait until the 737 had passed. In a statement, the agency said:

"The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 while the airplanes were taxiing."

UPS added in a statement that it was committed to working with authorities to determine what happened, adding that its crew was safe. The extent of the damage to either aircraft has not yet been officially confirmed, although images posted on social media reveal significant damage to the 767's nose.

The winglets depict the upward-curling of bird features to gain efficiency.

There is a suggestion that a runway change may have added to the UPS crew's workload shortly before the collision. During the radio exchange, one of the pilots told the controller that they were in the middle of a checklist for a runway change. This can require pilots to update the flight management computer, a task that can be demanding while an aircraft is already taxiing.

However, pilots are expected to maintain situational awareness and follow instructions during checks. The FAA's taxiing guidance recommends keeping cockpit workload to a minimum and ensuring at least one pilot remains focused outside the aircraft.

The Miami incident is not an isolated case, with several similar collisions involving commercial aircraft reported at major international airports over the past year. Only last month, a Delta Air Lines Airbus A350-900 struck the horizontal stabilizer of an Air Canada Boeing 777-200LR while taxiing at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). The Air Canada aircraft was being towed to its gate when the Delta jet's left wingtip became lodged in its tail.

#6105. American Airlines Concierge Key: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. In this post, I’d like to take a close look at this elite status, and talk about what it is, how you can earn it, what the benefits are, etc. The truth is that very little is officially published about this, so we mostly have to go off of data points.

The reality is that these invitation-only elite tiers are kind of genius from the perspective of airlines. That’s because a not-insignificant portion of the frequent flyer community finds this status to be rather “sexy,” and will go out of their way to earn it. Since the qualification requirements aren’t published, it keeps people on the hamster wheel, booking as many expensive tickets as possible.

On the most basic level, Concierge Key is American’s invitation-only elite status level. There’s no published criteria to earn it, and it has to be renewed every program year, so you can earn it one year and lose it the next.

Going back many years, Concierge Key was completely separate from the AAdvantage program, but that’s no longer the case. Nowadays Concierge Key is a formal part of the AAdvantage program, and it’s a tier above Executive Platinum status (American’s highest elite tier with published qualification criteria).

I think it’s also worth mentioning that Concierge Key is perhaps the most well-known invitation-only elite status in the industry, as it was a major theme of the popular 2009 movie “Up In The Air,” starring George Clooney. Ugh, I can’t believe that was over 15 years ago.

The criteria to earn Concierge Key is not published, but generally there are a few ways to earn it.

One way is to spend a ton on American Airlines travel. We’re talking $50,000+ of spending per year. That’s not to say that spending $50,001 will get you Concierge Key status, but rather that if you spend less than that, don’t assume you have any real chance of being invited. As a matter of fact, nowadays you might need to spend significantly more than that. So you absolutely can earn Concierge Key purely through your own travel, and that’s probably the most common way it’s earned.

We don’t fully know what American looks for in this regard, though. Does the airline care purely about the dollar amount you spend, the typical fare classes you fly in (consistently full fare first class, for example), or something else? There are also some indications that the qualification criteria vary based on markets, so you have a better chance of earning it if you’re not living in a major hub city of American.

In other words, on some level it’s competitive, and you’re ranked against other travelers in similar markets. Expect that it takes more effort to earn Concierge Key if you primarily fly out of Charlotte (CLT), Dallas (DFW), or Miami (MIA), rather than out of Atlanta (ATL), Seattle (SEA), or Tampa (TPA).

Keep in mind that nowadays American Airlines elite status is based on the Loyalty Points program, so you can even earn elite status through credit card spending. So, does non-flying activity similarly count toward Concierge Key status? The reports I’ve seen suggest that it does, but you need to engage with the program a lot. For example, I’ve heard of people earning Concierge Key through credit card spending, but we’re talking about many hundreds of thousands of dollars in spending, if not over a million dollars.

You can also earn Concierge Key through the influence you have over others’ travel. Sometimes American Airlines will give Concierge Key nominations as part of a big corporate contract, or to key travel planners who have influence over a lot of others’ travel.

American Airlines is even known to comp Concierge Key to some “influencers.” For example, going back several years, YouTuber Casey Neistat was comped Concierge Key status and was really unhappy when it was taken away.

For avoidance of doubt, I’ve never been offered Concierge Key status, and I’m totally fine with that. 😉

Just for context on how these requirements compare to Executive Platinum, that requires 200,000 Loyalty Points per year. All AAdvantage members earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on credit cards, and Executive Platinum members earn 11x Loyalty Points per dollar spent on flights. So Executive Platinum requires $200,000 in credit card spending or around $18,200 in spending on flights.

American Concierge Key has quite a few published benefits, but some would argue the biggest benefit of the status is better “soft” treatment in the event of irregular operations.

The first thing worth understanding is that Concierge Key automatically comes with all Executive Platinum benefits. This includes everything from oneworld Emerald status, to space available first class upgrades, to complimentary Main Cabin Extra seating, to 120% bonus miles on flights, to three free checked bags, to a free drink & snack in economy, to priority services, to same day flight changes & standby.

This also includes access to the Loyalty Point Rewards program, allowing members to select additional perks, ranging from systemwide upgrades to bonus miles. Beyond that, benefits of American Concierge Key include the following:

Assistance during irregular operations is probably both potentially the most valuable perk, and also the most inconsistent one. On a good day, Concierge Key members may get proactive rebookings when flights are canceled and delayed.

American even has a fleet of cars at hubs for Concierge Key tarmac transfers, so during a short connection you may be picked up planeside and driven to your connecting flight. At the same time, there are also instances where you’ll likely be disappointed, because Concierge Key agents aren’t going to deliver 100% of the time.

If you’re looking to at least get Concierge Key levels of airport support with a particular trip, keep in mind that American offers Five Star Service, which is a paid program for more attentive service at the airport.

In the interest of being thorough, let me also mention some perks that Concierge Key used to offer, but no longer does:

American Airlines understandably hasn’t revealed how many Concierge Key members there are, so the best we can do is speculate. If I had to guess, I’d say there are somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 Concierge Key members. To be more exact, my assumption is that the number is roughly in the middle of that range.

In 2019 there was a clue — American worked with a company to send out chocolate to Concierge Key members, and the company posted that 11,300 packages had been prepared. Now, not all Concierge Key members received this chocolate, suggesting to me that there are more members than that.

If you’re curious how other elite ranks compare, I’d guess the number of Executive Platinum members is maybe 4-5x as high as the number of Concierge Key members. Again, that’s purely speculation on my part, and with the Loyalty Points system nowadays, the number may be even higher than that.

It’s hard to say whether something like Concierge Key is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Concierge Key varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Flagship Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal — you’ll get to board first, but there’s not necessarily all that much more to it.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including Delta 360 and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, though, I’d say that Concierge Key is probably the strongest of the tiers, in terms of the number of perks, including additional lounge access to the carrier’s most premium lounges. A couple of thoughts, though:

Concierge Key is American Airlines’ invitation-only elite status. It gives you priority over Executive Platinum members for just about everything, lounge access, and also (hopefully) proactive help in the event of irregular operations. However, don’t expect it to earn it if you don’t spend at least $50,000 per year on American Airlines flights, and even then it’s not a sure bet.

Is the status life changing? While I’ve never had it, I’m inclined to say “no.” But others certainly may disagree…

If you’re a Concierge Key member (or have been one in the past), what has been your experience with the status? How does it compare to Executive Platinum status?

#6104. How the Electoral College Dies

Blue-state activists are about to be perfectly positioned to execute an end run around the constitutional system.

In the wake of the 2026 midterms, we are on the cusp of a total transformation of the U.S. election system. After decades of Republican dominance in state legislatures, Democrats now control enough state governments to push the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact past its 270-vote activation threshold and dismantle the Electoral College from below.

But it seems like the right has barely realized the importance of the fight that’s about to begin.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.
