#6103. Which Hotel Credit Cards Offer Free Night Awards, And Are They Worth It?

Hotel credit cards are among the most underrated out there. Understandably a lot of people get cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) to maximize the rewards they’re earning for their spending, and that’s a great idea. These cards offer valuable bonus categories, no foreign transaction fees, great travel coverage, and more.

But I think supplementing one of those cards with hotel credit cards can make a lot of sense. That’s because hotel credit cards largely offer some incredible perks that more than justify the annual fee, including free hotel elite status, and even some free night certificates. So even if you’re not loyal to a hotel group, it’s easy to get outsized value.

In this post, I’d like to specifically look at which credit cards offer free nights as part of their rewards structure, how you can earn them, and if they’re worth it.

There are hotel credit cards issued by Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, and World of Hyatt, which offer the opportunity to earn free night awards. To be clear, I’m not talking about the ability to earn points, but instead, the ability to earn free night awards that can be redeemed at a set of properties.

These free nights come in different forms — some free night awards are offered for spending a certain amount on a card, and some free night awards are offered as an annual benefit just for having a card, with no spending required.

So let’s take a look at the details of how these free night awards work, and then we’ll talk about whether they’re worth it. Note that I’m focusing specifically on cards that offer free night awards on an ongoing basis (rather than as part of a welcome offer), and am also limiting this to cards that are open to new applicants.

Hilton Honors has two credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Hilton Honors free night awards are my single favorite hotel free night awards out there, given that they have no category caps, and they’re valid for 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Hilton points at 0.5 cents each.

Hilton free night awards can be redeemed for standard rooms at properties costing up to 250,000 points per night, and there’s only a small list of excluded properties. They’re even valid at Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH) properties that are part of the Hilton Honors partnership. It’s easy to redeem these at properties costing $1,000+ per night.

IHG One Rewards has three credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

IHG One Rewards free night awards are also potentially quite valuable, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value IHG points at 0.5 cents each.

While IHG free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, what I really like is how you can top them off with an unlimited number of points. So if a hotel requires 100,000 points, you could use a 60,000 point free night certificate, and then top it off with 40,000 points.

Marriott Bonvoy has four credit cards that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

Marriott Bonvoy free night awards are also extremely lucrative, and they expire 12 months from when they’re issued. I value Marriott points at 0.7 cents each.

While Marriott free night awards are capped at properties costing a certain number of points, you can top them each off with up to 25,000 points, to redeem at more expensive properties. So you could book a hotel costing 60,000 points per night by redeeming a 35,000 point free night award, and then redeeming 25,000 additional points.

World of Hyatt Honors has one credit card that give cardmembers the ability to earn free night awards:

World of Hyatt free night awards are valuable, but definitely the most restrictive of the bunch. Free night awards issued with the card expire 12 months after they’re issued. I value World of Hyatt points at 1.4 cents each.

Category 1-4 covers a lot of Hyatt properties (these can cost up to 25,000 points per night), but the catch is that you can’t use these certificates to redeem at more expensive properties by topping them off. Still, it should be very easy to get outsized value.

I’ll let my credit card portfolio speak for itself — I have quite the selection of hotel credit cards. They’re not necessarily cards that I spend a ton on, but instead, they’re cards I largely have because of the very strong perks that they offer, which to me, more than justify the annual fee. Let me just give a few direct examples…

I have the Hilton Honors Aspire Card, and it’s my single favorite hotel credit card. The card offers a massive number of perks, but in particular, the free night alone more than justifies the annual fee for me. I try to use this at properties that would retail for $1,000+ per night, so it’s pretty awesome to get that, along with all kinds of other perks, just for having the card.

I also think there’s merit to spending $60,000 per year on the card, if you can swing it. That spending would earn you a minimum of 180,000 points (since you earn at least 3x points per dollar spent with the card), plus two additional free night awards, potentially worth up to 500,000 points. So this is a great card to consider if you’re making a big purchase.

In the case of Marriott Bonvoy, I have both the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Card and Marriott Bonvoy Business Card, which get me free night awards worth 85,000 and 35,000 points, respectively. These also in and of themselves more than justify the annual fees on the cards. I generally redeem the larger free night award for a luxury hotel stay, while I redeem the lesser free night award for a stay at a mid-range property.

Lastly, I also have the World of Hyatt Credit Card, and that free night award also more than justifies the annual fee in and of itself. Admittedly I wish the free night award cap would be increased to reflect inflation, but even so, I get a ton of value out of this. At an absolute minimum, I use it when I have an overnight near JFK to stay at the Hyatt Regency JFK, which typically costs $300+ if paying cash.

There are potentially lots of great benefits to hotel credit cards, including big welcome bonuses, easy opportunities to earn hotel status, generous rewards structures for spending, and more.

The best part is that most issuers let you have multiple credit cards, meaning you can potentially earn more than one free night certificate per year. In the case of just about all of the above cards, I’d say the free night certificates more than justify the annual fees.

What’s your favorite hotel credit card free night certificate?

Some of the most aspirational business-class award redemptions are increasingly hard to find, even for the most experienced points and miles enthusiasts.

Cathay Pacific is a prime example. It's harder and harder to find award availability in the Hong Kong-based airline's premium cabins, especially with partners.

But one trick still works: Look for award availability when airlines launch new routes or bring back old ones.

I was able to fly from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points. That is a screaming deal. But there was only saver-level availability for a limited time when the schedule was first loaded.

It turned out to be a fantastic redemption, with excellent service, delicious food and a comfortable lie-flat seat for the long journey across the Pacific.

I'll have more details later in this story on how to find some of these incredible deals in business class, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

Here's what my experience was like aboard Cathay Pacific's Airbus A350-900 and how you can use a similar strategy to find these elusive business-class awards.

Cathay Pacific relaunched its service to Hong Kong from Seattle in March 2026, after suspending the route during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The route originally launched in March 2019 and was canceled in November of the following year. The airline's CEO told TPG that the carrier had always wanted to restore the route, which was Seattle's first nonstop service to Hong Kong since the pandemic.

The plane was a nine-year-old A350-900 with the ship number B-LRL, with 38 business-class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 214 economy seats.

It was a very comfortable way to cross the Pacific and opens up fun new ways to get to Asia from the U.S. West Coast. It also adds another way to use points and miles to fly to Hong Kong, though as you'll read below, it's no easy task to find the lowest-level award availability.

Business-class guests on Cathay Pacific are invited to use The Club at Seattle in the South Satellite area, which is connected to the main terminal by an underground train.

The Club SEA is an independent lounge that participates in Priority Pass. It offers a buffet of hot and cold food items and free drinks. It's basic, and it doesn't hold a candle to Cathay Pacific's own lounges in places like San Francisco and Hong Kong (no noodle bar here). However, it will do the trick for a quick drink and bite.

It was crowded during my quick visit, and I didn't spend much time at this lounge, since I'd had access to the beautiful Alaska Airlines lounge in the N Concourse. I grabbed a bite there before heading to the S Concourse, which is about to get a major, modern $2.5 billion renovation. It should be a much nicer place to hang out once the renovations are done.

Cathay Pacific has 38 business-class seats, split between two cabins. I was in the forward cabin with 30 seats arranged in a 1-2-1 configuration. There is a smaller cabin with just eight business-class seats behind a small galley/boarding area, which looked like a good option for a more intimate experience.

The seats fold down to 75 inches in length to become fully flat beds, though the footwell is a bit narrow.

Cathay Pacific gave out British lifestyle brand Bamford amenity kits that had moisturizer, cooling body gel, pillow mist, an eye mask, earplugs, a toothbrush and toothpaste and mouthwash. There were also noise-canceling headphones and a bottle of water at the seat.

The seat had lots of little storage areas, along with slippers (but no pajamas, as Cathay only has pajamas on select planes with first class).

Bathrooms are plentiful, with two in the front of the main business-class cabin and one more behind. The coolest thing was that the two bathrooms in front have windows — something you don't see that often on airplanes. Amenities were provided by Bamford and included a moisturizing spray and lotion.

The inflight entertainment was great, with an 18.5-inch HD touchscreen and plenty of movies and entertainment. I was able to choose from hundreds of movies and television shows (including a documentary on Cathay Pacific's 80th anniversary). There was also a tail camera and a moving map. A handheld controller is available to navigate the screen.

Cathay Pacific provides free Wi-Fi for business-class passengers, and I found it worked well on my flight. It's not as fast as Starlink, but it was still easy for me to get some work done.

I really like Cathay Pacific's business-class seats on these planes, though I'm excited to try one of Cathay's newer Aria Suite business-class products someday. Those suites are currently being installed on their Boeing 777-300ER fleet.

I'm especially hoping to see it on flights to and from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), which the airline has hinted could come as soon as next year. (The timing of that rollout remains to be confirmed.)

A friendly and attentive crew, delicious food and good bedding made for a great flight across the Pacific. I had especially good service with flight attendants Mei, Amanda and Elsa, all of whom were super friendly and chatty.

Service wasn't as formal as some Asian airlines I've flown, and the crew was fun to be around.

A predeparture beverage of orange juice or water was served during boarding.

Not long after takeoff, flight attendants served drinks. I went with a nonalcoholic Cathay Delight, the airline's signature nonalcoholic drink, made with kiwi, coconut and mint.

That was followed by a lovely amuse-bouche of a deviled egg. I could have happily eaten 20 of them.

The egg dish was served with a Betsy Free, Cathay Pacific's nonalcoholic version of its signature Betsy beer, in a vintage-style Cathay Pacific beer can.

That was followed by an absolutely delicious lunch: a roast carrot soup with a selection of breads, a hearty buffalo mozzarella and rocket pesto salad with grilled radicchio and toasted hazelnuts, and a roasted chicken breast in a maple-chipotle barbecue sauce, served with corn on the cob, creamed spinach and garlic mashed potatoes.

The dessert cart was filled with things like cheese and fruit plates, a yogurt panna cotta, ice cream, or a raspberry tiramisu and, of course, port or wine.

The flight attendants saw me snapping a ton of pictures, so they ended up letting me sample a little bit of almost everything. What a feast!

As if that weren't enough, flight attendants later brought around a chocolate sampler.

There were also snacks set out in the area between the two business-class cabins.

I was able to pre-select a second meal before the flight, and went with a classic beef burger.

There was a nice set of options available on the pre-order menu.

That meal was served after I'd gotten a few hours of shut-eye. Cathay Pacific is well-known for its burgers, and this one didn't disappoint.

I'm not sure how they managed to make a burger served at 30,000 feet taste good, but they did.

The flight attendants helped make my bed with a Bamford-branded mattress pad, duvet and large pillow. I managed to get about five hours of sleep — not too bad.

Before landing, there was yet another meal.

Breakfast was a more traditional Chinese meal of congee with shrimp dumplings and siu mai. Honestly, at that point, I was so full that I didn't eat much of it, but I did enjoy about four cappuccinos.

I'll tell you one thing: Come hungry when flying international on Cathay Pacific.

I was able to score that business-class seat on Cathay Pacific's newly resumed flight to Hong Kong for just 75,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in federal security tax. You can also book Cathay flights with American Airlines AAdvantage miles.

Unfortunately, low-level award space has been increasingly hard to come by using partners lately. That's why I always look when a new or newly resumed route goes on sale. I've often found low-level awards when the route first comes up for booking.

That also happened recently when American Airlines announced new service to Prague and newly resumed flights to Budapest,. The airline made business-class redemptions widely available for just 55,000 Alaska Atmos Rewards points.

So when a new route starts or resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

Related: 9 flight award booking hacks every traveler should know

Of course, you'll likely find more availability using Cathay Pacific's own program: Asia Miles. Cathay Pacific often releases more award availability to its own members. You can transfer miles 1:1 from multiple Cathay Pacific banking partners — including Bilt and Citi ThankYou Rewards, among others — directly to Asia Miles. American Express Membership Rewards also transfers to Asia Miles but at a reduced 5:4 ratio.

Award search tools are increasingly a big part of my deal hunt. Some of my favorites include Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel. I also rely on the Points Path award tool, which runs in my browser, so I can see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

Flexibility is another key to finding award availability like this. You'll often need to travel whenever a seat is available, not on a specific date. If you're open to multiple destinations, you'll also have better luck finding the cheapest awards, especially to destinations like Asia. Consider using wherever you find the best redemption as a jumping-off point to see other destinations in the region.

Business class on Cathay Pacific's A350-900s may not have all the excitement of its newer Aria Suite, but it's still a super-compelling product, as my recent flight from Seattle to Hong Kong showed. This trip proved once again why Cathay Pacific is one of my favorite airlines, and the newly resumed service from Seattle adds another option for American travelers.

Friendly service, a great seat, and incredible food and beverages made this trip one to remember. The best part was getting all that for just 75,000 Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points.

Keep an eye out for newly launched (or relaunched) routes when you are looking for your next great redemption. You might get a happy surprise.

#6101. How The Boeing 737 MAX 10 Is Growing First Class On US Airlines

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 is now certified, and airlines will soon begin taking delivery of the aircraft. WestJet should be the launch operator of the aircraft in early 2027, while Alaska Airlines and United Airlines will take delivery of their first examples shortly afterwards. Delta Air Lines is expected to start taking its first 737 MAX 10s later in 2027, while American Airlines will take its first MAX 10s in 2029. Altogether, four US airlines have ordered 550 737 MAX 10s, making its long-awaited arrival hugely important.

Not only will the aircraft itself be a staple of each airline's narrowbody fleet, but the airlines are planning to try some new ideas with the MAX 10 as well. American and Delta have both confirmed that they will install 24 first class seats, as opposed to the previously expected 20-seat cabin. Alaska Airlines, meanwhile, plans to operate a subfleet of 737 MAX 10 with lie-flat business class seats, hoping to directly take on the dominant legacy carriers on the lucrative transcontinental market.

As it currently stands, the narrowbody with the largest first class cabin in American Airlines' fleet is the Airbus A321-200 and A321neo, both of which have 20 first class seats. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines both operate the Boeing 757-300 with 24 first class seats, but the 757-300 is also a much larger aircraft than an A321 or 737. For both airlines, their A321s and 737s max out at 20 first class seats. It was believed that these airlines' 737 MAX 10s would also come with 20 first class seats.

Delta Air Lines had previously revealed that its 737 MAX 10s would feature 20 Delta First seats and 182 seats in total, but later statements from company leadership have confirmed that the planes will have 24 Delta First seats instead. This is despite the aircraft being about the same size as the carrier's A321neos, which have 20 Delta First seats. American Airlines has also publicly confirmed that its 737 MAX 10s, which are coming later than Delta's, will have 24 first class seats and a larger Main Cabin Extra section.

The primary reason why US airlines are growing first class cabins is due to rising premium demand. First class is in high demand, and airlines therefore want to capitalize on this by growing the cabins. As the 737 MAX 10 is all three airlines' next narrowbody aircraft type, it makes sense to expand first class on this aircraft type first, especially given its size. Should the results prove successful, the carriers will surely expand this idea to other types as well.

Delta Air Lines currently holds orders for 100 737 MAX 10s, which will begin arriving in 2027, and they will arrive with Delta First seats. This is the same amount as the carrier's 757-300 fleet, of which the carrier has only 16 examples. However, neither aircraft is the one with the largest first class cabin in Delta's fleet, as the carrier is currently operating a subfleet of Airbus A321neos with a 44-seat Delta First cabin. This is by far the largest first class cabin offered by any US airline.

These seven planes were originally intended to feature a three-cabin layout with lie-flat business class seats, but delays with the seats have led Delta to simply install eight additional rows of Premium Select and market the 11-row cabin as Delta First. While this is a temporary solution to make use of planes that have been sitting in storage, the cabin is consistently almost full, which means that the 20-seat cabins are leaving money on the table.

More than likely, Delta had already decided earlier to increase the size of the 737 MAX 10's first class cabin, and the results of the 44-seat cabins on these A321neos are simply validating the carrier's earlier plans. However, the results of the experiment demonstrate much stronger demand for first class than the current supply, and Delta CCO Joe Esposito has previously stated that the 'sweet spot' is somewhere between 24 and 44 seats. As such, it's possible that future deliveries of 737s or A321neos may have even more Delta First seats.

The Canadian airline has more than 100 Boeing 737 MAX 10s on order.

American Airlines first ordered the 737 MAX 10 in 2024 and currently holds orders for 115 examples, set to start coming in 2029. In August 2026, the carrier made a significant announcement that it would upgrade the interiors of its narrowbody fleet, add seatback screens to all aircraft, install Starlink WiFi, and add more first class and main cabin extra seating. This includes configuring the 737 MAX 10 with 24 first class seats and additional Main Cabin Extra seats.

American more or less installs the same number of first class seats as its competitors, but the carrier tends to sell fewer Main Cabin Extra seats and has not been performing as well financially. American has been making a push to become more 'premium' through a variety of different methods, which now includes upgrading the cabins of its narrowbody jets and adding premium capacity. Features like seatback screens and more extra legroom seats have benefited competitors, while larger first class cabins are now clearly the future.

For both Delta and American, the 737 MAX 10 is simply their next aircraft, which is why both have chosen it to implement their latest domestic premium cabin strategies. While both airlines also fly the A321neo, they both ordered and specced their aircraft before the current rise in premium travel. Notably, American has also stated that its A321neos will be reconfigured with more first class seats, but did not explicitly say that they would have 24 seats like the 737 MAX 10. This could mean an even larger first class cabin.

Alaska Airlines currently holds orders for 163 737 MAX 10s, making it the second-largest customer for the MAX 10. Most of these aircraft will be in a domestic layout with an unspecified number of first class seats. However, the carrier has revealed that at least 25 737 MAX 10s will have a three-cabin layout with lie-flat seats and a premium economy cabin, named 'Premium Reserve'. This is the first time that Alaska will be flying narrowbodies with lie-flats, directly taking on American, Delta, JetBlue, and United on transcontinental routes.

The 737 MAX will feature 12 'Aurora' Suites and 12 Premium Reserve seats, which is fairly conservative compared to the competition. Notably, the Aurora Suites and Premium Reserve seats will be equipped with seatback screens, also a first on an Alaska Airlines narrowbody, but the economy seats won't. Passengers will instead have to rely on personal device streaming and the Starlink WiFi system, and Alaska Airlines will be the only carrier in this market not to offer screens in economy.

For the other US operators of the 737 MAX 10, the aircraft is complementing the A321neo, which is set to be used as a standard domestic aircraft as well as for transcontinental flights by all three US carriers. Alaska Airlines, however, does not have any A321neos under the Alaska brand (there are 18 A321neos flying under the Hawaiian Airlines brand). As such, the 737 MAX 10 will be serving multiple roles for Alaska, including as a new premium transcontinental narrowbody.

United may never find a use for the seats it ordered when it expected 737 MAX 10 deliveries to begin several years ago.

United Airlines holds 167 orders for the 737 MAX 10, making it the largest customer for the MAX 10. The airline has ordered 514 737 MAX aircraft in total, split between 123 MAX 8s, 224 MAX 9s, and 167 MAX 10s. At one point, however, United held orders for 277 MAX 10s, but it later converted 110 orders to the MAX 9 due to delays with certification. In addition, United has continued to increase its A321neo order count to 210 in total, not including the A321XLR orders.

The 737 MAX 10 was intended to be United's workhorse narrowbody, but the A321neo and 737 MAX 9 fleet will both be larger. In addition, the airline has planned a subfleet of 50 A321neos with a three-class configuration to operate premium transcontinental routes, a role that it originally planned to assign to the 737 MAX 10. For the most part, the 737 MAX 10 will serve the same role as the standard A321neo, and United has not announced anything new or unique for the aircraft yet.

It's been reported that United had planned 20 United First seats and 189 seats in total for the MAX 10, and it's unknown if the airline has changed this to add more first class seats. In addition, United's A321neos have all arrived with 20 United First seats so far. While nothing has been announced from United, the recent announcements from American and Delta suggest that this could become a new shift in the US airline industry, and it wouldn't be surprising to see United follow.

#6100. What Amenities Make An Airport Lounge Good? Here’s My Take…

I write a lot about airport lounges on the blog, ranging all the way from domestic lounges in the United States, to the best business class lounges, to the best first class lounges. When I rank the lounges that I like the most, some readers understandably have very different takes.

I thought it would be fun to start a discussion about basic expectations of airport lounges, and what makes them exceptional.

Obviously lounge standards should differ depending on whether you’re using Priority Pass to access a lounge or are traveling in international first class, so we’ll get into more detail on that below.

Broadly speaking, what I’m looking for in a lounge is a (relatively) quiet place to sit, connect to Wi-Fi, recharge electronics, use a clean bathroom, and maybe have some water or coffee. Other things are good to have, but not something I necessarily expect.

There are also some deal killers for me when it comes to airport lounges. Personally, if a lounge is packed, I have no interest in being there, and that largely reflects that over the years, terminals have become much better places to spend time:

I figured I’d share my expectations for lounges, and I’ll break it up into three tiers of lounges (admittedly some of the lines are blurred here):

I think it’s also important to note that everyone is looking for different things in lounges:

I think the two below videos from Cathay Pacific from several years ago oh-so-beautifully sum up what makes lounges great. The commentary in the videos is almost poetic.

With that out of the way, let me share my basic expectations of various types of lounges, and admittedly these reflect my preferences and biases.

My expectations for Priority Pass lounges, airport contract lounges, airline membership lounges, and credit card lounges, are pretty simple. I’m happy if I can actually consistently get in and have a quiet place to sit. Sadly that’s not as straightforward as it may sound, with so many stories of lounges denying entry to club members, Priority Pass members, etc.

What sets a “basic” lounge apart? I’d say showers, bathrooms that are significantly nicer than in the terminals, workstations, a good food selection (ideally with hot food), good coffee, and employees who actually make you feel welcome.

Just to give some examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be exceptional:

My expectations are a bit higher for purpose-built international business class lounges. In addition to what I expect from the more “standard” lounges above, I hope that international business class lounges will have hot food, a more premium drink selection, showers, and workstations.

What sets an international business class lounge apart? I’d say a la carte dining, nap rooms, barista-made coffee drinks, and generally elevated decor.

Just to give a few examples of lounges in this category that I consider to be quite good (we’re actually pretty lucky in North America):

International first class lounges are as premium as they get, so expectations should be high. In international first class lounges I expect a la carte dining, barista-made coffee, some sort of an area to rest, a truly tranquil environment, and staff who make you feel welcome.

What sets an international first class lounge apart? Dining that’s (high-end) restaurant quality, an amazing drink selection, individual nap rooms, spa treatments, and a ground experience that extends beyond the lounge. That’s to say either tarmac transfers or an escort to the gate, and that’s no doubt an area where many airlines fall short.

I’ve reviewed the world’s top first class lounges in detail, so it’s no secret what my favorite options are the Air France La Premiere Lounge Paris and Lufthansa First Class Terminal Frankfurt.

We’re all looking for different things from airport lounges, and I think that’s totally fair. Standards should differ based on what kind of a flight you’re taking, how you access the lounge, what you’re trying to accomplish by visiting a lounge, etc.

Everyone will have a different take on which lounges are great vs. just okay, and that’s fine. While I care about tranquility and good coffee, others care about great food and drinks.

I’m curious to hear from OMAAT readers — what makes a lounge great, in your book?

#6096. Why Airlines Don’t Want First Class Anymore

Josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom. He started at Simple Flying as a Commercial Aviation Journalist before taking a less writing-focused role as Content & Growth Lead for Simple Flying's Flight Tracker.

In recent years, travellers have noticed a subtle yet significant shift in the configuration of aircraft cabins. Once a hallmark of luxury and exclusivity, first class sections are quietly disappearing from the fleets of many major airlines. These changes have sparked curiosity among both frequent flyers and industry observers.

Why would carriers move away from offering their most prestigious service, often associated with premium pricing and elite comfort? The answer lies in a mix of evolving passenger preferences, changing economic pressures, and strategic decisions being made behind the scenes. As airlines continue to adapt to post-pandemic realities and long-term shifts in global travel demand, the role of first class in their business models is being reevaluated.

For airlines, every square foot of cabin space must justify its existence in terms of revenue. First class cabins, while luxurious and prestigious, often occupy significant space that could be used more efficiently. A single first class seat can occupy the same footprint as two or even three business class seats, which are often more profitable on a per-square-foot basis.

Many airlines have found that passengers are willing to pay a premium for upgraded business class experiences, which offer similar amenities to first class but at a more sustainable cost structure for both the carrier and the traveller. The percentage of seats filled on a flight has also become a critical metric for airline success.

First class cabins often fly with a lower load factor, making them less efficient from a revenue perspective. Business class, in contrast, tends to have higher occupancy rates, especially on corporate-heavy routes. Faced with tighter margins and growing pressure to operate efficiently, some airlines are choosing to reduce or eliminate first class seating in favor of more financially viable alternatives.

This evolution hasn’t happened by accident. Indeed, airlines have invested in business class products because they appeal to high-end leisure travellers and corporate clients, two of the most profitable segments. Unlike first class, which often caters to a smaller, more niche market, business class offers broader appeal and a higher return on investment.

As a result, many carriers have doubled down on premium business seating, introducing branded experiences like ANA's 'The Room' or Qatar Airways' 'Qsuite.' The convergence of luxury and practicality in business class has made first class harder to justify.

Travellers who once paid a premium for first class now find business class meets all their needs, especially on long-haul international routes. Airlines, recognizing this shift, are reallocating resources to expand and enhance business class cabins, effectively replacing the need for traditional first class while still delivering a top-tier passenger experience.

However, today's premium flyers often prioritize features that are now standard in many business class products. This shift is especially evident among corporate travellers, who make up a substantial portion of high-revenue passengers. Companies, even large ones, have tightened travel budgets and scrutinized expenses more carefully in recent years.

Growth rate of international premium class travel (first + business) in 2024

Growth rate of international economy class travel in 2024

Number of international premium class passengers in 2024

116.9 million (6% of all international passengers)

Leading region in premium growth (Asia Pacific) statistics

22.8% growth to 21 million premium passengers; economy class in Asia Pacific grew 28.6% to 500.8 million passengers.

Region with the highest share of premium travel

In the Middle East, 14.7% of travellers are in premium cabins; Europe has the largest number of premium passengers at 39.3 million.

First class fares are harder to justify when business class offers comparable comfort at a lower cost. As a result, corporate policies increasingly favor business class travel, reducing demand for the ultra-luxury segment that first class occupies. Leisure travellers with more disposable income, meanwhile, often opt for premium economy or business class, seeing them as better value for money.

Premium air travel continued to gain momentum in 2024, growing slightly faster than economy travel. Although premium passengers still represent a small portion of the market, their steady rise highlights ongoing demand for higher-end experiences.

Notably, the Asia-Pacific region is driving much of this growth, though economy travel there is expanding even more rapidly. Meanwhile, the Middle East stands out for having the highest share of premium passengers, suggesting a strong regional preference for luxury travel, while Europe leads in total premium traveller volume.

Long-haul flights have traditionally been the stronghold of first class, offering unparalleled luxury travel and exclusivity on journeys that can last 10 hours or more. These routes, often operated by widebodies, provided an ideal setting for airlines to showcase their best products. With growing demand for business class, airlines are increasingly allocating more space to these seats.

They deliver a strong balance of comfort and profitability, while scaling back or removing first class altogether. Furthermore, the evolving competitive landscape on international routes has driven airlines to reassess their cabin configurations. Airlines face pressure to maximize revenue on these expensive-to-operate long-haul flights.

After all, fuel costs, crew expenses, and operational complexity are significantly higher than on short-haul sectors. Business class cabins, with their relatively higher load factors, have become a more reliable revenue driver. Additionally, emerging trends in long-haul travel, such as the rise of ultra-long-haul flights and the expansion of premium economy, are influencing cabin design decisions.

Ultra-long-haul flights, which can last 16 hours or more and generally cost more due to their length, demand passenger comfort and rest, but also emphasize operational efficiency. Airlines are experimenting with innovative business class products that can provide near-first class comfort without the high costs of full first class suites.

Simultaneously, premium economy serves as a middle ground, capturing travellers who seek an upgrade from economy but cannot justify or afford business or first class fares. These evolving factors further reduce the economic justification for maintaining traditional first class cabins on many long-haul international routes.

Airlines are increasingly driven by the need to maximize profitability per available seat mile, and this imperative has placed significant pressure on premium cabin configurations. First class cabins, while luxurious, occupy a disproportionately large amount of space on aircraft relative to the revenue they generate.

The cost of outfitting, maintaining, and servicing these premium suites is substantially higher than for business class or economy seats. When first class cabins suffer from low load factors, the revenue shortfall becomes even more pronounced, eroding the potential profit margin for each flight.

Increasing / Introducing First Class or Premium Seats

Introducing first‑class suites on its A321LR narrowbody aircraft.

Re‑introducing First Class cabins on its A350‑1000s with private suites.

New premium First Class products ('Allegris First Class,' revamped 'La Première') to enhance the ultra‑luxury offering.

Eliminating first class on international long‑haul flights, replacing it with expanded business class (Flagship Suites) because demand for first class fell.

Removed first class from most long‑haul routes (except some flagship/high-demand routes) during/after the pandemic.

Planning to discontinue Royal First Class over the next 2–3 years as part of restructuring.

This economic reality is compelling airlines to reconsider the viability of maintaining such an expensive product. Finally, operating costs beyond the seats themselves also factor into decisions. First class cabins often require additional crew, specialized catering, and dedicated lounge facilities.

All of these contribute to higher operating expenses. By reducing or eliminating first class cabins, airlines can simplify operations and reduce onboard service complexity. Ultimately, the economic benefits of focusing on business class rather than first class are reshaping how airlines design their premium cabins.

The future of premium travel is shifting, shaped by changing passenger expectations and evolving airline strategies. While demand for comfort and value is growing, especially in business class and premium economy, traditional first class is becoming less common. In effect, there seems to be a pull among airlines in opposite directions.

These upgrades are redefining what premium travel means, focusing less on exclusivity and more on experience. Sustainability is also influencing the future of premium cabins, as airlines face pressure to reduce emissions while maintaining high service standards. This is pushing a shift toward lighter materials, smarter aircraft design, and more fuel-efficient operations, ensuring that premium travel remains viable in a more climate-conscious world.

#6094. Livery of the Week: Etihad Partners with McLaren

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

While traditional marketing theories advise airlines to avoid sponsoring events such as motor racing because of perceived associations with “danger” and “uncertainty” — concepts that could reflect negatively on air transport operators — the past couple of decades have seen several airlines establish partnerships with Formula One teams and events.

Today, some carriers are title sponsors of their home Grands Prix. Gulf Air, for example, has been the title sponsor of the Bahrain Grand Prix since its inception in 2004. Singapore Airlines, which has held the same role at the Singapore Grand Prix since 2014, has extended its commitment through 2028.

Abu Dhabi-based Etihad Airways has been the title sponsor of the UAE Grand Prix since the race’s debut in 2009. This year, it also entered into a partnership with McLaren Racing, bringing together “two organizations with a shared commitment to innovation, ambition, and delivering exceptional experiences for fans and customers around the world”.

To mark the partnership, Etihad has painted one of its Boeing 787-10 aircraft in a special livery, taking McLaren Racing’s distinctive color to the skies.

The livery features McLaren’s signature papaya orange across most of the fuselage — the same color used on its racing cars and team uniforms. The “Etihad” and “McLaren” names appear side by side above the cabin windows, while the McLaren logo is displayed toward the rear of the aircraft against a black background. The tail fin retains Etihad’s signature mosaic pattern, with its colors adjusted to complement the fuselage’s black-and-orange scheme.

Papaya has taken flight 🧡✈️Keep your eyes on the skies and let us know if you spot us 👀#McLarenF1 | #BeyondBorders | @etihad pic.twitter.com/NCHxsdAMTi

The aircraft chosen to showcase the special livery is a Boeing 787-10, registered A6-BMI. It was delivered to Etihad directly from the manufacturer on Oct. 14, 2020.

The aircraft features one of Etihad’s older cabin designs, introduced in 2018. It has 327 seats in a two-class configuration: 32 business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout and 295 economy class seats in a 3-3-3 layout. The first 10 rows of the economy cabin are designated “Economy Space,” offering a seat pitch of 35 inches rather than the standard 31 inches.

Not your usual livery 👀 ✈️ See the making of our special edition @etihad x McLaren Racing livery 🧡 #McLarenF1 #BeyondBorders pic.twitter.com/I2SaS0hyR7

Looking for a new airplane model? Head over to our friends at the Midwest Model Store for a wide selection of airlines and liveries.

#6093. How To Redeem World Of Hyatt Points For Best Value, Maximize Award Chart

I write a lot about the value of hotel loyalty programs, and in this post, I’d like to talk about World of Hyatt. What are the best ways to redeem World of Hyatt points, how many points do you need for a free night redemption, how does the award chart work, etc.?

Let’s start by talking about the basics of redeeming World of Hyatt points — how much should you expect to pay for free nights, are there blackout dates, how much are World of Hyatt points worth, etc.?

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each. There’s no science to that, but rather I think that’s a fair, conservative valuation for what the points are worth. In other words, I won’t redeem points for a hotel stay with Hyatt unless I’m getting well over 1.4 cents of value per point (and that has to factor in the points I’m forgoing by redeeming rather than paying cash, etc.).

It’s important to come up with a points valuation for yourself (it can be different than mine), so that you can decide whether to pay cash or redeem points for a hotel stay.

I have lowered this valuation a little recently, in light of the World of Hyatt award chart devaluation we’ve seen, where Hyatt has gone from three tiers of pricing within each category to five.

World of Hyatt has no blackout dates, which is to say that if a standard room is available for sale with cash, it can also be booked with points.

Now, the important thing to keep in mind is that some hotels have a very small pool of “standard” rooms, and a vast majority of rooms at a hotel may be considered “premium.” If a hotel has 150 rooms, it’s possible that only 10 rooms are considered “standard,” so that’s the major issue you’ll run into when redeeming points at some properties.

Unfortunately in the hotel industry overall, we’ve seen a reduction in the number of standard rooms at many properties that are popular for redemptions, which is essentially a way for hotels to create indirect capacity controls.

Keep in mind that Hyatt has a great points availability calendar, which at least makes it easy to find the nights that are available with points, for those properties that are challenging.

Hopefully this isn’t an issue anyone runs into, but just keep in mind the World of Hyatt points expiration policy. World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. Any points earning or redemption activity resets the expiration of your points by a further 24 months.

Unlike Hilton Honors, IHG One Rewards, and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt continues to publish award charts for award redemptions (the exception is Mr & Mrs Smith properties, which I’ll talk more about in a bit).

The catch is that at this point, World of Hyatt has five tiers of award pricing for standard room redemptions — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper, and Top — and the variance within each category is huge. So while I appreciate that there’s not technically dynamic pricing, when a Category 1 hotel can cost 3,000 or 9,000 points, and a Category 8 hotel can cost 35,000 or 75,000 points, you’re not exactly getting a lot of assurance.

The standard award chart applies at a vast majority of properties globally, including most Hyatt branded properties. There are eight categories of hotels, and 40 different pricing tiers, given the five pricing bands within each tier. Pricing ranges from 3,000 points for a Category 1 property during the “Lowest” period, and 75,000 points for a Category 8 property during the “Top” period.

Next, World of Hyatt has an all-inclusive award chart, which applies to an ever-growing number of properties across Hyatt’s all-inclusive brands. Hotels fall into one of six categories, with the similar five bands of pricing, all based on double occupancy. Pricing ranges from 12,000 points for a Category A property during the “Lowest” period, to 85,000 points for a Category F property during the “Top” period.

Lastly, World of Hyatt has an award chart for Miraval properties, which are Hyatt’s super-luxurious wellness resorts. Pricing varies based on single or double occupancy, and then there’s also the five bands of pricing.

Note that unlike Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy, World of Hyatt doesn’t offer a fifth night free on award redemptions. So you’ll pay the points that correspond to the number of nights you’re staying.

World of Hyatt is the only major hotel loyalty program that lets you efficiently redeem your points for suites. This can come in the form of free night redemptions, or in the form of an upgrade award. Unlike with standard room availability, there are capacity controls on suite redemptions, so these won’t always be available just because a suite is for sale.

You can find the standard suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, the premium for a standard suite can range from around 20% to 100%, so there’s quite a bit of variance here. In many situations this could represent a good deal. Of course the ways that hotels choose to designate suites differs by property, so in some cases this can represent a huge upgrade, while in other cases it doesn’t.

You can find the premium suite award chart below, for the same Category 1-8 properties as above. As you can tell, there’s also quite a bit of variance here in terms of how much of a premium you’re paying.

World of Hyatt also lets you upgrade to club rooms, suites, and premium suites, using points. You can find the chart for that below, though note that this is only possible when booking a fully paid stay at the flexible rate directly with Hyatt. This requires a rate code, so it’s not even combinable with Hyatt Privé rates.

There are also more capacity controls here than you’d have if redeeming Hyatt suite upgrade awards, which are issued through the Milestone Rewards program.

World of Hyatt offers Points + Cash awards, whereby you can book a stay at a hotel using a combination of points and cash. This might sound appealing to those who want to reduce the cash cost of a stay using points, or those who don’t have quite enough points for a stay.

Points + Cash redemptions follow an award chart. The way this works, you can redeem 50% of the standard points required, plus you’ll receive around 50% off the cash component of a stay, in comparison to the flexible rate.

It’s always worth taking a look at this, though more often than not I don’t find this to be as good of a deal as just outright redeeming points. Also note that Points + Cash redemptions have capacity controls, unlike free night redemptions.

Hyatt acquired luxury travel company Mr & Mrs Smith, and you’ll find that many Mr & Mrs Smith properties are bookable through Hyatt channels. This is an opportunity to earn and redeem Hyatt points for stays at all kinds of independent luxury properties that you’d not otherwise have access to with a major loyalty program.

While the opportunity to earn points is potentially exciting, the catch is that points redemptions largely represent a bad value. Award pricing is fully dynamic, and you’ll find that in many cases, points only get you around a cent each toward a stay. That’s significantly less than I value them, so I wouldn’t recommend redeeming that way.

While I wouldn’t say it’s my favorite use of points, World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, whereby you can redeem points toward a folio credit that can be applied to on-property dining and spa awards. With this, you’ll get anywhere from 1.0 to 1.54 cents of value per point.

While there are some restrictions to be aware of, this is still something that has the potential to be useful for those with lots of points, who are looking to splurge on incidentals during a stay.

With the Milestone Rewards program, World of Hyatt members can earn Guest of Honor certificates. This extends World of Hyatt Globalist status benefits over the course of a stay, for up to seven nights. These can be applied to any eligible revenue stay or points stay, and offer lots of value.

Those booked with a Guest of Honor certificate receive the standard Globalist perks, including complimentary breakfast, suite upgrades subject to availability, and much more. This is one of my favorite loyalty perks out there.

World of Hyatt has a generous policy when it comes to letting members transfer or combine points between accounts. World of Hyatt members can transfer points between accounts at a 1:1 ratio.

Members can transfer a minimum of 1,000 points, and can transfer in increments of 500 points above that. Members can transfer up to 525,000 points per transaction, and may transfer or receive up to that many points across accounts per calendar year. World of Hyatt accounts must be at least 60 days old in order to send or receive points.

World of Hyatt members are also limited to making one free points transfer every calendar month, and six free points transfers every calendar year. Transfers generally happen within 24 hours, but in rare cases could require additional review, and could take up to 10 business days.

This can be a great way to combine points in order to have enough for a particular redemption, or even to transfer points in order to make a booking out of an elite member’s account, or using a Guest of Honor award.

Nowadays many properties charge resort fees or destination fees, which are essentially a money-grab. All World of Hyatt members don’t have to pay these when redeeming points, which can add significant value. Furthermore, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay these even on revenue stays.

As a further perk, World of Hyatt Globalist members don’t have to pay for parking on award stays (however, non-Globalist members do have to pay for parking).

World of Hyatt has three elite tiers — Discoverist (10 elite nights), Explorist (30 elite nights), and Globalist (60 elite nights). While status isn’t quite as easy to earn as with some other hotel groups, there are still some opportunities to earn status with credit cards. World of Hyatt’s co-branded credit cards include the World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) and World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more). You can earn elite qualifying nights and status with these cards:

Even if you’re not a Hyatt loyalist, the great news is that earning World of Hyatt points is pretty easy. However, the ratios aren’t as consistently good as in the past.

In addition to being able to earn World of Hyatt points with the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card, you can also transfer points from both Bilt Rewards and Chase Ultimate Rewards:

On top of that, World of Hyatt frequently has promotions for purchasing points. The reason this matters is because there are lots of situations where you could get outsized value simply by buying points from Hyatt and then immediately redeeming them for a hotel stay.

With the above basics out of the way about redeeming World of Hyatt points, how do you get the most value with your points? Let me share my approach to redeeming Hyatt points.

As a Hyatt Globalist member, I exclusively redeem my points for free night award redemptions in standard rooms. While I think there can be value in redeeming points for standard or premium suites, my general strategy is to redeem for standard rooms, and then use suite upgrade awards to confirm suites.

The reality is that I get huge value with my World of Hyatt points throughout the award chart, and not just at aspirational properties. Generally I decide to redeem points if I’m getting at least two cents of value per World of Hyatt point. There are several things I factor into that, though. When deciding whether to redeem points:

With World of Hyatt charging such vastly different amounts across the five bands of pricing, in some cases you’ll get the most value per point when redeeming during an off-peak period, while in other cases you’ll get the most value when redeeming during a peak period. You of course always want to compare the cash rates to the points redemption rates.

With a little bit of effort, I have no issues redeeming a vast majority of my Hyatt points for well over two cents each, in comparison to the cash cost.

Ultimately the reason I collect airline miles and hotel points is for aspirational redemptions. I try to redeem for things that I typically wouldn’t pay for in cash, where I’m getting outsized value.

So just as airline miles are best redeemed for first & business class travel, hotel points are often best redeemed for five-star properties that would cost a lot in cash. So the main reason I earn Hyatt points is to be able to redeem at properties belonging to brands like Alila and Park Hyatt. From Alila Napa Valley, to Alila Ventana Big Sur, to Alila Jabal Akhdar, to Park Hyatt Kyoto, to Park Hyatt Milan, to Park Hyatt Paris, I’ve had some amazing award redemptions over the years.

World of Hyatt is my all-around favorite hotel loyalty program. I greatly value the elite perks I receive as a Globalist member, and I also consistently get great value with my points, especially for aspirational properties. I also love how World of Hyatt points can efficiently be transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, providing an easy pathway to racking up this currency.

Personally my favorite use of World of Hyatt points is for stays at Hyatt’s top luxury hotels, where you’ll almost consistently get the best value, assuming you can find award availability. However, I’ve gotten great value at lower end properties as well.

Now, in fairness, the value of Hyatt points is definitely decreasing a bit at the moment, and on top of that, the reduced transfer ratio from other currencies is frustrating, and definitely eats into the value a bit. That being said, that’s true of the industry at large, as we’ve also seen endless devaluations with Hilton Honors and Marriott Bonvoy. I do still get the most value with Hyatt.

What has your experience been with redeeming World of Hyatt points?

#6092. FAA Issues Nationwide Ground Stop, Shuts Down The Skies: What’s Going On?

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop, which is pretty unprecedented. Admittedly we’ve had our fair share of air traffic control issues in the United States over the years. But this is really on a different level, unlike anything we’ve seen since 9/11, in terms of operational disruptions. I guess it’s fitting that this is happening on Friday the 13th.

At 3:54PM ET today (Friday, November 13, 2026), the FAA issued a ground stop for flights across the country, as pilots received the following message:

DUE TO EXTRAORDINARY CIRCUMSTANCES AND FOR REASONS OF SAFETY. ATTENTION ALL AIRCRAFT OPERATORS, BY ORDER OF THE FEDERAL AVIATION COMMAND CENTER ALL AIRPORTS ARE GROUND STOPPED. ALL DEPARTING TRAFFIC SHOULD REMAIN GROUND STOPPED UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE. INBOUND INTERNATIONAL FLIGHTS WILL BE MANAGED ON A CASE BY CASE BASIS.

As of now, the ground stop is through 11:30PM ET, though it’s possible that it’s lifted before then. That timeline clearly reflects the extent to which the current situation is a complete mess, and this won’t be an easy fix.

As usual, JonNYC was among the first to break the news, and he even reported on this before the official ground stop was issued, when airports in the Northeast started having issues, prior to this going nationwide.

Kind of major, started at approx 3:15pmBoston Center, New York Center, Chicago Center, New York Approach have all lost numerous frequencies. All facilities are in ATC Alert. Some sectors in New York Center are unable any traffic currently. Numerous— I mean NUMEROUS frequencies…

“All airspace is currently being sterilized and centers are preparing for ATC Zero operations. Airborne’s should NOT be majorly effected— i.e, at least for now, this is not a “9/11 type of event” where airbornes are being forced to land at the closest airport available. All…

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed this development a while later, sharing that there were “communication issues impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers,” and he stated that “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

As of now, there’s no timeline for this ground stop ending. To my knowledge, I believe this is now the most significant ground stop we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years (since 9/11).

If you’re flying this weekend, expect that things will be a mess. To those flying right now, good luck. Ford is on a flight that was supposed to depart at 3:59PM, so suffice it to say that he had some pretty bad luck here, as they pushed back, and then this happened. I hope not too many others are in the same situation.

There’s a major issue when you have flights landing but flights can’t depart, since you have way more planes than gates. So get ready to be patient if you’re onboard a flight, given the complicated logistics.

What could explain an air traffic outage of this scale? As of now, all we can do is speculate, though there are a few interesting things to point out.

First, it remains to be seen if this is related, but the FAA reportedly began its rollout of the new AI-powered air traffic management tool this week, known as SMART (which stands for “Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories”).

Timing-wise, it seems like there’s a possibility this could be related. At the same time, you wouldn’t assume this leads to communication issues, which is what seems to be going on here. So it’s worth pointing out the timing, but we have no reason to believe the two things are related.

Yes the FAA began its nationwide rollout of the SMART AI for ARTCCs to use this week. It’s not clear at this time if the rollout is related to this outage, but if it’s a rolling communications issue, it’s much more likely it’s within already established equipment pilots-ATC use https://t.co/PXqSFdOA1q

One can’t help but wonder if a cyber attack might be to blame. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin insists that there are no indications of this being a cyber attack. However, if they’re still investigating the cause, it seems hard to rule anything out.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the agency had no indications of outages being tied to a cyberattack or potential terror threat, adding that the nationwide ground stop was “just a telecommunications outage." https://t.co/cb8xON9Xrz

If this is truly “just a telecommunications outage,” then that represents a major failure. How can air traffic control nationwide have that issue, rather than it just being isolated to one region? Are there no redundancies?

I don’t want to be a conspiracy theorist, but it sure feels to me like some very unusual things are going on. We just saw a huge Microsoft outage, and it has been a very strange week in general. Those two things can of course be completely unrelated, but you can’t help but point it out.

The FAA has grounded flights nationwide, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” For nearly two hours now, no flights have taken off in the United States, making this the largest outage since 9/11, to my knowledge.

It remains to be seen what the cause of this was, and whether this is a tech glitch, a cyber attack, or what. To those flying now (or this weekend), good luck… you’re going to need it!

What do you make of this strange ATC outage?

#6091. The Republican Party Must Be Bigger Than Any One Person

The GOP’s future depends on putting principles first.

President Ronald Reagan gives his acceptance speech at the 1984 Republican National Convention in Dallas, Texas

In 1967, Ronald Reagan offered a reminder about the Republican Party that is as relevant today as it was nearly 60 years ago: “Unity does not require unanimity of thought.” Reagan understood something fundamental about political leadership: A party is not a personality cult. It is a coalition of Americans united by shared principles, even when they disagree about policy specifics.

In the aftermath of the midterm elections, Republicans have serious questions to confront. The results demand reflection and an examination of what we believe and what kind of political institution we intend to be. I believe in the Constitution, limited government, individual liberty, fiscal responsibility, and personal accountability. Those convictions have not changed because of political pressure, nor are they dependent on who occupies the White House.

#6090. Why United Airlines Flies Its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners On Domestic Routes

FiledIMAGE | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

The Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is engineered and purpose-built to conquer vast oceanic expanses, connecting distant continents on ultra-long-range intercontinental missions. In actuality, travelers booking domestic flights across the United States frequently encounter this twin-aisle flagship operating high-density trunk routes between major domestic hubs. Far from being an anomaly, widebody deployment on domestic sectors is a sophisticated operational strategy network carriers use to maximize asset utilization and manage peak passenger flows.

Why does United Airlines schedule its premier widebodies on domestic legs? This article explores the core commercial, logistical, and operational drivers behind domestic widebody flying, looking closely at how aircraft positioning, premium cabin introductions, cargo yields, and schedule flexibility converge to put the Dreamliner on domestic routes.

Airline networks operate on tightly synchronized banking structures where widebody aircraft cannot afford to sit idle for hours between international arrivals and departures. When a 787-9 touches down from an overnight intercontinental flight at a hub like San Francisco International Airport (SFO), its scheduled transoceanic departure might not occur until late evening. Leaving a multi-million-dollar asset parked on the tarmac is a real economic waste, making high-volume domestic trunk routes ideal operational bridges to keep the airframe generating revenue.

Network planners schedule the 787-9 onto high-demand domestic legs connecting key hubs, such as flights linking San Francisco to Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) or Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). These high-volume corridors experience heavy passenger flows throughout the day, providing an ideal passenger volume to fill a widebody cabin. The idea is to keep the aircraft active on a domestic rotation, ensuring continuous asset utilization and minimal disruption to its overarching international schedule.

This hub-to-hub positioning also ensures that aircraft arrive precisely where they are needed for outbound international banks without requiring empty ferry flights. Operating a revenue-generating flight between domestic hubs while repositioning the airframe achieves double operational efficiency, covering fuel and crew costs while satisfying heavy regional passenger demand. Consequently, a widebody on a domestic sector is often the visible outcome of a complex, highly synchronized global aircraft-routing puzzle.

Beyond routine scheduling mechanics, network airlines often deploy newly delivered widebodies on domestic sectors as a controlled proving ground for upgraded interior products. When United Airlines introduced its latest batch of 787-9 aircraft featuring premium-heavy Elevated cabins and advanced Polaris business class configurations, the carrier did not immediately thrust them into intercontinental service. Instead, management scheduled initial revenue flights across domestic trunk routes as a live integration phase, helping to show that the hardware performed flawlessly under real-world operating conditions before committing the jets to remote international stations.

The domestic deployment plan is an invaluable training environment for both flight deck and cabin crew members experiencing newly certified cabin layouts for the first time. Operating a widebody packed with hundreds of passengers means flight attendants must master unfamiliar galley layouts, complex emergency equipment stowage, and multi-zone inflight entertainment systems. Running these systems on shorter domestic hops lets crews build operational familiarity and troubleshoot minor cabin discrepancies near major domestic maintenance bases, avoiding costly delays thousands of miles from home hubs.

For instance, United used select domestic rotations, such as high-profile flights connecting San Francisco (SFO) to Houston (IAH), as direct introductory lanes ahead of pushing the new 787-9s across the Atlantic to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) or deep into Asia-Pacific markets, as noted by AeroExplorer. By vetting the passenger experience, Wi-Fi connectivity, and seat performance on domestic sectors, the airline ensures that when the aircraft finally enters long-haul rotation, the product is fully polished.

An aircraft that has proven its capability across all corners of the globe for a powerhouse of aviation. Here is where United operates the Dreamliner.

Scheduling widebody aircraft on domestic trunk routes provides powerful commercial advantages in premium passenger revenue and belly-cargo capacity. Major domestic connectors, such as transcontinental paths or high-frequency hub links, regularly attract heavy concentrations of corporate travelers, high-net-worth flyers, and priority freight forwarders. Deploying a widebody like the 787-9 on these high-density domestic corridors allows carriers to capture exceptional ticket yields from business class and premium economy seats that consistently outperform standard narrowbody capacity.

Premium revenue generation is especially critical as airlines see sustained corporate demand for lie-flat comfort on longer domestic hops, as noted by Getaway. A single 787-9 equipped with high-density premium configurations can house dozens of business-class suites and make a routine domestic flight become a high-margin revenue generator. Passengers booking connecting itineraries appreciate the continuity of flying in a flagship long-haul suite right from their initial domestic departure, creating a seamless premium travel experience that builds brand loyalty early on.

At the same time, widebody deployment provides substantial under-floor cargo capacity that narrowbody aircraft lack. High-volume domestic sectors frequently move valuable commercial freight, express parcels, and time-sensitive cargo that feeds international widebody departures waiting at the hub. With air cargo markets demonstrating robust yields, using the massive belly-hold space of a 787-9 on domestic legs adds an extra layer of financial success, which can be vital to a route's profitability.

When passenger demand surges past what standard narrowbody frequencies can accommodate, major network hubs face rigid operational delays and gate limitations. Adding extra daily narrowbody departures to handle rising volume is often impossible at congested airports constrained by hourly arrival caps or limited gate availability. Instead of increasing flight frequency, network planners turn to aircraft gauge optimization, utilizing widebody capacity to scale passenger volume within existing slot allocations.

Upgrading a high-density domestic rotation from a single-aisle jet to a 787-9 Dreamliner increases seat capacity by over 100 passengers per departure without consuming an additional scarce takeoff or landing slot. At mega-hubs where slot controls and ramp congestion restrict extra movements, upgauging is the most efficient mathematical solution to handle heavy passenger flows. This is because it maximizes the passenger throughput of a single movement, avoiding constraints that limit frequency expansion.

Of course, operating smaller narrowbody aircraft multiple times a day provides a varied schedule for business travelers, but it quickly overwhelms crowded terminal concourses and ramp space during peak hours. Deploying a widebody on these heavy domestic corridors lets carriers consolidate passenger loads into fewer departures while optimizing ground infrastructure use.

Is there a possibility that Boeing will make an extended-range version of the 787 Dreamliner?

Domestic widebody deployments are inherently fluid and are not so much considered permanent fixtures. Instead, these deployments shift dynamically in response to seasonal international travel demand. During shoulder seasons or troughs in transatlantic and transpacific travel, long-haul aircraft availability fluctuates, creating strategic windows for network planners to route widebodies onto domestic trunk lines. This flexibility allows carriers to maximize asset productivity year-round, importantly ensuring that expensive multi-million-dollar airframes continue generating revenue when international route demand contracts.

Sometimes, equipment swaps and tactical network adjustments place the 787-9 onto domestic schedules to solve short-term operational hurdles. If unexpected passenger surges or maintenance schedule revisions occur at a primary hub, airlines can rapidly upgauge domestic rotations without disrupting long-term fleet allocations.

Ultimately, the ability to weave long-range widebodies into domestic loops highlights the sophisticated adaptability needed to manage modern airline networks. When global travel patterns shift or maintenance routing needs to be near major engineering bases, domestic widebody operations provide the operational elasticity needed to keep fleets balanced. By treating these aircraft as versatile assets rather than rigid intercontinental specialists, carriers like United can achieve both strong financial performance and network resilience.

The presence of a long-haul flagship like the 787-9 on domestic routes highlights the complex operational and commercial calculus governing modern network airlines. Far from an accidental routing choice, deploying twin-aisle widebodies across high-density domestic corridors lets carriers optimize asset rotation, test advanced premium cabin hardware, capture lucrative business yields, and relieve slot congestion that limits so many airlines worldwide. Turning highly valued intercontinental aircraft into flexible domestic workhorses during turnaround windows means that airlines like United can extract maximum value from every airframe in the fleet.

United Airlines is just one of many carriers that are refining their domestic hub connectivity and introducing next-generation cabin configurations. What this means is that flexible widebody utilization will still be an indispensable strategic lever well into the future. Whether balancing seasonal international demand shifts or scaling passenger capacity without consuming scarce airport slots, domestic widebody operations are a clear example of how aircraft versatility is as vital as raw range. As aviation networks evolve, mastering this balance between long-haul capability and domestic synergy can offer real competitive advantages for airlines.

#6088. Beond Airlines Suspends Flights For The Rest Of The Year: Better Luck In 2027?

Back in April 2026, we saw Beond Airlines suspend all scheduled operations for the summer, as the airline claimed it would resume flights as of late October. Then in October, it announced it would return in December. There’s now another update, as the airline has just announced that it will resume flights in January. That doesn’t sound so good, does it?

Beond Airlines launched operations in 2023, and it brands itself as the world’s first premium leisure airline. The company is headquartered in Dubai, but primarily operates flights to and from the Maldives. I reviewed the airline in 2024, and the onboard product was super pleasant. The airline currently has a fleet of two aircraft, including one A319 and one A321.

Anyway, in mid-April 2026, the company announced that it would suspend its scheduled operations for the entire summer. The airline promised to resume flights in October, for the winter season.

Then in October, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through November 30, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of December 1, 2026. Then just yesterday, the airline announced that it would suspend operations through December 31, 2026, meaning it will resume flights as of January 1, 2027.

So I guess it remains to be seen if we actually see a resumption of flights as of January, or if the timeline will get pushed back again. If you can’t make all-business class flights to the Maldives work for the festive season, then prospects seem pretty grim.

Beond Airlines does have its “commitment” to customers when plans change, which includes the ability to change destinations or travel dates, receive a travel credit valid for 18 months, or to receive a full refund. A change of destinations or dates, plus a travel credit, isn’t worth a whole lot for an airline that keeps pushing back its relaunch.

Interestingly, but perhaps not surprisingly, earlier this year the airline deleted its customer promise webpage, which used to guarantee rebooking on another airline in business class in the event a flight is canceled, or else the airline would offer a free flight. That page is now gone, and there’s no mention of rebooking on another airline.

So the airline will “support you every step of the way,” unless you actually want to take the vacation you booked, in which case you’re out of luck (which is less than ideal, given that many Maldives properties have very strict cancelation policies).

While Beond Airlines’ business plan was questionable under the best of circumstances, the crisis of this year makes matters worse:

So I feel bad for Beond, and I’m not trying to do a “told you so, I was right” thing, because these are of course exceptional circumstances. The thing that made me suspicious about Beond for so long is that the airline would repeatedly make outlandish growth announcements, only to rarely follow through on them. That’s neither here nor there, though.

Keep in mind that since operations were initially suspended in April, we’ve seen some interesting developments:

My assumption is that Saudi Arabia is to some extent funding the Red Sea flights, given how the country is throwing money at any airline willing to fly there. However, one wonders if that’s enough money to make the math work, or if Beond even has the general funding right now to keep things operating.

It’s just all so strange, because it feels like half of the announcements from Beond Airlines are really targeting prospective investors, constantly promoting how it’s going to open new subsidiaries all over the world, launch dozens of new routes, etc.

As I said in April, I didn’t think it was a sure bet that flights would resume in October. Now we’ll see if flights actually resume in January. I wouldn’t count on it. One bizarre angle to this is that Beond has claimed it will launch flights to London Heathrow (LHR). Best I can tell, there’s no public record of the airline getting slots for that. And if the airline did have slots, it would be under a “use it or lose it” clause, so not operating the route would make the airline lose them.

In the spring of 2026, all-business class airline Beond suspended scheduled operations through October 2026. Then the airline announced it would resume flights in December 2026. Now the airline claims it will relaunch flights in January 2027. Over the summer, we learned that the airline wasn’t paying many staff for months, and the airline is now pivoting to operating service via Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Airport.

We’ll see what happens in the coming weeks. Presumably the Red Sea service gets the airline some money from the Saudi government, but it remains to be seen if that’s enough to keep this operation afloat.

It’s understandable that the current situation is really challenging, between the price of jet fuel, plus overall sentiment about the Middle East. However, I have to imagine the airline didn’t have great financial health before this whole mess started, and suspending flights in some ways only makes things even worse.

How do you see this playing out for Beond?
