#6087. Duffy And Mullin’s FAA Ground Stop Press Conference: Self-Praise, A $50 Billion Ask, And Conflicting Stories

Yesterday, we saw the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issue a nationwide ground stop, which wasn’t fully lifted for over four hours. This represents the single biggest grounding of flights in the United States since 9/11, so the scale of whatever happened is pretty wild.

At around 8PM last night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin held a press conference to update people on the state of things. I can’t help but cover this, because it felt like something between an SNL skit and a shakedown, and they couldn’t even keep their story straight… all while praising themselves for doing an unprecedented job!

Below you can find the press conference last night regarding the FAA shutdown, which happened around the time that the ground stop was lifted. First Mullin and Duffy spoke for around 10 minutes, and then they took questions for around 20 minutes.

The gist of the story is that they claim there were no signs of this being a cyber attack, and basically they broadly blame the outdated air traffic control system.

Mullin didn’t speak for long, and his primary comment was this:

“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like, by the organization and team he has put together. We are built to handle crises like this, and that’s exactly what we’re doing. We’re moving at an unprecedented pace, as a whole of government, to make sure we’re doing the public justice by making sure everyone is safe, which everyone is.”

Isn’t this a little self-congratulatory, especially while he’s also claiming that they don’t fully know the cause here? Just objectively, the pace was indeed unprecedented… it was the longest ground stop since 9/11!

Then you have Duffy speak, and this basically just turned into a demand for Congress to give him $50 billion to modernize our aviation infrastructure, while not actually being honest about the state of things:

“The President, for the last year, has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a new air traffic control system.”

That’s just not accurate at all. In July 2025, Congress authorized $12.5 billion for modernizing air traffic control, which Duffy described as a “down payment.” Since then, the size of the request kept changing, and the formal ask only went to Congress this week, when Duffy asked lawmakers for $30.1 billion for air traffic control and airport upgrades.

So it’s a bit rich to claim that Congress has been uncooperative over the past year, especially when you consider Republicans have controlled the White House, House, and Senate.

He then tried to explain what happened, which just feels like a complete deflection to me, as it’s about an overall need to modernize ATC, rather than what actually went wrong here:

“What happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data, and they went down… I shouldn’t say they went down… they started to give us inconsistency with the data from those routers, and because of that, we shut the system down. Now, I have already replaced some of those switches with President Trump, and our new IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down, and I think the question for the American people is, ‘do you want your Congress to fund this?'”

“I think the Congress at a point looked at the history of the FAA, and said ‘we don’t trust you.’ Well with President Trump, and what we’ve done, I think they do trust, because what we’ve done with that first tranche of money.”

“I’ve asked the President to ask for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

Obviously our air traffic control technology is really outdated and does need updating, there are no two ways about it. However, what was different yesterday, and caused an outage to this scale?

You can see I quoted Duffy above as saying that he claimed that “what happened is that our switches, actually got overloaded with data,” and that this caused the shutdown. I’m not a tech expert, but how exactly does that happen and cause the systems nationwide to have issues? At most, you’d assume it would be regionalized, no?

So this is where the questions from reporters come in handy. Mullin seemingly threw Duffy under the bus, saying:

“What it appears to be right now is that as Secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches in the system, they were putting new equipment, and new technology, and that new equipment and new technology was overwhelming the older system.”

You can see Secretary Duffy’s reaction as Secretary Mullin says the newer technology was overwhelming the system. pic.twitter.com/IeoW5nM4aY

Duffy was then asked what was different yesterday, given that the system had been in place for years. As you’d expect, there was no good answer.

Initially Duffy made it sound like they knew exactly what happened, but then he backtracked on that, and said “we’re still working on the details of what went wrong, I’ll be happy to give you more information, but I don’t want to give you the wrong information.”

Very good set of questions from Luke Radel for Secretary Duffy and Secretary Mullin. pic.twitter.com/f6tlfDtbJG

I also appreciate how someone actually asked the question about this being blamed on Congress, given that the Republicans have had full control for the past two years. As you’d expect, Duffy’s response was first to ask what network the person was from.

DUFFY: How many times does this have to happen before congress gives the money to fix it?R: You’ve been in office almost two years now, Republicans controlled both chambers of congress and still do.DUFFY: What your network are you from? pic.twitter.com/xuX5arTwjl

What’s amazing to me is the overall tone of the press conference. They feel bad for themselves, with Duffy pointing out that he hopes he doesn’t have to give another press conference after 8PM. You know what’s not mentioned once, though? Thanking travelers for their patience throughout all of this, or apologizing to the public for the disruption. Not once.

I’m 100% in support of funding and modernizing air traffic control. But when you have the biggest outage you’ve had in over 25 years, it seems a bit rich to say “give us $50 billion” and “we’re doing an unprecedented job.” And again, if Mullin is to be believed, the system updates that were put in place were to blame.

#6086. Iran Is Still a Menace

A member of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at a military training center for citizens in Tehran, Iran, November 2, 2026.

Majid Asgaripour/WANA (West Asia News Agency) via Reuters

The American public may not be interested in the Iran war, but it is still interested in us.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his home to a military base after credible Iranian threats against his life. Bessent helps oversee the crippling financial sanctions imposed on Iran, making him a particular target for the regime.

In the past several years, former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Adviser John Bolton, and President Trump himself have also been the targets of Iranian assassination plots.

With the Iran war playing a prominent role in the GOP’s stunning defeat in last week’s elections, there is renewed pressure — both from incoming Democrats and critics on the right — to put an end to the conflict.

On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that JD Vance had become lead negotiator with Iran, to the point of even contemplating direct talks with a top Iranian security official. The same article related that Trump had started to second-guess the wisdom of the June memorandum of understanding that Vance negotiated and that Trump gladly signed, wondering whether it allowed time for Iran to regroup and earn more oil revenue.

On Thursday morning, Trump, who has been vacillating between threatening to bomb Iran and touting imminent peace almost by the day, poured cold water on the idea of any renewed negotiations. The president took to Truth Social to say that he was asking Vance to focus on corruption in Democrat-run cities. “We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Bombast aside, a status quo in which the U.S. maintains a naval blockade against Iran and escorts ships through the Strait of Hormuz may be the least bad of the remaining options. While maintaining that pressure, the U.S. should also look for ways to actively support the Iranian opposition, something President Trump implicitly promised in January with his “help is on its way” comments. But we obviously cannot bank on the Iranian regime falling or moderating any time soon. It is hard to see what can be accomplished strategically through another weeks-long air campaign, but the immediate diplomatic prospects are dim, as well.

Presumably, any deal that Iran would agree to in the aftermath of what it considers its victory in the midterms would be a bad one for the U.S., likely a repeat of Barack Obama’s disastrous Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, if not worse. Under that agreement, Iran enjoyed hundreds of billions of dollars in sanctions relief, preserved its ability to enrich uranium, and maintained its ballistic missile program. The scandal of the Iran deal was that even if it worked exactly as intended, it would have still allowed Iran to continue to develop a more powerful conventional military, to sponsor terrorism, and to exert a malign influence within the region and around the world. All the while, restrictions on its nuclear program were set to expire over time, putting the regime on a long-term glide path to weaponization. If any eventual agreements are to be reached with Iran, they must meet two tests: First, do no harm, and second, trade nothing for any promises of future conduct by the Iranians.

Iran’s plots against one of the most important U.S. cabinet officials, as well as Americans throughout the Middle East, underline the malignity of an Iranian regime that has been in a conflict with the United States for a half century. In short, it is still very interested in the war, and in doing us harm.

#6085. Spool Up Vs. Turn & Burn: Which Takeoff Concept Is More Effective?

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

Every takeoff begins with a carefully managed increase in engine power, but the way an aircraft starts moving can vary. In a static takeoff, the aircraft remains stationary while the engines are brought to the required stabilization setting before the takeoff roll begins. A rolling takeoff, meanwhile, allows the aircraft to begin moving before takeoff thrust is fully applied. Both techniques are used in aviation, with the appropriate procedure depending on the aircraft, operating conditions, and manufacturer guidance.

Although the distinction may appear minor, the timing of thrust application can influence how evenly engines accelerate and how easily pilots maintain directional control during the early stages of the takeoff roll. Neither method is universally better, and the choice is not simply about getting airborne as quickly as possible. Understanding how each technique works helps explain why aircraft manufacturers provide specific procedures for managing engine power on departure.

A static takeoff begins with the aircraft stationary on the runway. After completing the required checks and receiving takeoff clearance, the flight crew applies an initial engine power setting and allows the engines to stabilize. Once the required conditions are met, the crew advances the thrust levers to the appropriate takeoff setting and begins the takeoff roll. The aircraft therefore starts accelerating after the engines have reached the prescribed stabilization point.

A rolling takeoff begins differently. Instead of holding the aircraft stationary while completing the initial power-setting sequence, the pilot allows it to start moving while applying an intermediate power setting. The engines are still given time to stabilize before the crew advances to takeoff thrust. The aircraft is already accelerating along the runway during this process, making the timing and coordination of thrust application particularly important.

The key distinction is when the aircraft begins moving in relation to the initial engine power setting. A rolling takeoff does not mean that pilots immediately select full takeoff thrust from idle, nor does a static takeoff necessarily mean that maximum thrust is applied while the aircraft is stationary. Both techniques involve controlled power management, and the exact sequence depends on the aircraft's approved operating procedures.

When an aircraft takes off, pilots must make some of the quickest reactionary decisions anyone can make. Only two seconds can make or break the flight

The choice between a static and rolling takeoff depends on several operating conditions. Aircraft type, engine characteristics, runway length, surface condition, wind direction, and aircraft weight can all influence the procedure. Pilots must follow the applicable aircraft flight manual, manufacturer guidance, and airline standard operating procedures rather than selecting a technique based on preference alone.

Wind is particularly important because crosswinds and tailwinds can affect the airflow entering an engine. Airbus explains that significant crosswind or tailwind conditions can disturb airflow around the engine inlet. Its guidance describes a progressive increase in thrust after the stabilization step to help the aircraft accelerate and reduce the effects of disturbed airflow. The procedure is aircraft-specific, but it demonstrates why environmental conditions can influence how thrust is applied.

Determines the approved thrust-setting procedure

Determines the available distance for acceleration

Influences acceleration and stopping performance

Influence engine performance and aircraft acceleration

Runway conditions and available distance also matter. A rolling takeoff requires sufficient runway for the aircraft to accelerate through the prescribed sequence and reach the required takeoff speeds. A static takeoff may provide a more controlled starting point for a particular aircraft or operating situation, but it does not automatically produce better runway performance. The crew must use approved performance calculations that account for weight, temperature, pressure altitude, wind, runway condition, and other relevant factors.

The second UltraFan 80 demonstrator is soon expected to run as Rolls-Royce develops a new generation of engines for widebody and narrowbody airliners.

Aircraft manufacturers emphasize that takeoff thrust must be managed according to the specific aircraft and engine combination. Airbus' Engine Thrust Management – Thrust Setting at Takeoff explains that engines must reach the required stabilization point before pilots advance to takeoff thrust. This procedure helps ensure that both engines respond appropriately and reduces the potential for asymmetric thrust during the early stages of the takeoff roll.

Airbus explains that engines on the same aircraft can have slightly different acceleration characteristics. Applying takeoff thrust directly from idle may cause one engine to accelerate faster than the other, creating asymmetric thrust that can make directional control more difficult at low speed. The manufacturer also clarifies that engine stabilization remains necessary during rolling takeoffs. The Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Airplane Flying Handbook similarly describes a rolling takeoff in which pilots begin moving the aircraft, apply an intermediate power setting, and allow the engines to stabilize before proceeding with takeoff.

These recommendations demonstrate that a rolling takeoff is not intended to bypass engine stabilization, nor is a static takeoff automatically the preferred procedure. Both techniques require pilots to monitor engine response and maintain directional control while following aircraft-specific guidance. The appropriate method depends on the aircraft's approved procedures and operating conditions.

In practice, the main difference is how the initial acceleration and engine stabilization stages are managed. During a static takeoff, the aircraft remains stationary while the engines reach the required stabilization setting. This allows the crew to establish the prescribed engine conditions before the aircraft begins accelerating. Once the takeoff roll starts, the crew monitors engine indications and maintains directional control as the aircraft gains speed.

During a rolling takeoff, the aircraft begins accelerating while the engines are being brought to the stabilization setting. This means pilots must manage the aircraft's movement and monitor engine response at the same time. The technique can be useful when permitted by the aircraft's procedures and when sufficient runway is available. However, it does not remove the need to monitor engine indications or maintain directional control throughout the takeoff roll.

Neither technique automatically shortens takeoff distance. A rolling takeoff may avoid a complete stop before acceleration, but the distance required to reach takeoff speed still depends on the aircraft's performance and the conditions on the day. Similarly, a static takeoff does not guarantee a shorter or safer departure simply because the engines are stabilized before movement begins. The relevant comparison must be based on approved performance data for the specific aircraft and operating conditions.

Neither a static nor a rolling takeoff eliminates the risk of asymmetric thrust. Although engines on the same aircraft are designed to operate together, their acceleration characteristics can differ. If thrust is increased too quickly from idle, one engine may respond faster than the other, creating a yawing moment that makes directional control more difficult at low speed. Engine stabilization is therefore an important part of either procedure.

Airbus documented an A320 event in which differences in the engines' initial operating speeds and subsequent acceleration rates contributed to a loss of directional control during a static takeoff. The aircraft veered off the runway at a relatively low groundspeed. Separately, a 2019 United Technologies patent, Takeoff Power Management System and Method for Gas Turbine Engines, describes a proposed system that could select between static and rolling takeoff procedures using operating information, including ground wind. Its rolling sequence uses intermediate power before applying full takeoff thrust at a predetermined groundspeed.

Differences in engine acceleration can affect directional control

Must be respected during both static and rolling takeoffs

Crosswinds and tailwinds can affect airflow around engine inlets

Requires directional control while the aircraft is already moving

The 2019 patent describes a proposed system, not confirmed widespread airline implementation

Pilots must follow the aircraft manufacturer's procedures and verify that the selected takeoff method is appropriate for the prevailing conditions. They should pay particular attention to engine indications, wind conditions, runway limitations, and any required stabilization settings. If an engine or directional-control problem develops, the crew must respond according to the aircraft's approved rejected-takeoff procedures.

There is no universal winner between a static and rolling takeoff. Each method has a place in aviation, and the more effective option depends on the aircraft's approved procedures, engine characteristics, runway conditions, weather, and performance requirements. A static takeoff allows the engines to reach the required stabilization setting before the aircraft moves, while a rolling takeoff starts acceleration earlier without removing the stabilization requirement.

The most important consideration is not whether the aircraft starts moving immediately or waits at the runway threshold. It is whether the crew follows the correct thrust-setting sequence and maintains control throughout the takeoff. Engine response, wind conditions, and available runway distance all influence how the departure should be managed. A technique that is appropriate for one aircraft or set of conditions may not be suitable for another.

Ultimately, both methods are designed to achieve the same objective: a controlled takeoff within the aircraft's performance limits. Manufacturer procedures and approved performance calculations determine which technique is appropriate. Rather than treating one as inherently faster, safer, or more efficient, pilots must use the method that best meets the aircraft's operating requirements on that particular departure.

#6084. Delta 360: Benefits & How To Earn This Invitation-Only Status

All of the “big three” carriers in the United States have invitation-only elite status. I’ve written about how American has Concierge Key and United has Global Services, and in this post, I’d like to take a look at Delta 360, which is Delta’s invitation-only elite status. I’d argue it’s the most mysterious, least talked about, and perhaps the rarest, of the three.

What is Delta 360 status, how do you earn it, what are the benefits, and how many members are there? I’ll share everything I know…

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite status. It’s my understanding that this is the most exclusive of the invitation-only elite tiers, in the sense that there are the fewest members. Despite that, the benefits are actually pretty weak, at least on paper. For that matter, Delta 360 isn’t even a formal elite tier, which is to say that you separately still have to qualify for status in the Delta SkyMiles Medallion program.

For what it’s worth, here’s how Delta describes Delta 360 status on its website:

Delta 360° is an annual, invitation-only membership for our most loyal SkyMiles Members. A Delta 360° Membership offers Delta’s most premium suite of benefits and services exclusive to our top SkyMiles Members. Entry into Delta 360° will be extended to a very small percentage of Diamond Medallion Members. Considerations include, but are not limited to: overall Delta flight activity, premium product purchases (Delta One, Delta Premium Select, Delta First) and spending on Delta SkyMiles American Express Cards.

As is the case with the invitation-only status of American and United, the requirements to earn Delta 360 status aren’t published. However, based on the data points I’ve seen, the criteria are even more confusing. With American and United, as a general rule, you need to spend well over $50,000 per year to have a shot at the status. In the case of Delta, you probably need to spend even more.

As Delta officially states, getting an invitation to Delta 360 is for the “most loyal SkyMiles members.” Generally speaking:

Some suggest that you’d have to spend $100,000 per year on Delta flights to be invited as a Delta 360 member at major hubs, while the number could be much lower if you’re not based at a hub.

Note that qualification for Delta 360 is annual (so it expires at the end of the elite year), and criteria could change year-to-year. So it’s possible you have the same activity in two years, and earn Delta 360 one year, but not the other. There’s also no way to ask for or request the status (at least not in a way that will achieve the intended result). Instead, you’ll be contacted if you’re eligible, and you’ll see your account updated to reflect that.

There’s one other way to earn Delta 360 status. As part of the SkyMiles lifetime elite status program, you can receive Delta 360 status for life if you rack up five million lifetime miles. This metric is based on the number of eligible miles flown on Delta.

Just for some context on all of this, Delta’s top published tier is Diamond Medallion, and that requires earning 28,000 Medallion Qualifying Dollars (MQDs) in a program year. That would require $28,000 in spending on Delta tickets, or $280,000 to $560,000 in spending on select co-branded Delta credit cards.

Interestingly, Delta 360 isn’t a separate tier in the SkyMiles program. That’s to say that Delta 360 members still have to earn status in the SkyMiles Medallion program. Most Delta 360 members are also Diamond Medallion members, but in theory it’s possible to earn Delta 360 without being a Diamond Medallion member.

This is different than American AAdvantage and United MileagePlus, where Concierge Key and Global Services are separate tiers, above the published top tier levels.

What are the benefits of Delta 360 status?

Those are all the Delta 360 benefits that I’m aware of. There’s no upgrade priority for Delta 360 members beyond their standard Diamond Medallion status, so Delta 360 doesn’t factor into upgrade priority. Furthermore, any confirmed upgrades would be earned through the standard Choice Benefits program, as this is how you can earn Global Upgrade Certificates (GUCs) and Regional Upgrade Certificates (RUCs).

So the benefits of Delta 360 are weak, though I’d imagine that the “soft” treatment is very good — Delta has great service to begin with, and I imagine it’s even better for Delta’s best customers.

I also think it’s noteworthy how Delta is much quieter about this status than American and United. There’s just not as much public acknowledgement of invitation only status at Delta as at American and United (and that might be by design).

This is a real mystery, and all I can do is speculate. For context, I’ve speculated that there are 10,000-20,000 American Concierge Key members, and I’ve speculated that there are 15,000-25,000 United Global Services members.

This is purely a guess on my part, but I think the number of Delta 360 members is probably in the 5,000-10,000 range. That’s simply because the status seems to be more difficult to earn. Like I said, this is purely a guess on my part, and I could be wrong. If anyone has any data or info, I’d love to hear it.

It’s hard to say whether something like Delta 360 is “worth it.” For one, the qualification requirements aren’t even published, so how can one say whether it’s worth it when you don’t know what it will take? Second, I’d say the value of something like Delta 360 varies greatly based on the type of traveler you are.

If you’re a domestic road warrior doing 200 segments per year, you might actually get significant upside from the improved assistance during irregular operations, the Delta One Lounge access, etc. Meanwhile if you take a handful of international long haul business class trips per year, the upside will likely be very minimal, above and beyond what you’d otherwise get.

So I absolutely don’t think it’s worth going out of your way to try to earn something that doesn’t even have published qualification requirements. But if you earn it anyway, of course, it’s a nice thing to have!

The “big three” US carriers all have their own invitation-only elite status, with other programs including American Concierge Key and United Global Services. So how do they all compare?

The reality is that all three tiers are primarily about better improved “soft” treatment, including during irregular operations. On paper, I’d say Delta 360 probably offers the fewest official perks of the three tiers. The one exception is that Delta One Lounge access is an absolutely awesome benefit, given the quality of lounges (though the lack of free guests limits the usefulness for those not usually traveling alone).

Here are a couple of thoughts on the comparable status tiers at American and United:

Delta 360 is Delta Air Lines’ invitation-only elite tier. It’s the US airline status that’s probably hardest to earn. Historically the benefits have been weaker than comparable status with American and United, though with access to Delta One Lounges, that’s perhaps no longer the case. Delta 360 offers dedicated customer support, a Sky Club membership, Delta One Lounge access, good odds of tarmac transfers, and more.

To earn Delta 360, be prepared to spend a lot on Delta flights, especially if you’re based out of a Delta hub.

Are any OMAAT readers Delta 360 members? If so, what has your experience been like?

Flight cancellations are on the rise in 2026. Since Jan. 1, U.S. carriers have canceled roughly 2% of all flights, according to FlightAware, putting this year on pace for the highest cancellation rate since 2022. And delays remain common: About one in four departures nationwide was delayed between Memorial Day and Labor Day, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

While most flights leave on time, delays and cancellations remain a reality of air travel — whether due to bad weather, mechanical issues, scheduling problems or other unforeseen circumstances, including the recent nationwide ground stop.

In case you experience flight delays or cancellations, here are tips on how to decrease your chances of getting stuck and increase your odds of arriving at your destination as quickly as possible. Plus, check out our advice on how to potentially get reimbursed for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation, depending on the reason that caused the delay.

In this era of full flights and easily available information, don’t wait for the airline to tell you there is a problem. You can keep an eye on general flight trends across the country by using FlightAware, which gives you a good overview of how a day in the sky looks.

FlightAware’s “MiseryMap” focuses on delays. In the 24 hours before travel, you can manually check the status of your flight on your airline’s website. If possible, be sure to check the plane's origin. Even if the conditions are clear where you are, there’s a good chance your plane won’t get to you on time if it’s sitting in a snowstorm somewhere else.

It’s also a good idea to sign up for flight notifications from your airline. Here are details on how to opt in to that process with American Airlines and United Airlines.

You can also get flight status updates sent directly from FlightAware. TPG staffers are also fond of the Flighty app, which offers a reliable "Where's My Plane?" feature to track your plane starting 25 hours before your flight.

Be sure to download your airline’s app on your phone, too. Many airlines will show you where your incoming plane is currently. In fact, your airline’s app often has more up-to-date flight departure information than what’s on the departure and arrival boards at the airport.

This can be a tricky one. If your flight is still listed as “on time” in the app, leave for the airport according to the original schedule.

Even if your flight shows as delayed in the app, that status is subject to change. So, in most cases, it’s best to be at the airport ready to go at the originally scheduled time. We’ve certainly heard stories of flights being delayed only to depart sooner than expected, leaving some passengers behind.

Sometimes, you’ll receive confirmation well in advance, letting you know if your flight will be significantly delayed. Say you are at an airport that isn’t a hub for the airline you are flying (meaning there's less chance of spare planes and crew), and the plane that's supposed to operate your flight is nowhere close to arriving at the airport. In that case, it's likely that your posted delay will be a real delay. However, it’s still safer to be at the airport, just in case.

Bad weather can sometimes cause a temporary ground stop at the airport. As soon as the weather improves and the stop lifts, airlines will try to get their flights off the ground ASAP. So, it’s best to be close by should things change on short notice.

Related: 3 things to do if your flight is delayed

It’s important to know your rights as an airline passenger, which have been changed in recent years.

For instance, if your flight is canceled or significantly delayed and you choose not to travel, you’re entitled to a refund, no matter the reason for the disruption. According to current rules from the U.S. Department of Transportation, passengers on domestic flights that are significantly changed, including arriving three or more hours late, and international flights arriving six or more hours late are entitled to automatic refunds if they choose not to travel and don't accept alternative transportation or travel credits. Those refunds must be issued within seven days for credit card purchases and 20 days for cash payments.

However, if you get stranded overnight, you may also be able to recoup costs for extra meals, hotel nights and ground transportation, depending on the reason for the delay. A widespread FAA ground stop, for example, is unlikely to be a covered reason.

You’ll find these and other passenger rights guarantees on flightrights.gov, the DOT’s dashboard.

On that website, you’ll find a rundown of what airlines guarantee in the event of “controllable” delays and cancellations — disruptions within an airline’s control. Keep in mind that these controllable situations typically exclude weather-related problems.

When looking at the dashboard, you’ll quickly see that some airlines promise to do more than others regarding overnight hotel stays, ground transportation, credit vouchers and rebooking on partners. Give that list a look not only when you’re deciding which airline to book with but also in the event of a long, controllable delay or cancellation. This way, you’ll know what the airline has promised to do in those situations. You can file a complaint with the DOT if the airline doesn’t hold up its end of the bargain.

Monitor weather patterns a few days before your flight to see if any major systems are anticipated. It’s vital to check the forecast the night before and on the day of travel to see how any issues could affect your departure and arrival airports.

Again, be sure to opt in to receive updates on your flight’s status. If you know bad weather is coming later in the day, ask for an earlier flight if you can. Alternatively, leaving the night before the weather arrives is a good idea if you want to minimize the risk of delays.

Many airlines will issue travel advisories during (and ahead of) severe weather, such as blizzards, ice storms or even heavy thunderstorms. These advisories allow travelers to make changes even when flying on a restrictive ticket that typically can’t be altered — like some basic economy fares. In some cases, the airline may even proactively change your flight.

If you know bad weather is on the horizon, visit your airline’s website and look for an advisory notice or call the airline to discuss options. If an airline gets ahead of weather issues, you may be able to reschedule your flight by a few days in either direction with no fees. Additionally, you can try asking for a nonstop flight if the weather jeopardizes your connecting flight.

However, if the airline hasn’t issued its own advisory, you might need to pay out of pocket for any fare differences if you really want to be proactive in changing plans.

Standing in a long line at the airport or waiting on hold by phone is usually no longer the most efficient (or most enjoyable) way to rebook when a flight is canceled or delayed.

Most major airlines will allow you to rebook yourself using a mobile app. You may be able to rebook for a new time or even to a new nearby origin or destination city. For that reason, the airline app should probably be your first stop when you learn of a hiccup in your travel plans.

United will even let you standby for up to three flights if something happens to your originally scheduled flight, while maintaining your original seat.

That said, there are times when automated rebooking systems are not your best option. Sometimes, the only automated option is a red-eye flight or a flight several days later that will head to your destination. That’s especially true when many flights are full.

If you can’t locate what you need on the app, find an airline employee who can work the ticketing desk. Check their uniforms and name tags to ensure you get a ticket agent, versus a baggage handler or a similarly outsourced contractor who is less likely to be able to help.

If the U.S. call center has long hold times (which can happen during widespread issues), you can try dialing an international number for faster service. You can often find those numbers on the airline’s website. You might also find success reaching out to an airline on the social platform X or other social media channels when customer service lines are busy.

For example, when the first leg of an American Airlines flight from New York to Arkansas, scheduled just before Christmas, was delayed, TPG Managing Editor Madison Blancaflor missed her connection. She contacted American Airlines on X to help ensure she was rebooked on the earliest possible flight. She still had to endure a long layover in Charlotte, but it was better (and less stressful) than rushing to the customer service desk to try to rebook upon arrival.

Additionally, some airlines offer live online chat or text options that can be quicker than calling.

If there are no reasonable booking options left with your carrier, ask whether there are options available on another airline. If the delay is weather-related and you are on a basic economy ticket or are flying on a low-cost carrier, there might not be other airline options at your fingertips. Still, it’s worth asking — and, if possible, presenting options you have researched yourself.

Related: Don’t wait on hold: Here’s how to reach airline customer service quickly

If you have airline lounge access at a United Club, a Delta Sky Club or something similar, you can head there for help from experienced agents with potentially shorter lines. Use it as a spot to gather your thoughts, charge your phone and make level-headed decisions. The agents there might be able to help you change or track your flight, as there are usually agents with that knowledge and ability in the airline lounges.

In third-party lounges, such as an American Express Centurion Lounge, you won’t be able to get that type of airline-specific assistance, but you’ll probably be in a better spot to wait out the storm than in a crowded terminal.

Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access

Sometimes, if you really need to get home, you may need to do the work and pay for a new flight yourself.

In some of our prior experiences, the airlines we originally booked with couldn't get us home within 24 hours of our flights being canceled. In cases like these, you may be able to book a nonstop flight with at least one last seat available on another carrier.

Keep in mind, though, that rebooking yourself is typically not covered by any insurance provider or carrier. Still, you should be able to get a refund for your original ticket, which will at least offset some of the pain of a new one. The extra work may be worth it to control your own destiny and avoid being stuck as options narrow.

Your credit card’s built-in trip delay or trip cancellation coverage can help with many unexpected expenses in the face of delays and cancellations, but a brand-new flight home isn’t likely to be one of them. Still, in some cases, it may be the only way home for a while, so you’ll have to weigh the pros and cons.

Fortunately, many airlines now allow you to cancel main cabin tickets and, at the very least, get airline trip credit; you can use this credit to book a future flight — even if you are being proactive to try and avoid possible delays and, ultimately, your originally scheduled flight does not experience a delay. (This does not necessarily apply to basic economy fares or low-cost carriers' flights.)

Related: Should you get travel insurance if you have credit card protection?

While thinking through what to do in case of a flight delay or cancellation, consider your options at airport hotels; they can fill up during major delays and cancellations. Sometimes, it is best to call it a day, get some rest and try again in the morning.

Airport hotels are generally pretty affordable on points, but cash rates can skyrocket when demand surges. Accommodations are typically covered by trip delay protection in the event of cancellations or very long delays via cards like the (see rates and fees) and .*

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Why my favorite use of Hyatt points is a Category 1 airport hotel

If you know in advance that your flight will be canceled or delayed, heading to the airport early could score you a same-day standby flight that gets you to your destination on time.

For example, one TPG staffer used this strategy to avoid getting stuck overnight when a hiccup with his flight from Austin to New York would have caused him to miss a connection in Dallas. He arrived at the airport a bit early and was placed on the standby list for an earlier flight connecting to a different city.

Getting on the standby list isn’t foolproof, especially if the earlier flight is almost full. This is a case where having elite status can help since you’ll have priority over non-elite travelers. Additionally, some airlines charge non-elite travelers a fee to be added to the standby list for an earlier flight.

Related: The best credit cards to reach elite status

The hard truth is that in the event of airline delays and cancellations caused by weather, the airline itself is not going to help you out with the extra expenses you incur due to the change in plans, since the weather is outside its control. Travel insurance may have your back if you purchased it, but beyond that, the credit card you booked your flight with may also be able to reimburse you for unexpected expenses due to your flight delay or cancellation — even if it was caused by weather.

Many rewards credit cards confer valuable travel protections when you have a delayed or canceled flight (if you used one of them to book your flight). Below are just a few examples of cards that provide some built-in coverage:

*Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

Related: Best credit cards with travel insurance

To highlight how valuable this can be, a couple of years ago, one TPG staffer's flights home from Colorado during the busy winter holiday season were canceled due to a snowstorm.

She was faced with an unexpected $1,100-per-night hotel stay during peak season in a pricey ski town, based on what was still available at the last minute. Ultimately, her eligible Chase card covered not only the $1,100 unexpected hotel stay but also the unexpected car service and meals during the delay. Within 26 days of the unexpected cancellation and delay, she had a check for $1,401.74 in her hand, thanks to using the right credit card to book the flight.

Unfortunately, some situations are not covered by the built-in trip delay and trip cancellation protections that commonly come with some rewards credit cards, but it never hurts to save receipts and try.

Last but not least, we recommend being decisive when making travel decisions amid delays or cancellations.

The longer you wait to switch flights or book a hotel, the greater the chances you’ll be at the mercy of whatever dwindling options are left as hundreds (or thousands) of other passengers rebook their plans.

Most of the time, your flight will get you where you need to be, close to when you want to be there. Still, flight delays and cancellations are a reality of air travel. If your flight is delayed by an hour or two, there’s not usually much to do other than be patient. However, when facing a long delay or cancellation, it’s good to have a plan to reduce the odds of getting stuck.

Given the common theme of full flights these days, acting quickly, researching options and making a speedy decision will put you ahead of the pack.

#6082. FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop

Flights were grounded across the U.S. Friday afternoon over suspected air traffic control communications issues.

The FAA issued a highly unusual mass ground stop shortly after 3 p.m.

“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety, attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped,” the agency said in an advisory. “All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis.”

In a separate statement, the FAA said a communications issue affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers is to blame. Agency technicians are now investigating the issue.

According to ABC News, this is only the second time since the 9/11 attacks that departures across the country have been stopped. Flights currently in the air are believed to still be in contact with ATC.

National media outlets showed footage of commercial airplanes queued up but not moving at numerous major airports, including Los Angeles, Boston, Reagan National, New York-LaGuardia, Houston Bush, Dallas/Fort Worth, and Raleigh–Durham.

The ground stop will almost certainly cause a cascade of cancellations and delays lasting into the weekend.

The first Cabinet-level official to comment in person on the incident was Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who spoke to reporters outside the White House. Mullin said there is no indication that the outage is a cyberattack, or connected to the recent Microsoft outage.

The situation is close to “unprecedented,” the secretary added, but there is no threat to public safety or reason to panic. Mullin said it is still too early to say when the problem will be resolved.

It was not immediately clear if the outage is connected to ongoing upgrades on ATC systems and infrastructure. The FAA has been moving rapidly to replace outdated equipment, such as old radios and floppy disks, and install more automated technology. The agency is also ripping out old copper wiring and replacing it with fiber optic cables.
